topic: AA Amyloidosis secondary to chronic arthritis

page.mentor_intro: AA amyloidosis is a complication of sustained inflammation, so control of the underlying disease is the treatment. Autoinflammatory syndromes (FMF, CAPS, TRAPS), uncontrolled adult-onset Still's disease and injecting-related soft-tissue infection are recognised causes.

teaching_points.claim: In familial Mediterranean fever, IL-1 inhibitors are effective and relatively safe for colchicine non-responders, and tocilizumab might be of interest in selected patients with established AA amyloidosis resistant to colchicine and IL-1 inhibitors.

A systematic review of causes listed 48 disease associations as strong, 19 weak, 23 unclear and 60 unlikely, and proposed a pragmatic diagnostic approach for AA amyloidosis without an obvious underlying disease.

In cryopyrin-associated periodic syndrome, AA amyloidosis occurred in nearly all subtypes; deaths were in patients who never received IL-1 inhibitors, and 89% of those treated had a greater than 50% fall in proteinuria.
TRAPS is revealed by AA amyloidosis in most cases, so clinical features of TRAPS should be screened for in AA patients, and IL-1 antagonists can preserve renal function.

AA amyloidosis is a rare, severe complication of uncontrolled active adult-onset Still's disease that could be prevented by early diagnosis and better disease control, including more frequent use of biologic therapy.
There is strong evidence linking skin and soft-tissue infections to AA amyloidosis among people who inject drugs.

page.standard_overview: AA (secondary/reactive) amyloidosis results from sustained overproduction of serum amyloid A (SAA) protein by hepatocytes during chronic systemic inflammation (rheumatoid arthritis, ankylosing spondylitis, adult-onset Still's disease, or chronic infection). Insoluble amyloid fibrils deposit in tissues, predominantly causing nephrotic-range proteinuria, progressive renal failure, and hepatosplenomegaly, while cardiac involvement is rare compared to AL or ATTR amyloidosis. Diagnosis requires Congo red staining of tissue biopsies (abdominal fat pad, rectum, or kidney) showing apple-green birefringence under polarized light and positive anti-SAA immunohistochemistry. Management centers aggressively on suppressing underlying chronic inflammation (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6 [tocilizumab], or colchicine in FMF) to lower SAA below 10 mg/L, which arrests amyloid deposition and permits regression of proteinuria.

standard_knowledge.claim: AA amyloidosis is driven by chronic elevation of acute-phase reactant serum amyloid A (SAA); sustained suppression of SAA to < 10 mg/L halts renal progression and improves survival.
Renal involvement is the primary clinical manifestation (> 90% of cases), presenting initially as asymptomatic albuminuria progressing to nephrotic syndrome and end-stage kidney disease.
Biopsy confirmation using Congo red stain demonstrates characteristic apple-green birefringence under cross-polarized light, with immunohistochemistry differentiating AA from AL and ATTR amyloidosis.

Targeted biologic therapies suppressing chronic inflammation (IL-6 receptor antagonist tocilizumab or TNF inhibitors in inflammatory arthritis) produce dramatic biochemical and renal remissions in AA amyloidosis.

page.standard_overview: Abatacept is a soluble recombinant fusion protein consisting of the extracellular domain of human CTLA-4 linked to the modified Fc portion of human IgG1 (CTLA-4-Ig). It selectively modulates T-cell co-stimulation by binding to CD80 and CD86 on antigen-presenting cells, thereby blocking CD28 interaction on T cells and inhibiting T-cell activation. In the landmark AMPLE trial (first head-to-head biologic comparison in RA), subcutaneous abatacept demonstrated non-inferior clinical efficacy to adalimumab with comparable radiographic inhibition, but with fewer injection-site reactions and fewer serious infections. Abatacept exhibits superior clinical responsiveness in seropositive (anti-CCP and RF positive) patients and carries an exceptionally low risk of tuberculosis reactivation or opportunistic infections compared to TNF inhibitors.

standard_knowledge.claim: The landmark head-to-head AMPLE trial proved subcutaneous abatacept is non-inferior to adalimumab in achieving ACR20 response (64.8% vs 63.4%) and inhibiting radiographic progression at 2 years.
Abatacept selectively binds CD80/CD86 on antigen-presenting cells to prevent CD28 co-stimulation, uniquely dampening adaptive T-cell priming without broad systemic lymphopenia.
Clinical efficacy is significantly higher in seropositive patients (high-titer anti-CCP and RF), reflecting targeted suppression of autoantibody-generating T-cell help.

ACR guidelines recommend abatacept as an optimal first-line biologic choice in RA patients with a history of serious infections, recurrent cellulitis, or latent TB due to its favorable infectious safety profile.

page.standard_overview: Abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA) is defined as an infrarenal aortic diameter >= 3.0 cm (or > 50% increase over normal). Rupture carries > 80% overall mortality. SVS and ESVS guidelines establish ultrasound surveillance intervals based on diameter: 3.0-3.9 cm (every 3 years), 4.0-4.9 cm (annually), and 5.0-5.4 cm (every 3-6 months). Elective repair is indicated at diameter >= 5.5 cm in men, >= 5.0 cm in women, or with rapid expansion (> 1.0 cm/year or > 0.5 cm in 6 months), or symptomatic aneurysms. Landmark trials (EVAR-1, DREAM, OVER) proved that Endovascular Aneurysm Repair (EVAR) significantly reduces 30-day perioperative mortality compared to open surgical repair (1.2-1.7% vs 4.7-5.0%), but this early survival benefit converges by 2-3 years, with EVAR carrying higher lifetime re-intervention rates for endoleaks (especially Type I and III) requiring lifelong CT/ultrasound surveillance.

standard_knowledge.claim: Elective threshold for repair is >= 5.5 cm in men and >= 5.0 cm in women, or rapid growth > 1.0 cm/year or > 0.5 cm in 6 months (SVS/ESVS guidelines).
Landmark trials (EVAR-1, DREAM) demonstrated a 3-fold lower 30-day operative mortality with EVAR compared to open surgical repair (1.7% vs 4.7%).

Long-term trial follow-up out to 10-15 years shows convergence of all-cause mortality between EVAR and open repair, with EVAR having significantly higher rates of secondary rupture and re-intervention for endoleaks.

Classification of endoleaks: Type I (attachment cuff leak; requires urgent repair), Type II (collateral lumbar/IMA back-bleeding; observe unless sac expands), Type III (graft fabric/modular disconnection; requires urgent repair).

page.standard_overview: Abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS) is defined by the WSACS consensus as a sustained intra-abdominal pressure (IAP) > 20 mmHg (with or without an abdominal perfusion pressure [APP = MAP - IAP] < 60 mmHg) associated with new or worsening single- or multiple-organ dysfunction. Intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH) is defined as sustained IAP >= 12 mmHg. Measurement of bladder pressure via an indwelling Foley catheter at end-expiration in the supine position is the gold standard diagnostic method. High IAP compresses the IVC (lowering venous return and cardiac output), impedes renal vein and parenchymal perfusion (oliguria and acute tubular necrosis), and elevates hemidiaphragms (peak airway pressures rise, producing hypercapnia and hypoxemia). Medical therapy encompasses nasogastric/colonic decompression, paracentesis of ascites, neuromuscular blockade, and judicious fluid management; refractory ACS is a surgical emergency mandating decompressive laparotomy with temporary open abdominal closure.

standard_knowledge.claim: WSACS consensus defines ACS as sustained IAP > 20 mmHg associated with new-onset organ failure; IAH is defined as sustained IAP >= 12 mmHg.
Transvesical bladder pressure measurement at end-expiration instilling 20-25 mL sterile saline with transducer zeroed at mid-axillary line is the clinical gold standard.

ACS pathophysiology produces a triad of cardiovascular collapse (decreased preload, elevated SVR), respiratory compromise (high peak airway pressures), and oliguric renal failure resistant to fluid challenges.
Emergency surgical decompressive laparotomy is the definitive life-saving intervention for refractory ACS (IAP > 20 mmHg with worsening organ dysfunction failing medical decompression).

page.standard_overview: Abnormal uterine bleeding (AUB) in non-pregnant reproductive-age women is classified according to the FIGO PALM-COEIN system into structural causes (Polyp, Adenomyosis, Leiomyoma, Malignancy/hyperplasia) and non-structural causes (Coagulopathy, Ovulatory dysfunction, Endometrial, Iatrogenic, Not otherwise classified). Initial workup requires pelvic transvaginal ultrasound, complete blood count, and endometrial biopsy in women aged >= 45 years (or < 45 with risk factors: obesity, nulliparity, chronic anovulation/PCOS, tamoxifen, Lynch syndrome). First-line medical therapy for ovulatory or non-structural AUB is the 52 mg levonorgestrel intrauterine system (LNG-IUS; Mirena), which reduces menstrual blood loss by > 70-90%, followed by oral tranexamic acid, combined oral contraceptives, or cyclical oral progestins. Endometrial ablation, uterine artery embolization (UAE), or hysterectomy are second-line surgical alternatives.

standard_knowledge.claim: The FIGO PALM-COEIN classification categorizes AUB etiologies into structural (PALM: polyp, adenomyosis, leiomyoma, malignancy) and non-structural (COEIN: coagulopathy, ovulatory, endometrial, iatrogenic, not classified).

ACOG guidelines mandate endometrial tissue sampling to rule out hyperplasia/cancer in any woman aged >= 45 with AUB, or < 45 with chronic unopposed estrogen (PCOS, obesity) or failed medical management.

The 52 mg levonorgestrel-releasing intrauterine system (LNG-IUS) is the most effective medical therapy, reducing menstrual blood loss by > 70-90% and outperforming oral agents in quality-of-life improvements.

Acute severe AUB in hemodynamically stable patients is managed medically with high-dose oral tranexamic acid (1.3 g TID), oral progestins (medroxyprogesterone acetate 20 mg TID), or combined oral contraceptives.

page.standard_overview: Childhood Absence Epilepsy (CAE) and Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (JME) are idiopathic generalized epilepsies (IGEs) characterized by bilateral, synchronous 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges on EEG (CAE) or rapid 4-6 Hz polyspike-and-wave discharges (JME). Ethosuximide is the drug of first choice for pure absence seizures: the landmark NIH randomized controlled trial proved ethosuximide and valproic acid have superior seizure freedom rates (~53-58%) compared to lamotrigine (29%), with ethosuximide causing significantly fewer attentional/cognitive side effects. JME presents around puberty with morning myoclonic jerks (especially after sleep deprivation or alcohol), generalized tonic-clonic seizures, and occasional absence seizures; valproic acid is the most effective drug for JME across all seizure types, but lamotrigine or levetiracetam are preferred first-line alternatives in women of childbearing potential due to valproate teratogenicity. Sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, phenytoin) exacerbate absence and myoclonic seizures.

standard_knowledge.claim: The landmark NIH double-blind trial demonstrated that ethosuximide and valproate achieve superior 16-week seizure freedom in absence epilepsy compared to lamotrigine, with ethosuximide having the best cognitive/attentional profile.

In Juvenile Myoclonic Epilepsy (JME), broad-spectrum agents (valproate, levetiracetam, lamotrigine) control multiple seizure types; valproate is the most potent but restricted in females of reproductive age due to teratogenicity and neurodevelopmental harms.

Narrow-spectrum sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin, vigabatrin) are strictly contraindicated in absence epilepsy and JME as they worsen absence seizures and precipitate status myoclonicus.

EEG hallmarks: pure absence shows generalized, symmetric 3-Hz spike-and-wave discharges provoked by hyperventilation; JME exhibits 4-6 Hz polyspike-and-wave discharges triggered by photic stimulation and sleep deprivation.

page.standard_overview: Acute acalculous cholecystitis (AAC) is an acute necroinflammatory gallbladder disease occurring without cholelithiasis, accounting for ~5-10% of acute cholecystitis cases but carrying 30-50% mortality. It typically arises in critically ill ICU patients, severe trauma, extensive burns, sepsis, major surgery, or prolonged total parenteral nutrition (TPN). Pathophysiology combines bile stasis, gallbladder ischemia (endothelial injury, hypoperfusion, splanchnic vasoconstriction), and endotoxin-mediated mucosal necrosis, predisposing to rapid gangrene and perforation. Ultrasound and CT criteria include gallbladder wall thickening (> 3 mm), pericholecystic fluid, intramural gas, and subserosal halo sign without gallstones. Initial management requires broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and prompt gallbladder decompression: percutaneous cholecystostomy (PC) is the preferred minimally invasive intervention in critically ill unstable patients, reserving laparoscopic or open cholecystectomy for stable candidates or those with gallbladder perforation/gangrene.

standard_knowledge.claim: AAC occurs in critically ill, burned, trauma, or post-cardiac surgery patients through a combination of bile stasis (TPN, fasting) and microvascular ischemia.
Ultrasound and contrast CT diagnostic criteria include gallbladder wall thickening >= 3.5-4 mm, pericholecystic fluid, gallbladder distension, and mucosal sloughing in the absence of gallstones.

Tokyo Guidelines (TG18) recommend ultrasound-guided percutaneous transhepatic cholecystostomy (PTC) as the definitive or stabilizing procedure of choice in critically ill patients unfit for emergent surgery.

Antibiotic therapy must cover enteric Gram-negative bacilli, Enterococcus, and anaerobes (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam or meropenem); cholecystostomy catheters are typically maintained for 4-6 weeks until mature tract formation before removal.

page.standard_overview: Systemic autoimmune and chronic inflammatory diseases (Rheumatoid Arthritis, Systemic Lupus Erythematosus, Psoriatic Arthritis, Ankylosing Spondylitis) confer a 2- to 3-fold higher risk of premature atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), rivaling diabetes mellitus as an independent cardiovascular risk equivalent. Chronic circulating pro-inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1beta, IL-6, interferon-alpha) trigger endothelial dysfunction, vascular smooth muscle proliferation, macrophage foam-cell activation, oxidation of LDL, and destabilization of coronary fibrous caps. EULAR guidelines mandate a 1.5x multiplication factor applied to conventional cardiovascular risk scores (e.g. SCORE2, Framingham) in patients with RA who have disease duration >= 10 years, seropositivity (RF or anti-CCP), or extra-articular manifestations. Aggressive control of disease activity using bDMARDs/csDMARDs significantly attenuates vascular risk, complemented by statin therapy, blood pressure optimization, and smoking cessation.

standard_knowledge.claim: EULAR recommendations mandate multiplying calculated cardiovascular risk scores by 1.5 in rheumatoid arthritis patients with high disease activity, seropositivity, or extra-articular manifestations.

Chronic systemic inflammation drives endothelial injury, increases circulating adhesion molecules (ICAM-1, VCAM-1), promotes dense necrotic core lipid plaques, and doubles premature myocardial infarction rates.
Aggressive disease suppression with methotrexate and biologic DMARDs (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6) reduces vascular inflammation and decreases incident cardiovascular events by 20-30%.
Statin therapy provides lipid-lowering and pleiotropic anti-inflammatory vascular plaque stabilization, safe in combination with DMARDs under transaminase monitoring.

page.standard_overview: Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) inhibitors - ACE inhibitors and Angiotensin Receptor Blockers (ARBs) - are foundational therapies for hypertension, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), post-myocardial infarction, and proteinuric chronic kidney disease (diabetic and non-diabetic). By blocking angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar vasoconstriction, they decrease intraglomerular hydrostatic pressure, which provides long-term nephron protection and slows GFR decline, but causes an acute, predictable, hemodynamic decline in eGFR. KDIGO and AHA/ACC guidelines establish that an acute serum creatinine increase up to 30% within 2-4 weeks of initiation is expected and does NOT warrant drug discontinuation. Routine monitoring of serum creatinine and potassium is required 1-2 weeks post-initiation. True hyperkalemia (> 5.5 mmol/L) is managed with dietary potassium restriction, dose reduction of concomitant potassium-sparing medications, adding loop or thiazide diuretics, or introducing modern potassium binders (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) to maintain RAAS inhibitor organ protection.

standard_knowledge.claim: KDIGO and ACC/AHA guidelines establish that an acute serum creatinine elevation <= 30% from baseline upon RAAS inhibitor initiation reflects benign intraglomerular hemodynamics and should NOT prompt discontinuation.
Serum creatinine and potassium should be measured 1-2 weeks following initiation or dose escalation of ACE inhibitors or ARBs.

Routine combination therapy of an ACE inhibitor with an ARB or direct renin inhibitor is strictly contraindicated due to elevated risks of hyperkalemia, syncope, and acute kidney injury without cardiovascular benefit (ONTARGET and ALTITUDE trials).

Modern gastrointestinal potassium binders (patiromer, sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) enable continuation and optimization of guideline-directed RAAS inhibitors in heart failure and CKD patients with recurrent hyperkalemia.

page.standard_overview: Achalasia is a primary esophageal motility disorder characterized by incomplete lower esophageal sphincter (LES) relaxation and absent esophageal peristalsis due to autoimmune loss of inhibitory nitric oxide/VIP-producing ganglion cells in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus. Diagnosis is confirmed by High-Resolution Manometry (HRM) according to the Chicago Classification v4.0, defining three subtypes based on panesophageal pressurization: Type I (classic, no pressurization), Type II (panesophageal pressurization; highest therapeutic success > 90%), and Type III (spastic, premature contractions). Definitive treatment aims to mechanically disrupt the LES and encompasses Per-Oral Endoscopic Myotomy (POEM), Laparoscopic Heller Myotomy with partial fundoplication (LHM), and Graded Pneumatic Dilation (PD; serial 30, 35, 40 mm balloons). POEM provides superior dysphagia relief for Type III spastic achalasia and comparable long-term success to LHM for Types I and II, but carries higher rates of post-procedure gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) requiring daily proton pump inhibitor therapy.

standard_knowledge.claim: High-Resolution Manometry (Chicago Classification) is the gold standard diagnostic tool, classifying achalasia into Type I (classic), Type II (panesophageal pressurization), and Type III (spastic).
POEM achieves excellent dysphagia relief (> 90%) across all subtypes and is the treatment of choice for Type III (spastic) achalasia due to the ability to perform a long proximal esophageal myotomy.
Laparoscopic Heller Myotomy combined with partial fundoplication (Dor or Toupet) provides durable 5-10 year clinical success with lower rates of post-procedure reflux compared to POEM.

Pneumatic dilation with graded balloon sizes (30, 35, 40 mm) achieves success comparable to myotomy in older adults with Type II achalasia, but carries a 1-3% perforation risk requiring emergency surgical backup.

page.standard_overview: Advanced Cardiovascular Life Support (ACLS) guidelines from the AHA and ERC structure adult cardiac arrest resuscitation around rapid rhythm identification, high-quality cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), and prompt defibrillation for shockable rhythms. Shockable rhythms (Ventricular Fibrillation [VF] and Pulseless Ventricular Tachycardia [pVT]) mandate immediate unsynchronized defibrillation (120-200 J biphasic), resumption of CPR for 2 minutes, and IV/IO epinephrine 1 mg administered after the second shock, alternating with amiodarone (300 mg first dose, 150 mg second dose) or lidocaine (1-1.5 mg/kg first dose, 0.5-0.75 mg/kg second dose) after the third shock (ALPS trial). Non-shockable rhythms (Asystole and Pulseless Electrical Activity [PEA]) require immediate epinephrine 1 mg as early as possible and urgent investigation of reversible etiologies using the 'H's and T's' framework (Hypovolemia, Hypoxia, Hydrogen ion acidosis, Hypo/hyperkalemia, Hypothermia, Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis PE/coronary).

standard_knowledge.claim: AHA/ERC guidelines mandate high-quality CPR: chest compression rate 100-120/min, depth 5-6 cm (2-2.4 inches), complete chest recoil, and minimizing interruptions (chest compression fraction > 60-80%).

In shockable rhythms (VF/pVT), amiodarone (300 mg initial, 150 mg second dose) and lidocaine (1-1.5 mg/kg initial) achieve equivalent survival-to-hospital-discharge rates in refractory cardiac arrest (ALPS trial).
In non-shockable rhythms (asystole/PEA), early administration of epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO within 5 minutes of arrest significantly increases return of spontaneous circulation (ROSC) and survival.

Targeted Temperature Management (TTM) in comatose post-cardiac arrest patients targeting strict normothermia (36-37.5 C) to actively prevent fever is non-inferior to 33 C hypothermia in survival and functional recovery (TTM-2 trial).

page.standard_overview: Acromegaly is a chronic systemic endocrine disease caused by excessive growth hormone (GH) secretion, in > 98% from a benign pituitary somatotroph adenoma. Elevated serum Insulin-like Growth Factor 1 (IGF-1) is the screening test of choice. Confirmation requires an Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT; 75 g oral glucose), where failure to suppress nadir GH < 1.0 ug/L (or < 0.4 ug/L with ultrasensitive assays) confirms autonomous GH hypersecretion. Transsphenoidal pituitary adenomectomy is the first-line definitive therapy, achieving biochemical cure in > 70-85% of microadenomas and 40-50% of macroadenomas. For persistent or recurrent disease, first-line medical therapy is first-generation long-acting Somatostatin Receptor Ligands (SRLs: octreotide LAR, lanreotide autogel; targeting SSTR2). Second-line therapies for SRL-resistant disease include the growth hormone receptor antagonist pegvisomant (normalizes IGF-1 in > 90% without lowering GH), pasireotide LAR (multi-receptor SRL targeting SSTR5; carries high hyperglycemia risk), or cabergoline (dopamine agonist for modest IGF-1 elevation).

standard_knowledge.claim: Endocrine Society guidelines establish serum IGF-1 as the initial diagnostic test of choice; confirmation requires lack of GH suppression (< 1.0 ug/L or < 0.4 ug/L) during a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test.
Transsphenoidal surgery is the primary definitive treatment of choice, performed by an expert neurosurgeon to achieve rapid decompression of visual pathways and biochemical cure.
First-generation somatostatin receptor ligands (octreotide LAR, lanreotide) normalize IGF-1 and control tumor volume in ~40-50% of surgical non-cured patients by targeting SSTR2.

Pegvisomant, a recombinant GH receptor antagonist, normalizes serum IGF-1 in > 90% of patients refractory to somatostatin analogues by blocking peripheral GH action without shrinking pituitary tumors.

page.standard_overview: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) encompasses ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI), Non-ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI), and Unstable Angina (UA), defined by myocardial ischemia with or without high-sensitivity cardiac troponin (hs-cTn) elevation. STEMI mandates immediate primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) with door-to-balloon time < 90 minutes (or fibrinolysis within 120 minutes if PCI is unavailable). NSTEMI requires validated risk stratification (GRACE score > 140) to direct early invasive coronary angiography (< 24 hours). ESC and AHA/ACC guidelines mandate dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT) combining aspirin with a potent P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor 90 mg BID or prasugrel 10 mg daily in PCI) over clopidogrel (PLATO and TRITON-TIMI 38 trials), anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin, bivalirudin, or enoxaparin, high-intensity statin therapy (atorvastatin 80 mg), beta-blockers in reduced LVEF, and early ACE inhibitors.

standard_knowledge.claim: STEMI mandates emergency primary PCI with target door-to-balloon time < 90 minutes, or fibrinolytic therapy within 10 minutes of ECG if primary PCI transfer time exceeds 120 minutes.

In NSTEMI, an early invasive coronary angiographic strategy (< 24 hours) is recommended for high-risk patients (GRACE score > 140, dynamic ST changes, elevated troponins) to reduce recurrent ischemia and hospitalizations.
Potent P2Y12 inhibitors (prasugrel or ticagrelor) are superior to clopidogrel in ACS, significantly reducing ischemic death and stent thrombosis (TRITON-TIMI 38 and PLATO trials).
Prasugrel demonstrated superior reduction in ischemic events without increased bleeding compared to ticagrelor in invasive ACS in the randomized ISAR-REACT 5 trial.

page.standard_overview: Active pulmonary tuberculosis (TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, presenting with chronic cough, hemoptysis, fevers, drenching night sweats, weight loss, and upper lobe cavitary or nodular infiltrates on chest radiography. Diagnosis is confirmed via rapid molecular testing (Xpert MTB/RIF assay on sputum), sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear, and mycobacterial culture. Standard first-line therapy for drug-susceptible TB consists of a 6-month regimen: a 2-month intensive phase with 4 drugs (Rifampin [RIF], Isoniazid [INH], Pyrazinamide [PZA], and Ethambutol [EMB] - 'RIPE'), followed by a 4-month continuation phase with Rifampin and Isoniazid (2RH). Pyridoxine (vitamin B6; 25-50 mg daily) must be co-administered with isoniazid to prevent dose-dependent peripheral neuropathy. Baseline visual acuity and red-green color discrimination must be verified before starting ethambutol to detect optic neuritis; baseline and serial hepatic transaminases must be monitored for drug-induced liver injury (PZA > INH > RIF).

standard_knowledge.claim: ATS/CDC/IDSA guidelines recommend a 6-month regimen for drug-susceptible pulmonary TB: 2 months of daily RIPE (rifampin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) followed by 4 months of daily RH (rifampin, isoniazid).
Rapid molecular testing (Xpert MTB/RIF) achieves sensitivity > 90% and simultaneously detects rpoB gene mutations conferring rifampin resistance within 2 hours.

Pyridoxine (vitamin B6, 25-50 mg daily) must be co-prescribed with isoniazid to prevent sensory peripheral neuropathy, particularly in diabetics, alcoholics, pregnant women, and malnourished patients.

Drug-induced liver injury (DILI) rules: discontinue all hepatotoxic drugs (PZA, INH, RIF) if transaminases rise >= 3x upper limit of normal with jaundice/nausea, or >= 5x ULN in asymptomatic patients.

page.standard_overview: The acute abdomen encompasses rapid-onset, severe abdominal pain reflecting life-threatening surgical emergencies (perforated viscus, acute peritonitis, bowel obstruction, acute mesenteric ischemia, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, or ruptured AAA). Diagnostic evaluation prioritizes hemodynamic stability, early resuscitation, and structured clinical evaluation: localized peritoneal signs (involuntary guarding, percussion tenderness, rebound) mandate emergent surgical consultation. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis is the diagnostic gold standard, offering sensitivity and specificity > 95% for identifying surgical pathology. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) rapidly detects hemoperitoneum (FAST), abdominal aortic aneurysm rupture, and acute cholecystitis at the bedside. Analgesia with IV opioids should NOT be withheld as it facilitates physical examination without masking surgical pathology.

standard_knowledge.claim: Contrast-enhanced abdominal/pelvic CT is the diagnostic imaging modality of choice, achieving sensitivity > 95% and significantly reducing negative laparotomy rates.
Early administration of intravenous opioid analgesia does NOT obscure abdominal examination or impede diagnostic accuracy, and is standard of care (WSES consensus).
Peritoneal signs (involuntary abdominal rigidity, focal rebound tenderness, percussion pain) warrant emergent surgical evaluation for peritonitis or hollow viscus perforation.

page.standard_overview: The acute abdomen encompasses rapid-onset, severe abdominal pain reflecting life-threatening surgical emergencies (perforated viscus, acute peritonitis, bowel obstruction, acute mesenteric ischemia, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, or ruptured AAA). Diagnostic evaluation prioritizes hemodynamic stability, early resuscitation, and structured clinical evaluation: localized peritoneal signs (involuntary guarding, percussion tenderness, rebound) mandate emergent surgical consultation. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis is the diagnostic gold standard, offering sensitivity and specificity > 95% for identifying surgical pathology. Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) rapidly detects hemoperitoneum (FAST), abdominal aortic aneurysm rupture, and acute cholecystitis at the bedside. Analgesia with IV opioids should NOT be withheld as it facilitates physical examination without masking surgical pathology.

standard_knowledge.claim: Contrast-enhanced abdominal/pelvic CT is the diagnostic imaging modality of choice, achieving sensitivity > 95% and significantly reducing negative laparotomy rates.
Early administration of intravenous opioid analgesia does NOT obscure abdominal examination or impede diagnostic accuracy, and is standard of care (WSES consensus).

Immediate empiric broad-spectrum parenteral antibiotics covering enteric Gram-negative bacilli and anaerobes must be administered within 1 hour of identifying gastrointestinal perforation or peritonitis.

page.standard_overview: Pain assessment requires validated multidimensional scales and careful clinical differentiation between nociceptive, neuropathic, and nociplastic mechanisms. In acute pain, multimodal analgesia combining acetaminophen, NSAIDs (unless contraindicated by CKD, peptic ulcer, or cardiovascular disease), regional/neuraxial anesthesia, and non-pharmacologic interventions maximizes pain control while minimizing opioid requirements ('opioid-sparing strategy'). For chronic non-cancer pain, CDC guidelines emphasize non-opioid pharmacotherapies (gabapentinoids, SNRIs, tricyclics, topical agents) and non-pharmacologic modalities (CBT, physical therapy). When opioids are necessary, clinicians should prescribe immediate-release formulations at the lowest effective dose for <= 3-7 days in acute pain; for chronic therapy, clinicians should assess opioid risk tools (ORT), check prescription drug monitoring programs (PDMP), avoid concurrent benzodiazepines (which quadruple fatal overdose risk), and co-prescribe take-home naloxone when daily morphine milligram equivalents (MME) exceed 50.

standard_knowledge.claim: CDC and APS guidelines emphasize multimodal analgesia combining non-opioid medications (acetaminophen, NSAIDs) and regional blocks as first-line strategy to minimize opioid exposure.

For acute pain requiring opioids, immediate-release formulations at the lowest effective dose should be prescribed for <= 3 to 7 days to prevent long-term physical dependence.

Take-home naloxone should be co-prescribed whenever opioid dosages equal or exceed 50 Morphine Milligram Equivalents (MME)/day, or in patients with sleep apnea, renal/hepatic dysfunction, or substance use history.

page.standard_overview: Acute pericarditis is diagnosed clinically by the presence of at least 2 of 4 cardinal ESC criteria: 1) sharp, pleuritic chest pain improved by sitting upright and leaning forward, 2) pericardial friction rub on auscultation, 3) widespread concave-upward ST-segment elevation with PR depression on ECG, and 4) new or worsening pericardial effusion. Viral infections (Coxsackie, echovirus, SARS-CoV-2) are the most common cause in high-resource settings. ESC guidelines mandate combination therapy with high-dose NSAIDs (e.g. ibuprofen 600-800 mg TID or aspirin 750-1000 mg TID) PLUS weight-adjusted oral colchicine (0.5 mg daily if < 70 kg, 0.5 mg BID if >= 70 kg) for 3 months in acute pericarditis (ICAP trial) and 6 months in recurrent pericarditis (CORP trials). Colchicine inhibits tubulin polymerization and leukocyte chemotaxis, halving recurrence rates from 37% to 16%. Systemic corticosteroids are second-line agents strictly reserved for NSAID contraindications, autoimmune etiologies, or pregnancy, as early corticosteroid use independently increases the risk of chronic recurrence.

standard_knowledge.claim: ESC 2015 guidelines establish diagnosis by >= 2 of 4 criteria: pleuritic chest pain, pericardial rub, widespread ST elevation with PR depression, and pericardial effusion.
The landmark ICAP trial proved that adding colchicine to standard NSAID therapy halves the rate of recurrent or persistent pericarditis from 37.5% to 16.7% (NNT = 5).
Weight-adjusted colchicine dosing (0.5 mg daily if < 70 kg, or 0.5 mg BID if >= 70 kg) is maintained for 3 months for first-episode acute pericarditis and 6 months for recurrences.

Systemic corticosteroids should be avoided as first-line therapy because early steroid exposure independently promotes recurrence and chronicity; rilonacept (IL-1 inhibitor) is approved for refractory recurrent pericarditis.

topic: Acute aortic dissection diagnosis and management

page.mentor_intro: Retrieved evidence centres on outcomes rather than the diagnostic pathway: type A dissection carries organ-specific malperfusion risk that predicts in-hospital death, and for type B the question is whether and when to add TEVAR to medical therapy. Guideline-level recommendations were not in the retrieved set.

teaching_points.claim: In acute type A aortic dissection, in-hospital survival varies with the type of malperfusion; mesenteric, coronary and cerebral malperfusion carried the highest in-hospital mortality, so organ-specific malperfusion should inform perioperative risk and surgical planning.
Women with type A dissection more often had pericardial effusion or tamponade, while in-hospital surgical mortality did not differ by sex (RR 1.02), suggesting a personalised approach.

A meta-analysis found TEVAR was associated with lower mortality than best medical therapy in type B dissection, especially in patients aged 65 or older, at the cost of longer hospital and ICU stays, with randomised trials still needed.

For uncomplicated type B dissection, the role of TEVAR remains debated: it improves aortic remodelling but there is no definitive survival evidence, and trials and guidelines that include high-risk features are needed.
Meta-analyses of TEVAR timing found the subacute phase (14-90 days from onset) associated with better long-term outcomes, including lower aortic-related death and reintervention.
Retrograde type A dissection after TEVAR is rare but carries high mortality (about 42%), especially in the first month and with proximal bare-stent grafts.
The GERAADA score showed better calibration than EuroSCORE II for 30-day mortality after surgery for acute type A dissection, though discrimination of both was moderate.
AI tools can feasibly detect aortic dissection on CT but do not yet demonstrate clinical applicability, and most studies were low quality.

uncertainties: Whether pre-emptive TEVAR improves survival in uncomplicated type B dissection.

page.standard_overview: Acute Aortic Syndromes (AAS) encompass Acute Aortic Dissection (AAD), Intramural Hematoma (IMH), and Penetrating Atherosclerotic Ulcer (PAU), presenting with acute, tearing or ripping chest/back pain and severe hypertension. Stanford classification determines emergency management: Type A involves the ascending aorta (surgical emergency requiring immediate open surgical graft replacement to prevent pericardial tamponade, aortic rupture, or coronary malperfusion); Type B involves the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery (managed with medical anti-impulse therapy, reserving Thoracic Endovascular Aortic Repair [TEVAR] for complicated dissection: malperfusion, refractory pain, rapid expansion, or rupture). Initial medical therapy aims to reduce aortic wall shear stress (anti-impulse therapy): IV short-acting beta-blockers (esmolol, labetalol) must be initiated FIRST to lower heart rate < 60 bpm, followed by vasodilators (nitroprusside, nicardipine) to target systolic blood pressure 100-120 mmHg. Giving vasodilators before beta-blockers precipitates reflex tachycardia and accelerates dissection tear propagation.

standard_knowledge.claim: Stanford classification directs treatment: Type A (ascending aorta) is a surgical emergency with 1-2% hourly mortality requiring immediate operative repair; Type B is managed medically unless complicated.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography angiography (CTA) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis is the imaging modality of choice, providing rapid full-length aortic visualization and branch vessel assessment.
Emergency medical therapy requires anti-impulse control: intravenous beta-blockade (esmolol or labetalol) MUST precede vasodilators to lower heart rate < 60 bpm and SBP 100-120 mmHg.

Thoracic Endovascular Aortic Repair (TEVAR) is the standard of care for complicated Type B aortic dissection (visceral/limb malperfusion, refractory pain/hypertension, rupture, or aneurysm expansion).

page.mentor_intro: Acute asthma care centres on bronchodilators and systemic corticosteroids; high-dose inhaled corticosteroids may add benefit, and IV magnesium helps children. Prevention depends on adherence, eosinophilic phenotype and inhaler technique.

teaching_points.claim: The Italian paediatric acute-asthma guideline advises against epinephrine, allows IV magnesium sulfate in severe attacks or FEV1 below 60% unresponsive to inhaled therapy, allows heliox in life-threatening attacks, and does not recommend leukotriene receptor antagonists.

A meta-analysis found moderate evidence that high-dose inhaled corticosteroids added to systemic corticosteroids reduce hospital admission (OR 0.73) in ED treatment of moderate-to-severe exacerbations.
In children, intravenous magnesium sulfate improved pulmonary function and reduced hospitalisation and further treatment, whereas nebulised magnesium had no significant effect.
Adherence of 80% or more lowered the odds of severe exacerbation (OR 0.53), and discontinuing therapy raised it.
Blood eosinophils of 200 cells/microlitre or more are associated with exacerbation (a modifiable factor in asthma management).
Inhaler technique education reduced exacerbation rates in older adults with asthma or COPD (pooled risk ratio 0.71).
Oral timolol and infusion propranolol were associated with higher asthma attack risk and should be avoided in patients at risk of asthma.
GORD and asthma exacerbation are only weakly associated.

page.standard_overview: Acute severe asthma exacerbation is characterized by progressive dyspnea, wheezing, chest tightness, and airflow obstruction, quantified by Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF) < 50% predicted or personal best. Initial therapy mandates repetitive or continuous inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (SABA; albuterol 4-8 puffs or 2.5-5 mg nebulized) combined with inhaled ipratropium bromide (500 ug nebulized q20min x 3 doses), which reduces hospital admissions by 30%. Systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisone 40-50 mg daily for 5-7 days, or IV methylprednisolone 60-80 mg in severe cases) must be administered early within 1 hour of presentation to accelerate resolution of airway inflammation. In severe exacerbations unresponsive to initial nebulization, single-dose intravenous magnesium sulfate (2 g IV over 20 min) provides safe, potent bronchodilation and reduces hospitalizations. Controlled oxygen therapy should target SpO2 93-95% (avoiding hyperoxia, which worsens V/Q mismatch and hypercapnia). A 'normal' or rising PaCO2 (> 40 mmHg) or silent chest signals respiratory muscle fatigue and impending fatal respiratory arrest.

standard_knowledge.claim: GINA guidelines mandate immediate repetitive SABA plus ipratropium bromide nebulization, which significantly reduces hospital admissions compared to SABA monotherapy.

A 'normal' or elevated PaCO2 (> 40-45 mmHg) in a tachypneic asthmatic is an ominous sign of respiratory muscle exhaustion, signaling impending arrest requiring ICU monitoring and preparation for intubation.

page.standard_overview: Acute severe asthma exacerbation is characterized by progressive dyspnea, wheezing, chest tightness, and airflow obstruction, quantified by Peak Expiratory Flow (PEF) < 50% predicted or personal best. Initial therapy mandates repetitive or continuous inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (SABA; albuterol 4-8 puffs or 2.5-5 mg nebulized) combined with inhaled ipratropium bromide (500 ug nebulized q20min x 3 doses), which reduces hospital admissions by 30%. Systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisone 40-50 mg daily for 5-7 days, or IV methylprednisolone 60-80 mg in severe cases) must be administered early within 1 hour of presentation to accelerate resolution of airway inflammation. In severe exacerbations unresponsive to initial nebulization, single-dose intravenous magnesium sulfate (2 g IV over 20 min) provides safe, potent bronchodilation and reduces hospitalizations. Controlled oxygen therapy should target SpO2 93-95% (avoiding hyperoxia, which worsens V/Q mismatch and hypercapnia). A 'normal' or rising PaCO2 (> 40 mmHg) or silent chest signals respiratory muscle fatigue and impending fatal respiratory arrest.

page.standard_overview: Acute behavioural disturbance (ABD) and severe agitation in the emergency and acute inpatient setting represent medical emergencies that threaten patient and staff safety. Most common causes include acute delirium, intoxication (sympathomimetics, alcohol, synthetic cannabinoids), sedative withdrawal, severe psychiatric psychosis, metabolic derangements, and traumatic brain injury. Clinical management follows a staged de-escalation hierarchy: environmental adaptation and verbal de-escalation are attempted first. When non-pharmacologic measures fail and physical danger exists, parenteral pharmacotherapy is deployed: for delirium and undifferentiated agitation, low-dose atypical antipsychotics (haloperidol 2.5-5 mg IM or olanzapine 5-10 mg IM) are first-line. For stimulant toxicity or alcohol withdrawal, intravenous or intramuscular benzodiazepines (lorazepam 1-2 mg or midazolam 2.5-5 mg) are the treatments of choice. For violent, hyperactive excited delirium, intramuscular ketamine (3-4 mg/kg IM) achieves rapid sedation within 5 minutes under strict airway monitoring.

standard_knowledge.claim: A structured stepwise approach begins with non-pharmacologic de-escalation, reserving chemical sedation for patients presenting immediate physical danger to themselves or staff.

Antipsychotics (haloperidol, olanzapine, droperidol) provide effective sedation for psychotic agitation and delirium, but require ECG monitoring for QTc prolongation.
Intramuscular ketamine (3-4 mg/kg IM) produces rapid, reliable dissociation within 3-5 minutes in extreme, life-threatening violent agitation failing other agents, under dedicated airway monitoring.

page.standard_overview: Acute cholecystitis and acute cholangitis represent common biliary infections governed by the international Tokyo Guidelines (TG18). Acute cholecystitis is defined by local inflammation (Murphy's sign, RUQ tenderness), systemic inflammation (fever, elevated CRP/WBC), and confirmatory imaging (ultrasound showing gallbladder wall thickening >= 4 mm, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's sign). Laparoscopic cholecystectomy performed early within 72 hours of symptom onset (or during index admission) is the gold standard, achieving shorter hospital stays and fewer complications than delayed surgery. Acute cholangitis is a medical emergency caused by biliary tract obstruction (primarily choledocholithiasis) with bacterial superinfection, presenting with Charcot's triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain) or Reynolds' pentad (adding hypotension and altered mental status in septic shock). TG18 mandates immediate resuscitation, empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics, and emergency biliary decompression via Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) within 24 hours (or emergent < 12 hours for severe Grade III cholangitis).

standard_knowledge.claim: Tokyo Guidelines 2018 (TG18) recommend early laparoscopic cholecystectomy within 72 hours of symptom onset as the optimal treatment of choice for acute cholecystitis.
Acute cholangitis is diagnosed by systemic inflammation (fever, elevated WBC/CRP), cholestasis (jaundice, elevated transaminases/alkaline phosphatase), and biliary dilation on imaging.
Severe (Grade III) acute cholangitis with organ dysfunction mandates immediate fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, and urgent biliary drainage by ERCP within 12 hours.

In high-risk surgical patients with acute cholecystitis unfit for emergency surgery, ultrasound-guided percutaneous transhepatic gallbladder drainage (PTGBD) provides effective temporary or definitive decompression.

page.standard_overview: Acute confusion (delirium) is an acute, fluctuating neurocognitive disturbance characterized by inattention, altered level of consciousness, and disorganized thinking, triggered by underlying acute medical illness, surgery, or toxidrome. Diagnostic confirmation requires validated screening instruments, predominantly the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM; acute onset/fluctuation + inattention + disorganized thinking or altered consciousness) or 4AT. Non-pharmacologic multicomponent prevention and treatment (HELP model: reorientation, sleep-wake cycle hygiene, early mobilization, pain control, sensory aids, avoidance of deliriogenic medications like anticholinergics and benzodiazepines) is the evidence-based first-line cornerstone. Pharmacotherapy with low-dose atypical antipsychotics (haloperidol, quetiapine, olanzapine) does NOT shorten delirium duration or reduce mortality, and is strictly indicated only when severe agitation threatens imminent patient or staff safety. Formal mental capacity assessment must be decision-specific and time-specific, assessing the ability to understand, retain, weigh information, and communicate a choice.

standard_knowledge.claim: Diagnosis requires validated bedside tools; the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) requires features 1 (acute onset/fluctuating course) AND 2 (inattention), PLUS either 3 (disorganized thinking) OR 4 (altered level of consciousness).
Non-pharmacological multicomponent bundles (Hospital Elder Life Program [HELP]: early mobilization, hydration, cognitive reorientation, sleep protocols) reduce delirium incidence by > 30-40%.

Randomized clinical trials (MIND-USA trial) proved that routine antipsychotic administration (haloperidol or ziprasidone) does not alter delirium duration, ICU length of stay, or 30-day mortality compared to placebo.

Mental capacity is legally presumed unless proven otherwise, must be assessed specifically for the particular decision at that exact moment, and requires structured assessment of understanding, retaining, weighing, and communicating decisions.

page.standard_overview: Acute confusion (delirium) is an acute, fluctuating neurocognitive disturbance characterized by inattention, altered level of consciousness, and disorganized thinking, triggered by underlying acute medical illness, surgery, or toxidrome. Diagnostic confirmation requires validated screening instruments, predominantly the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM; acute onset/fluctuation + inattention + disorganized thinking or altered consciousness) or 4AT. Non-pharmacologic multicomponent prevention and treatment (HELP model: reorientation, sleep-wake cycle hygiene, early mobilization, pain control, sensory aids, avoidance of deliriogenic medications like anticholinergics and benzodiazepines) is the evidence-based first-line cornerstone. Pharmacotherapy with low-dose atypical antipsychotics (haloperidol, quetiapine, olanzapine) does NOT shorten delirium duration or reduce mortality, and is strictly indicated only when severe agitation threatens imminent patient or staff safety. Formal mental capacity assessment must be decision-specific and time-specific, assessing the ability to understand, retain, weigh information, and communicate a choice.

standard_knowledge.claim: Diagnosis requires validated bedside tools; the Confusion Assessment Method (CAM) requires features 1 (acute onset/fluctuating course) AND 2 (inattention), PLUS either 3 (disorganized thinking) OR 4 (altered level of consciousness).
Non-pharmacological multicomponent bundles (Hospital Elder Life Program [HELP]: early mobilization, hydration, cognitive reorientation, sleep protocols) reduce delirium incidence by > 30-40%.

Randomized clinical trials (MIND-USA trial) proved that routine antipsychotic administration (haloperidol or ziprasidone) does not alter delirium duration, ICU length of stay, or 30-day mortality compared to placebo.

Mental capacity is legally presumed unless proven otherwise, must be assessed specifically for the particular decision at that exact moment, and requires structured assessment of understanding, retaining, weighing, and communicating decisions.

page.standard_overview: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) management centers on rapid risk stratification, coronary revascularization, and potent antithrombotic therapy. Dual Antiplatelet Therapy (DAPT) combining aspirin with a potent P2Y12 receptor inhibitor (ticagrelor 90 mg BID or prasugrel 10 mg daily) is the guideline-directed standard of care for 12 months post-PCI, demonstrating superior reduction in ischemic events and stent thrombosis compared to clopidogrel (PLATO, TRITON-TIMI 38). In the randomized head-to-head ISAR-REACT 5 trial, prasugrel was superior to ticagrelor in reducing composite death, MI, or stroke (6.9% vs 9.3%) without increasing major bleeding. High-bleeding-risk (HBR) patients can safely undergo abbreviated DAPT (1-3 months) followed by P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy (ticagrelor or clopidogrel; TWILIGHT and STOPDAPT-2 trials), which halves major bleeding without increasing ischemic events. Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors (eptifibatide, tirofiban) are reserved for thrombotic bailout during PCI.

standard_knowledge.claim: Prasugrel and ticagrelor are significantly superior to clopidogrel in ACS, reducing ischemic death and stent thrombosis (TRITON-TIMI 38 and PLATO trials).

In high-bleeding-risk patients undergoing PCI, dropping aspirin after 1-3 months and continuing P2Y12 inhibitor monotherapy significantly reduces major bleeding without increasing stent thrombosis (TWILIGHT trial).

Triple antithrombotic therapy (OAC + DAPT) in patients with atrial fibrillation undergoing PCI should be minimized: transition to dual therapy (DOAC + clopidogrel) at hospital discharge reduces bleeding by > 40% (AUGUSTUS trial).

page.standard_overview: Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) requires aggressive, early decongestion to relieve elevated ventricular filling pressures and systemic congestion. Intravenous loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide) are the foundation of therapy: the landmark DOSE-AHF trial established that high-dose IV loop diuretic therapy (2.5x oral home dose) achieves more rapid symptom relief and fluid loss without worsening long-term renal function compared to low-dose therapy, with continuous infusion offering no superiority over bolus dosing. Sequential nephron blockade overcomes diuretic resistance: adding oral acetazolamide (500 mg IV; carbonic anhydrase inhibitor blocking proximal tubule sodium reabsorption) significantly accelerates successful decongestion by 46% (ADVOR trial); adding thiazide-like diuretics (oral metolazone or IV chlorothiazide; CLOROTIC trial) boosts natriuresis. SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) initiated early during index hospitalization improve decongestion and reduce cardiovascular mortality and readmissions (EMPULSE trial).

standard_knowledge.claim: The landmark DOSE-AHF trial showed that high-dose loop diuretic therapy (2.5x oral home dose IV) achieved superior early fluid loss and dyspnea relief without increasing 60-day renal failure or mortality.
Adding intravenous acetazolamide (500 mg daily) to loop diuretics significantly accelerates successful complete decongestion by 46% without increasing renal adverse events (ADVOR trial).
Adding a thiazide diuretic (CLOROTIC trial: oral hydrochlorothiazide added to IV furosemide) significantly enhances weight loss and diuresis in patients with loop diuretic resistance.

In-hospital initiation of SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin) in acute decompensated heart failure produces significant clinical benefit, weight reduction, and lower 90-day all-cause mortality (EMPULSE trial).

page.standard_overview: Acute Disseminated Encephalomyelitis (ADEM) is an acute, immune-mediated, monophasic inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system, predominantly affecting children and young adults typically 1-3 weeks following a viral illness or vaccination. Clinical presentation combines encephalopathy (altered behavior, lethargy, or coma - a mandatory diagnostic feature in pediatric consensus criteria) with multifocal neurologic deficits (ataxia, cranial nerve palsies, hemiparesis, optic neuritis). Brain and spine MRI with gadolinium is the imaging modality of choice, demonstrating large, bilateral, asymmetric, poorly marginated, fluffy hyperintensities on T2/FLAIR predominantly involving cerebral white matter, deep gray nuclei (thalami, basal ganglia), and spinal cord, with punctate or open-ring enhancement. Serum myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) antibodies are positive in > 50-60% of pediatric ADEM cases. First-line therapy is high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (30 mg/kg/day, up to 1 g daily for 3-5 days) followed by an oral prednisone taper; intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 2 g/kg over 2-5 days) or plasma exchange (PLEX) are second-line rescue therapies.

standard_knowledge.claim: International Pediatric Multiple Sclerosis Study Group (IPMSSG) consensus defines ADEM as a first polyfocal demyelinating event with encephalopathy (lethargy, irritability, altered behavior) not explained by fever.
Brain and spinal MRI typically reveals diffuse, poorly demarcated, large (> 1-2 cm) lesions involving subcortical and deep white matter, thalami, and brainstem with open-ring or punctate enhancement.
High-titer serum anti-MOG (myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein) antibodies are present in > 50% of pediatric ADEM cases, predicting a high rate of complete monophasic recovery if titers decline.

First-line therapy is high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3-5 days in adults, 30 mg/kg/day in children) followed by a 4- to 6-week oral taper, achieving complete functional recovery in > 70-80%.

page.standard_overview: Acute gouty arthritis is an intensely painful inflammatory arthritis driven by the deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in synovial fluid and periarticular tissues, triggering the NLRP3 inflammasome and interleukin-1beta (IL-1beta) release. page.standard_overview: Acute decompensated heart failure (ADHF) requires aggressive, early decongestion to relieve elevated ventricular filling pressures and systemic congestion. Intravenous loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide) are the foundation of therapy: the landmark DOSE-AHF trial established that high-dose IV loop diuretic therapy (2.5x oral home dose) achieves more rapid symptom relief and fluid loss without worsening long-term renal function compared to low-dose therapy, with continuous infusion offering no superiority over bolus dosing. Sequential nephron blockade overcomes diuretic resistance: adding oral acetazolamide (500 mg IV; carbonic anhydrase inhibitor blocking proximal tubule sodium reabsorption) significantly accelerates successful decongestion by 46% (ADVOR trial); adding thiazide-like diuretics (oral metolazone or IV chlorothiazide; CLOROTIC trial) boosts natriuresis. SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) initiated early during index hospitalization improve decongestion and reduce cardiovascular mortality and readmissions (EMPULSE trial).

standard_knowledge.claim: The landmark DOSE-AHF trial showed that high-dose loop diuretic therapy (2.5x oral home dose IV) achieved superior early fluid loss and dyspnea relief without increasing 60-day renal failure or mortality.
Adding intravenous acetazolamide (500 mg daily) to loop diuretics significantly accelerates successful complete decongestion by 46% without increasing renal adverse events (ADVOR trial).
Adding a thiazide diuretic (CLOROTIC trial: oral hydrochlorothiazide added to IV furosemide) significantly enhances weight loss and diuresis in patients with loop diuretic resistance.

page.standard_overview: Acute ischemic stroke management is defined by rapid reperfusion to salvage the ischemic penumbra. Intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase (0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg; NINDS trial) or tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg, max 25 mg; EXTEND-IA TNK trial) is indicated within 4.5 hours of symptom onset in eligible patients after intracranial hemorrhage is excluded on non-contrast CT head. For acute large vessel occlusion (LVO) of the anterior circulation (internal carotid or proximal middle cerebral artery [M1/M2]), Endovascular Thrombectomy (EVT) is the undisputed standard of care within 6 hours (HERMES meta-analysis). Furthermore, landmark trials revolutionized late-window therapy: the DAWN trial (6 to 24 hours using clinical-core mismatch on diffusion MRI or CT perfusion) and DEFUSE-3 trial (6 to 16 hours using perfusion-core mismatch: ischemic core < 70 mL, mismatch ratio >= 1.8) proved that EVT dramatically improves functional independence (mRS 0-2: 45-49% vs 13-17%; NNT ~2-3) in selected patients with salvageable penumbral tissue out to 24 hours.

standard_knowledge.claim: Intravenous thrombolysis (alteplase 0.9 mg/kg or tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg) administered within 4.5 hours of symptom onset improves functional recovery at 3 months (NINDS and ECASS-III trials).

Endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) for large vessel anterior circulation occlusions within 6 hours of onset achieves functional independence in 46% of patients compared to 27% with medical therapy (HERMES meta-analysis, NNT = 2.6).
The landmark DAWN trial proved that mechanical thrombectomy performed between 6 and 24 hours based on clinical-infarct core mismatch achieves marked functional independence (49% vs 13%, NNT = 2.8).

The DEFUSE-3 trial demonstrated that EVT performed between 6 and 16 hours in patients selected by CT perfusion or diffusion MRI (ischemic core < 70 mL, mismatch ratio >= 1.8) significantly reduces disability and 90-day mortality.

page.standard_overview: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) is an abrupt decline in glomerular filtration rate defined by KDIGO consensus as an increase in serum creatinine by >= 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours, a >= 1.5-fold increase over baseline within 7 days, or urine output < 0.5 mL/kg/h for >= 6 hours. Clinical evaluation categorizes etiology into prerenal (volume depletion, renal hypoperfusion), intrinsic renal (acute tubular necrosis [ATN], acute interstitial nephritis [AIN], glomerulonephritis), and postrenal (urinary tract obstruction). Urinalysis with microscopic sediment examination is essential: muddy brown granular casts indicate ATN, white cell casts/eosinophils suggest AIN, dysmorphic red cells and RBC casts signal glomerulonephritis, and bland sediment points to prerenal azotemia. Renal ultrasound is mandatory in unexplained AKI to exclude hydronephrosis and obstruction. Management prioritizes restoring euvolemia with balanced crystalloids, discontinuing nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast), and initiating renal replacement therapy for urgent refractory complications (AEIOU: Acidosis pH < 7.15, Electrolytes K+ > 6.5, Ingestion toxins, Overload pulmonary edema, Uremia encephalopathy/pericarditis).

standard_knowledge.claim: KDIGO consensus criteria stage AKI from Stage 1 (creatinine 1.5-1.9x baseline or urine < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6-12h) to Stage 3 (creatinine 3.0x baseline, >= 4.0 mg/dL, or anuria >= 12h).
Urinary sediment microscopy provides high diagnostic accuracy: muddy brown granular casts are pathognomonic for acute tubular necrosis (ATN); red cell casts indicate acute glomerulonephritis.
Balanced crystalloids (Lactated Ringer's, Plasma-Lyte) reduce the risk of major adverse kidney events (MAKE) compared to 0.9% normal saline in hospitalized patients (SMART and SALT-ED trials).

Urgent indications for renal replacement therapy follow the 'AEIOU' mnemonic: refractory Acidemia (pH < 7.15), refractory Hyperkalemia (K+ > 6.5 mmol/L), Intoxications, volume Overload, and Uremic pericarditis/encephalopathy.

RenalGuard is more secure than conventional hydration for preventing contrast-associated AKI, though its role in TAVR is questionable.

page.standard_overview: Contrast-associated acute kidney injury (CA-AKI) represents a frequent inpatient consult where historic dogma often drives unnecessary prophylactic interventions. Rigorous multicenter randomized trials (PRESERVE and AMACING) have clarified that routine intravenous sodium bicarbonate or oral N-acetylcysteine provides no benefit over standard isotonic saline, and that intravenous hydration itself may be withheld safely in stable outpatients with eGFR >= 30 mL/min/1.73m2. The primary protective strategies remain minimizing iodinated contrast volume (contrast volume to eGFR ratio < 3.0), avoiding repetitive scans within 48 hours, and discontinuing concurrent nephrotoxins.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the landmark PRESERVE trial of 5,177 patients undergoing angiography, neither intravenous sodium bicarbonate nor oral N-acetylcysteine reduced the 90-day risk of death, need for dialysis, or persistent decline in kidney function compared with intravenous isotonic saline.

The AMACING randomized trial established non-inferiority of withholding prophylactic intravenous hydration compared with standard hydration in elective contrast procedures for patients with eGFR 30-59 mL/min/1.73m2, showing no increase in contrast-induced nephropathy.

KDIGO guidelines recommend utilizing iso-osmolar or low-osmolar iodinated contrast media and titrating to the lowest diagnostic volume (contrast volume to eGFR ratio < 3.0 or contrast volume to weight ratio < 3.7 mL/kg).

The ACR-NKF consensus statement specifies that true contrast-induced acute kidney injury is exceptionally rare when baseline eGFR is >= 45 mL/min/1.73m2, and routine prophylactic hydration should be reserved primarily for non-emergent patients with eGFR < 30 mL/min/1.73m2 or AKI stage 1-3.

page.standard_overview: The KDIGO consensus definition harmonized previous RIFLE and AKIN diagnostic frameworks, standardizing AKI diagnosis around two cardinal physiological parameters: acute elevation in serum creatinine and/or sustained reduction in urine output. Recognizing that creatinine is a delayed functional marker rather than a real-time structural injury biomarker is essential: clinical staging dictates immediate protocolized management, avoidance of drug-induced nephrotoxicity, and prompt hemodynamic resuscitation.

standard_knowledge.claim: Under KDIGO criteria, AKI is formally diagnosed by an increase in serum creatinine by >= 0.3 mg/dL (>= 26.5 umol/L) within 48 hours, or an increase >= 1.5 times baseline within the prior 7 days, or urine volume < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 consecutive hours.

KDIGO staging stratifies severity: Stage 1 (creatinine 1.5-1.9x baseline or urine < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6-12h); Stage 2 (creatinine 2.0-2.9x baseline or urine < 0.5 mL/kg/h for >= 12h); Stage 3 (creatinine >= 3.0x baseline, creatinine >= 4.0 mg/dL, initiation of RRT, or anuria for >= 12h).

The historic RIFLE framework demonstrated a direct stepwise association between severity tiers (Risk, Injury, Failure, Loss, End-Stage) and inpatient mortality and duration of mechanical ventilation in intensive care.

ADQI consensus emphasizes combining functional criteria (creatinine, urine output) with cell-cycle arrest and damage biomarkers (such as TIMP-2 and IGFBP7) to identify subclinical AKI prior to overt filtration loss.

page.standard_overview: Preventing and managing established acute kidney injury requires proactive hemodynamic optimization, de-escalation of nephrotoxic medications, and judicious fluid stewardship. Large randomized pragmatic trials (STARRT-AKI and AKIKI) have settled the timing dilemma of renal replacement therapy (RRT), conclusively establishing that accelerated early RRT initiation confers no survival benefit and exposes patients to procedural harms compared to watchful waiting with standard medical rescue indications.

standard_knowledge.claim: The STARRT-AKI multinational trial (3,011 patients) showed that accelerated RRT initiation in critically ill patients with Stage 2-3 AKI did not reduce 90-day all-cause mortality (43.9% vs 43.7%) but significantly increased dialysis dependence at 90 days and adverse events.

The AKIKI trial demonstrated that a delayed strategy waiting for refractory hyperkalemia, severe metabolic acidosis, or refractory pulmonary edema allowed 49% of patients to avoid dialysis entirely with identical 60-day survival.

The AKIKI 2 trial demonstrated that delaying RRT beyond oliguria of > 72 hours or BUN > 112 mg/dL until mandatory life-threatening emergency thresholds were breached increased 60-day mortality, defining the upper safety boundary of waiting.

KDIGO guidelines recommend an individualized strategy based on refractory physiological criteria (refractory hyperkalemia, acidemia, volume overload, uremic pericarditis/encephalopathy) rather than arbitrary creatinine or urea numeric cutoffs.

page.standard_overview: Acute Leukemia of Ambiguous Lineage (ALAL) comprises rare, biologically aggressive leukemias that cannot be classified as purely myeloid or lymphoid. Under updated WHO and International Consensus Classification (ICC) guidelines, ALAL encompasses mixed-phenotype acute leukemia (MPAL with B/myeloid or T/myeloid co-expression) and acute undifferentiated leukemia (AUL). Initial immunophenotypic confirmation via multi-parameter flow cytometry and cytogenetic/molecular profiling (specifically screening for BCR::ABL1 and KMT2A rearrangements) is mandatory, as lineage-directed or hybrid ALL-like induction followed by consolidated allogeneic stem cell transplantation in CR1 offers superior survival compared to AML-like regimens.

standard_knowledge.claim: Diagnostic criteria for mixed-phenotype acute leukemia (MPAL) require strict lineage-defining markers: myeloperoxidase (MPO) or monocytic markers for myeloid lineage; strong CD19 with companion B-markers (CD10, CD22, CD79a) for B lineage; and cytoplasmic or surface CD3 for T lineage.

Retrospective and registry studies show that ALL-directed induction chemotherapy achieves higher complete remission rates (70-85%) and superior overall survival compared with standard AML-type induction regimens (30-50% CR).

For patients with MPAL harboring t(9;22)(q34.1;q11.2) / BCR::ABL1, upfront addition of a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (dasatinib or ponatinib) to induction backbone is standard and significantly deepens remission.

Due to high relapse rates with consolidation chemotherapy alone, allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) in first complete remission (CR1) represents the optimal curative consolidation for fit adult ALAL patients.

page.standard_overview: Acute limb ischemia (ALI) is a vascular emergency characterized by sudden hypoperfusion threatening limb viability within a 4-to-6 hour golden window. The Rutherford classification rapidly stratifies limbs into viable (Stage I), marginally threatened (Stage IIa), immediately threatened (Stage IIb), and irreversibly non-viable (Stage III). Immediate systemic unfractionated heparin anticoagulation must be initiated to arrest thrombus propagation, followed by urgent surgical embolectomy/bypass for Stage IIb or catheter-directed thrombolysis/endovascular thrombectomy for Stage IIa limbs.

standard_knowledge.claim: Rutherford classification defines clinical urgency: Stage I is viable without sensory/motor loss; Stage IIa is marginally threatened with minimal sensory loss and audible arterial Doppler; Stage IIb is immediately threatened with motor weakness and inaudible arterial Doppler; Stage III is irreversible with profound anesthesia and paralysis.

Immediate intravenous unfractionated heparin bolus and infusion prevents microvascular thrombosis propagation and reduces amputation risk, and should be administered immediately upon clinical suspicion before diagnostic imaging.

The TOPAS and STILE randomized trials demonstrated that for patients presenting within 14 days with viable or marginally threatened limbs (Rutherford IIa), catheter-directed thrombolysis achieved equivalent limb salvage and survival compared to open surgery, while reducing surgical morbidity.

For immediately threatened limbs (Rutherford IIb), emergent open surgical revascularization (balloon catheter embolectomy, endarterectomy, or bypass) is required to restore perfusion within 6 hours to prevent permanent neuromuscular necrosis; prophylactic four-compartment fasciotomy is indicated if ischemia duration exceeds 4-6 hours.

page.standard_overview: Acute liver failure (ALF) is a rapid-onset syndrome characterized by severe hepatocyte death, international normalized ratio (INR) >= 1.5, and hepatic encephalopathy in a patient without pre-existing cirrhosis, evolving within 26 weeks. Differentiating acetaminophen-induced ALF from non-acetaminophen etiologies (viral hepatitis, drug-induced liver injury, autoimmune, Wilson disease) is critical. Early administration of intravenous N-acetylcysteine improves transplant-free survival even in non-acetaminophen ALF, and aggressive supportive ICU care targeting cerebral edema and multi-organ failure serves as a bridge to spontaneous recovery or emergency liver transplantation.

standard_knowledge.claim: A prospective double-blind randomized controlled trial by Lee et al. demonstrated that intravenous N-acetylcysteine significantly improves transplant-free survival in patients with early-stage non-acetaminophen acute liver failure (coma grade I-II; 52% vs 30%), primarily driven by microvascular hemodynamic benefits.

ALF diagnosis requires biochemical evidence of acute hepatic injury (transaminitis), coagulopathy (INR >= 1.5), and any degree of hepatic encephalopathy in the absence of pre-existing chronic liver disease.

Infection is the leading cause of death in ALF; surveillance blood, sputum, and urine cultures must be performed routinely, with a low threshold for broad-spectrum empirical antimicrobial and antifungal therapy upon clinical deterioration.

Sedation and endotracheal intubation should be instituted early once Grade 3 or 4 encephalopathy manifests to protect the airway and facilitate neuroprotective management of intracranial hypertension.

page.standard_overview: Managing acute liver failure in the intensive care unit centers on preventing and mitigating severe intracranial hypertension resulting from hyperammonemia, cytotoxic astrocyte swelling, and disrupted cerebral autoregulation. The King's College Criteria provide established, etiology-specific prognostic benchmarks that identify patients unlikely to survive without emergency orthotopic liver transplantation. Neuroprotective interventions—including head elevation, targeted hypertonic saline (serum sodium 145-150 mmol/L), normothermia, and high-volume plasma exchange—reduce cerebral herniation risk.

standard_knowledge.claim: Under King's College Criteria for acetaminophen ALF: arterial blood pH < 7.30 after resuscitation, or all three of INR > 6.5, serum creatinine > 3.4 mg/dL, and Grade 3-4 encephalopathy; for non-acetaminophen ALF: INR > 6.5, or any 3 of unfavorable etiology, age < 10 or > 40, jaundice-to-encephalopathy interval > 7 days, INR > 3.5, bilirubin > 17.5 mg/dL.

In a randomized trial by Murphy et al., prophylactic infusion of 3% hypertonic saline to maintain serum sodium between 145 and 150 mmol/L significantly reduced the incidence and severity of acute intracranial hypertension in ALF.

Larsen et al. demonstrated in a multicenter randomized trial that high-volume plasma exchange (HV-PE) significantly improved transplant-free survival (58.7% vs 47.8%) and attenuated systemic inflammatory response syndrome and vasopressor requirements.

Arterial ammonia levels > 150-200 umol/L correlate strongly with intracranial hypertension and cerebral herniation; continuous renal replacement therapy is recommended early for ammonia clearance even in the absence of traditional dialysis indications.

page.standard_overview: Accurate, dynamic prognostication in acute liver failure is essential to prevent either premature transplantation in patients who would recover spontaneously or delayed listing resulting in fatal brainstem herniation. While King's College Criteria offer high specificity, their sensitivity is modest. Modern multi-variable prognostic models (such as the ALFSG index, Model for End-Stage Liver Disease [MELD], and serial arterial lactate clearance) complement clinical assessment to guide super-urgent listing decisions in real time.

standard_knowledge.claim: The Model for End-Stage Liver Disease (MELD) score is highly predictive of death in ALF, with MELD scores > 30-33 demonstrating diagnostic sensitivity superior to King's College Criteria for non-acetaminophen etiologies.

Serial arterial lactate kinetics provide critical prognostic insight: in acetaminophen ALF, arterial lactate > 3.5 mmol/L after early fluid resuscitation or > 3.0 mmol/L at 12 hours independently predicts mortality with > 90% positive predictive value.

EASL clinical practice guidelines emphasize combining static scores with dynamic trajectory: lack of reduction in INR and progressive elevation in serum bilirubin over 48-72 hours indicate failure of spontaneous hepatocyte regeneration.

The Acute Liver Failure Study Group (ALFSG) prognostic index integrates etiology, coma grade, INR, bilirubin, and arterial phosphorus to generate validated 21-day transplant-free survival probabilities.

page.standard_overview: Timely referral to a specialized liver transplant center is the single most vital intervention determining survival in acute liver failure. Listing for emergency liver transplantation (UNOS Status 1A / UK Super-Urgent Scheme) must occur before irreversible multi-organ failure, refractory sepsis, or fixed dilated pupils from cerebral herniation preclude surgery. Understanding the distinct pathophysiological criteria—King's College, Clichy-Villejuif criteria (Factor V < 20-30%), and contraindications to transplantation—enables frontline clinicians to coordinate transfer without fatal delay.

standard_knowledge.claim: Immediate contact with a liver transplant center is mandatory as soon as coagulopathy (INR >= 1.5) and any altered mental status occur, rather than delaying until full King's College Criteria listing benchmarks are reached.

Under the Clichy-Villejuif criteria (widely used in Europe), fulminant viral hepatitis patients with Factor V level < 20% (age < 30) or Factor V < 30% (age >= 30) in the presence of encephalopathy meet emergency transplant listing criteria.

Super-urgent transplant listing criteria (UNOS Status 1A) require fulminant liver failure with life expectancy < 7 days, manifesting as encephalopathy, mechanical ventilation, renal replacement therapy, or severe coagulopathy (INR > 2.0).

Absolute contraindications to emergency liver transplantation include irreversible catastrophic brain damage (fixed dilated pupils, sustained cerebral perfusion pressure < 40 mmHg), uncontrolled active septic shock, and severe active cardiopulmonary comorbidities.

page.standard_overview: Adult acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) management has been revolutionized by pediatric-inspired multi-agent chemotherapy regimens, molecular risk-stratification, and targeted immunotherapies. In Philadelphia chromosome-positive (Ph+) ALL, combining second- or third-generation tyrosine kinase inhibitors (dasatinib, ponatinib) with blinatumomab has enabled chemotherapy-free induction with high complete molecular remission rates. For relapsed/refractory B-ALL, antibody-drug conjugates (inotuzumab ozogamicin) and bispecific T-cell engagers (blinatumomab) demonstrate marked superiority over conventional salvage.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the phase 3 TOWER trial, blinatumomab (CD19/CD3 bispecific T-cell engager) significantly improved overall survival (median 7.7 vs 4.0 months) and complete remission rates compared to standard salvage chemotherapy in relapsed/refractory B-ALL.

The INO-VATE trial showed that inotuzumab ozogamicin (anti-CD22 calicheamicin conjugate) achieved significantly higher CR rates (80.7% vs 29.4%) and higher MRD negativity than standard chemotherapy, though requiring careful monitoring for hepatic sinusoidal obstruction syndrome prior to HSCT.

The D-ALBA trial established that first-line chemotherapy-free induction with dasatinib plus blinatumomab achieved a 98% hematologic complete response rate and high molecular clearance in adult Ph+ B-ALL.

Pediatric-inspired regimens (such as augmented Berlin-Frankfurt-Münster [BFM] or CALGB protocols) significantly improve event-free survival in adolescents and young adults (AYAs, ages 18-39) with Ph-negative ALL compared to historic adult protocols.

page.mentor_intro: Oral and intravenous steroids show no clear efficacy difference for acute MS relapse in adults, though oral steroids cause more insomnia. Relapse recovery is often incomplete, with relapse severity the strongest predictor.

teaching_points.claim: In adults with acute MS relapse, there were no clear differences in efficacy and overall tolerability between oral and intravenous steroids, with insomnia associated with the oral route (RR 1.25).
Relapse recovery is often incomplete, and relapse severity is the strongest and most consistent predictor of incomplete recovery.
