page.standard_overview: Acute relapses in multiple sclerosis (MS) present as subacute neurological deficits developing over hours to days in the absence of fever or infection. High-dose corticosteroids (intravenous or oral methylprednisolone 1,000 mg daily for 3-5 days) represent the first-line standard of care, accelerating functional recovery as proven in the Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT) and COPOUSEP trials. In patients with severe, disabling deficits refractory to high-dose steroids, therapeutic plasma exchange (PLEX) provides proven rescue therapy, demonstrating marked functional improvement when instituted early.

standard_knowledge.claim: The Optic Neuritis Treatment Trial (ONTT) demonstrated that high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 3 days) followed by oral prednisone accelerated visual recovery compared to placebo, whereas oral prednisone alone at standard doses increased relapse recurrence rates.

The double-blind COPOUSEP non-inferiority trial demonstrated that oral methylprednisolone (1,000 mg daily for 3 days) is clinically non-inferior to intravenous methylprednisolone in achieving functional recovery at day 28 in acute MS relapses.

In a sham-controlled randomized trial by Weinshenker et al., therapeutic plasma exchange (PLEX, 5-7 exchanges over 14 days) produced moderate to marked neurological recovery in 42.1% of patients with severe steroid-refractory acute inflammatory demyelinating relapses versus 5.9% with sham treatment.

Pseudo-relapses—transient re-emergence of previous neurological deficits triggered by infection (e.g., UTI), elevated core body temperature (Uhthoff phenomenon), or metabolic stress—must be ruled out before initiating high-dose immunosuppressive therapies.

page.standard_overview: Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) management is anchored in rapid cytogenetic and molecular risk stratification under the 2022 European LeukemiaNet (ELN) recommendations. For fit adult patients, traditional '7+3' cytarabine and anthracycline induction is now systematically enhanced by targeted agents: adding the FLT3 inhibitor midostaurin in FLT3-mutated AML (RATIFY trial), or the anti-CD33 antibody-drug conjugate gemtuzumab ozogamicin in favorable-risk cytogenetics (ALFA-0701 trial). Defining measurable residual disease (MRD) after induction guides the decision to pursue allogeneic stem cell transplantation in CR1.

standard_knowledge.claim: The ELN 2022 classification stratifies AML into Favorable (e.g., inv(16), t(8;21), mutated NPM1 without FLT3-ITD), Intermediate, and Adverse (e.g., mutated TP53, complex karyotype, adverse gene fusions, myelodysplasia-related gene mutations).

The international RATIFY trial established that adding the multikinase FLT3 inhibitor midostaurin to standard 7+3 induction and consolidation significantly prolonged overall survival (hazard ratio for death 0.78, p=0.009) in both FLT3-ITD and FLT3-TKD mutated AML.

The ALFA-0701 randomized trial demonstrated that fractionated gemtuzumab ozogamicin added to standard induction improved event-free and overall survival in patients with favorable and intermediate-risk cytogenetics, without increasing fatal toxicities.

Flow cytometric or molecular measurable residual disease (MRD) negativity after consolidation is the strongest predictor of long-term relapse-free survival and stratifies the necessity of allogeneic stem cell transplantation in intermediate-risk disease.

page.standard_overview: The combination of the selective oral BCL-2 inhibitor venetoclax with a hypomethylating agent (azacitidine or decitabine) has transformed the therapeutic landscape for older adults (>= 75 years) or younger patients unfit for intensive chemotherapy. In the landmark VIALE-A trial, venetoclax plus azacitidine demonstrated marked improvements in complete remission rates and overall survival over azacitidine monotherapy. Managing this regimen demands rigorous tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) ramp-up prophylaxis, protocolized bone marrow reassessment on day 28, and proactive dose delays or growth factor support for prolonged cytopenias.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the global phase 3 VIALE-A trial, venetoclax combined with azacitidine significantly improved median overall survival (14.7 months vs 9.6 months; hazard ratio for death 0.66, p<0.001) and composite complete remission rate (66.4% vs 28.3%) compared with azacitidine alone in patients ineligible for intensive chemotherapy.

In patients receiving low-dose cytarabine backbones, the VIALE-C trial demonstrated superior composite remission (48% vs 13%) and clinically meaningful survival extension with the addition of venetoclax.

Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) mitigation requires cytoreduction with hydroxyurea for white blood cell counts > 25,000/uL, vigorous hydration, rasburicase or allopurinol, and structured daily venetoclax ramp-up (100 mg, 200 mg, 400 mg daily).

When co-administered with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., posaconazole, voriconazole), venetoclax dosage must be reduced by 75% (to 100 mg daily), and by 50% (to 200 mg daily) with moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors (e.g., fluconazole).

page.standard_overview: Acute myocarditis encompasses an inflammatory spectrum ranging from mild chest pain with transient troponin elevation to fulminant cardiogenic shock and fatal ventricular arrhythmias. While historic Dallas histopathological criteria suffered from low sensitivity and biopsy sampling error, contemporary diagnosis centers on multiparametric cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) utilizing the updated Lake Louise Criteria (T1 and T2 mapping). Endomyocardial biopsy remains mandatory in progressive or fulminant presentations to identify specific subtypes—such as giant cell myocarditis or eosinophilic myocarditis—where emergency immunosuppressive regimens are life-saving.

standard_knowledge.claim: Under the 2018 Updated Lake Louise Criteria, CMR diagnosis of acute myocarditis requires at least one T2-based criterion (myocardial edema on T2-weighted imaging or elevated myocardial T2 relaxation time) and at least one T1-based criterion (late gadolinium enhancement, increased myocardial T1 relaxation time, or extracellular volume fraction).

AHA/ACC/ESC guidelines reserve endomyocardial biopsy for specific clinical scenarios: new-onset heart failure of < 2 weeks' duration associated with hemodynamic compromise, or heart failure of 2 weeks to 3 months with ventricular arrhythmias, conduction block, or failure to respond to standard therapy within 1-2 weeks.

Giant cell myocarditis carries a median survival of < 6 months without transplantation; Cooper et al. demonstrated that combined aggressive immunosuppression (cyclosporine, corticosteroids, and azathioprine or anti-thymocyte globulin) prolonged transplant-free survival to 12.3 months.

Routine immunosuppression is not recommended for mild lymphocytic myocarditis with preserved ejection fraction; management consists of standard guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure, arrhythmia surveillance, and strict avoidance of competitive exercise for 3 to 6 months.

page.standard_overview: Acute myocarditis represents myocardial inflammation precipitated predominantly by viral infections, autoimmune reactions, or immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Initial evaluation requires high-sensitivity cardiac troponin, 12-lead ECG, echocardiography, and multiparametric cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR; updated Lake Louise Criteria). In hemodynamically stable patients, supportive therapy with guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT: ACEi/ARB and beta-blockers) and physical rest for 3 to 6 months forms the management foundation. In fulminant myocarditis manifesting as cardiogenic shock, life-threatening ventricular arrhythmias, or advanced heart block, emergency mechanical circulatory support (ECMO, Impella) and endomyocardial biopsy (EMB) to detect giant cell or eosinophilic myocarditis for targeted immunosuppression are life-saving.

standard_knowledge.claim: The 2018 Updated Lake Louise CMR Criteria require both myocardial edema (elevated T2 signal or T2 mapping) and myocardial injury/necrosis (increased extracellular volume fraction, elevated native T1, or late gadolinium enhancement) for diagnostic confirmation.

European Society of Cardiology (ESC) guidelines recommend standard guideline-directed heart failure therapy for systolic dysfunction, avoidance of NSAIDs in acute myocardial inflammation due to increased mortality in animal models, and exercise abstinence for 3-6 months.

The AHA scientific statement specifies that patients with fulminant myocarditis refractory to pharmacological inotropes should receive early temporary mechanical circulatory support (VA-ECMO or microaxial ventricular assist devices) as a bridge to recovery or transplant.

In immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-associated myocarditis, early high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone (1,000 mg/day for 3 days) followed by rapid immunosuppressive intensification (abatacept, tofacitinib, or ATG) in refractory cases significantly mitigates the > 25-50% fatality rate.

page.standard_overview: Acute necrotizing pancreatitis occurs in approximately 20% of acute pancreatitis episodes and carries significant morbidity and mortality, particularly when secondary bacterial infection develops. The landmark PANTER trial revolutionized surgical dogma by establishing the 'step-up' approach—initiating treatment with percutaneous or endoscopic catheter drainage and reserving minimally invasive retroperitoneal necrosectomy (VARD) only for patients who fail to improve clinically. Compared to open necrosectomy, the step-up strategy slashes new-onset multi-organ failure and systemic complications by two-thirds and eliminates major abdominal wall hernias.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the landmark Dutch PANTER randomized trial (88 patients), the minimally invasive step-up approach reduced the composite endpoint of major complications or death by 43% compared with primary open necrosectomy, driven by lower rates of new-onset multi-organ failure (12% vs 40%).
Over one-third of patients (35%) treated in the step-up arm of the PANTER trial were successfully cured by percutaneous catheter drainage alone, avoiding surgical necrosectomy entirely.

The randomized TENSION trial demonstrated that an endoscopic step-up approach (transluminal endoscopic drainage followed by endoscopic necrosectomy) was comparable to the surgical step-up approach in mortality and major morbidity, with fewer pancreaticocutaneous fistulae and shorter hospital stays.

International Association of Pancreatology / American Pancreatic Association (IAP/APA) guidelines recommend delaying invasive drainage or debridement until walled-off necrosis (WON) has matured, typically at least 4 weeks after symptom onset, unless rapid clinical collapse dictates emergency drainage.

page.standard_overview: Acute otitis media (AOM) is a rapid-onset middle ear infection characterized by erythema, purulent middle ear effusion, and distinct bulging of the tympanic membrane. According to American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and NICE guidelines, diagnostic precision is paramount to combat inappropriate antimicrobial overuse. Watchful waiting (observation with analgesia for 48-72 hours) is recommended in children >= 2 years with mild unilateral AOM, while immediate antibiotic treatment (high-dose amoxicillin 80-90 mg/kg/day) is reserved for severe illness, children < 6 months, bilateral disease in children < 2 years, or otorrhea.

standard_knowledge.claim: AAP clinical guidelines emphasize that rigorous diagnosis of AOM requires moderate-to-severe bulging of the tympanic membrane or new-onset otorrhea not due to acute otitis externa, distinguishing AOM from uncomplicated otitis media with effusion (OME).

First-line antimicrobial therapy for confirmed bacterial AOM without penicillin allergy is high-dose amoxicillin (80-90 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses), ensuring adequate middle ear penetration against penicillin-nonsusceptible Streptococcus pneumoniae.

Amoxicillin-clavulanate (90 mg/kg/day amoxicillin component with 6.4 mg/kg/day clavulanate) is indicated if the patient has received amoxicillin within the preceding 30 days, has concurrent purulent conjunctivitis (otitis-conjunctivitis syndrome due to nontypeable H. influenzae), or is unresponsive to initial amoxicillin after 48-72 hours.

Routine observation (watchful waiting) with structured pain control for 48 hours without upfront antibiotics is safe in children >= 2 years with mild unilateral symptoms and reliable follow-up, reducing antibiotic exposure without increasing mastoiditis rates.

page.standard_overview: Acute pancreatitis is an acute inflammatory process of the pancreas diagnosed by fulfilling at least two of three criteria: characteristic epigastric abdominal pain radiating to the back, serum lipase or amylase elevated >= 3 times the upper limit of normal, and characteristic cross-sectional abdominal imaging findings. Under the Revised Atlanta Classification, pancreatitis is stratified into mild (no organ failure or local complications), moderately severe (transient organ failure < 48 hours or local complications), and severe (persistent organ failure > 48 hours). Management focuses on etiology identification, goal-directed moderate fluid resuscitation, and early enteral nutrition.

standard_knowledge.claim: Diagnosis under the Revised Atlanta Classification requires at least 2 of 3 features: (1) characteristic epigastric pain radiating to the back; (2) serum lipase or amylase > 3x upper limit of normal; (3) contrast CT, MRI, or transabdominal ultrasound demonstrating pancreatitis.

Persistent organ failure (> 48 hours)—defined using the modified Marshall scoring system for cardiovascular (hypotension), renal (elevated creatinine), or respiratory (decreased PaO2/FiO2) systems—is the primary determinant of mortality in severe acute pancreatitis.

The international multicenter WATERFALL trial proved that aggressive fluid resuscitation (20 mL/kg bolus followed by 3 mL/kg/h) resulted in a three-fold higher rate of fluid overload (20.5% vs 6.3%) without improving clinical outcomes compared to moderate fluid resuscitation (10 mL/kg bolus in hypovolemic patients followed by 1.5 mL/kg/h).

IAP/APA guidelines recommend early transabdominal ultrasound in all patients to identify gallstones, and early oral refeeding with low-fat solid or liquid diet as soon as abdominal pain is improving and ileus has resolved.

page.standard_overview: Fluid stewardship and nutritional support have undergone a paradigm shift in acute pancreatitis management. The historic practice of aggressive volume resuscitation ('forced hydration') was conclusively refuted by the landmark WATERFALL trial, establishing goal-directed moderate fluid resuscitation with balanced crystalloids (Ringer's lactate) as the modern standard. Similarly, the historic dogma of 'putting the pancreas to rest' via prolonged fasting has been replaced by early enteral nutrition: starting oral feeding immediately in mild pancreatitis and initiating enteral tube feeding (nasogastric or nasojejunal) within 24-72 hours in severe disease, preserving gut mucosal integrity and preventing infected pancreatic necrosis.

standard_knowledge.claim: The WATERFALL randomized trial showed that aggressive hydration doubled the incidence of fluid overload without accelerating clinical resolution; guidelines now advise moderate Ringer's lactate resuscitation (1.5 mL/kg/h maintenance after 10 mL/kg bolus only if hypovolemic).

In mild acute pancreatitis, immediate oral refeeding with a low-fat solid or soft diet is safe, reduces length of hospital stay by 1.5 to 2 days, and does not increase pain relapse compared to gradual step-up liquid regimens.

The multicenter Dutch PYTHON randomized trial demonstrated that very early nasoenteric tube feeding (within 24 hours) did not reduce infected necrosis or death compared to an on-demand strategy allowing oral diet at 72 hours in predicted severe pancreatitis, with 69% of patients tolerating oral food without needing a feeding tube.

Enteral nutrition is vastly superior to total parenteral nutrition (TPN), significantly reducing infectious complications, systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), multi-organ failure, and overall mortality by preserving intestinal barrier function.

page.standard_overview: Critically ill patients with severe acute pancreatitis in the ICU suffer high mortality (20-30%) driven by a biphasic clinical trajectory: early multi-organ failure from massive systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS), followed by late sepsis from infected pancreatic necrosis. Early bedside risk stratification utilizing the Bedside Index for Severity in Acute Pancreatitis (BISAP) or APACHE-II score identifies patients at risk of rapid deterioration. Management centers on lung-protective ventilation, restrictive fluid therapy after initial stabilization, avoiding prophylactic antibiotics or routine probiotics (disproven in PROPATRIA), and multidisciplinary coordination.

standard_knowledge.claim: The BISAP score (BUN > 25 mg/dL, Impaired mental status, SIRS >= 2 criteria, Age > 60, Pleural effusion) provides simple, accurate prognostic stratification within 24 hours, with scores >= 3 correlating with a > 7-to-12-fold increase in mortality.

Routine administration of prophylactic systemic antibiotics for sterile necrotizing pancreatitis is not recommended by IAP/APA guidelines, as randomized trials demonstrate no reduction in infected necrosis or mortality, but an increased risk of multi-drug resistant fungal superinfections.

The PROPATRIA multicenter randomized trial revealed that prophylactic probiotic administration in predicted severe acute pancreatitis significantly increased bowel ischemia and nearly doubled all-cause mortality (16% vs 6%), leading to a strict black-box contraindication against prophylactic probiotics.

Intra-abdominal hypertension (IAH, intra-abdominal pressure >= 12 mmHg) and abdominal compartment syndrome (ACS, IAP > 20 mmHg with new organ failure) are frequent in severe pancreatitis; protocolized decompression (nasogastric drainage, sedation, paracentesis, neuromuscular blockade) is critical to preserve renal and splanchnic perfusion.

page.standard_overview: Acute pericarditis is diagnosed by fulfilling at least two of four cardinal criteria: pleuritic chest pain, pericardial friction rub, new widespread PR-segment depression or ST-segment elevation, and new or worsening pericardial effusion. High-dose NSAIDs (e.g., ibuprofen 600-800 mg TID or indomethacin 50 mg TID) combined with weight-adjusted colchicine (0.5 mg BID, or 0.5 mg daily if weight < 70 kg) for 3 months represent the first-line evidence-based regimen. The landmark ICAP and COPE trials proved that adding colchicine halves recurrence rates and accelerates symptom remission, whereas systemic corticosteroids should be avoided as first-line therapy due to increased recurrence risk.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the landmark ICAP randomized trial (240 patients), adding colchicine (0.5 mg daily or BID for 3 months) to standard anti-inflammatory therapy halved the rate of recurrent pericarditis from 37.5% to 16.7% (relative risk reduction 56%) and significantly reduced symptom persistence at 72 hours.

The COPE trial confirmed in first-episode acute pericarditis that colchicine plus aspirin significantly reduced 18-month recurrence rates compared to aspirin alone (10.7% vs 32.3%) and shortened time to clinical remission.

The 2015 ESC Pericardial Diseases Guidelines recommend high-dose NSAIDs (ibuprofen 600-800 mg TID or aspirin 750-1000 mg TID) with gastroprotection plus colchicine for 3 months as first-line therapy, with tapering guided by symptom resolution and C-reactive protein (CRP) normalization.

Systemic corticosteroids are classified as second-line therapy for patients with contraindications or intolerance to NSAIDs/colchicine, or specific autoimmune etiologies; upfront steroid use independently predicts disease chronicity and multiple relapses.

page.standard_overview: Acute phosphate nephropathy is a form of kidney injury caused by the deposition of calcium phosphate crystals within the renal tubules and interstitium, typically following the ingestion of oral sodium phosphate (OSP) bowel purgatives for colonoscopy. Patients present with either acute kidney injury shortly after exposure or insidious, irreversible chronic kidney disease diagnosed weeks to months later. Advanced age, pre-existing chronic kidney disease (CKD), volume depletion, and concurrent therapy with renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibitors, NSAIDs, or diuretics are major risk factors; PEG-based bowel preparations are the safer standard of care.

standard_knowledge.claim: Markowitz et al. established that acute phosphate nephropathy is characterized histopathologically by abundant calcium phosphate tubular deposition, tubular epithelial atrophy, and interstitial fibrosis in the absence of significant glomerular disease.

The clinical course is frequently biphasic: an early acute asymptomatic rise in creatinine followed by progressive irreversible renal dysfunction, with fewer than 20% of affected patients recovering back to their baseline serum creatinine.

Major clinical risk factors include baseline CKD (eGFR < 60 mL/min/1.73m2), volume contraction, hypertension, advanced age (> 65 years), and concurrent medications that compromise renal hemodynamics: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, and NSAIDs.

KDIGO and FDA guidelines strongly discourage the use of oral sodium phosphate formulations for colonoscopy bowel cleansing in patients with CKD, congestive heart failure, liver cirrhosis, or electrolyte disturbances, mandating safer isosmotic polyethylene glycol (PEG) solutions.

page.standard_overview: Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a medical emergency driven by the t(15;17)(q24.1;q21.2) chromosomal translocation encoding the PML::RARA fusion oncoprotein, leading to severe consumptive coagulopathy (disseminated intravascular coagulation and hyperfibrinolysis) and catastrophic hemorrhage. Immediate initiation of all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) upon morphological suspicion—before cytogenetic confirmation—is mandatory. In standard- and intermediate-risk APL (WBC <= 10,000/uL), chemotherapy-free dual differentiation therapy with ATRA and arsenic trioxide (ATO) is the curative standard of care, achieving 95-98% complete remission and event-free survival rates superior to chemotherapy.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the landmark Italian-German APL0406 randomized phase 3 trial (Lo-Coco et al.), ATRA plus arsenic trioxide (ATO) proved non-inferior and statistically superior to ATRA plus idarubicin chemotherapy in low-to-intermediate risk APL, achieving 97% vs 80% 2-year event-free survival and zero secondary myelodysplasia.

The UK NCRI AML17 randomized trial confirmed that ATRA plus ATO significantly reduced relapse rates and improved 4-year event-free survival compared to standard chemotherapy across all risk groups, with lower treatment-related mortality.

European LeukemiaNet (ELN) guidelines emphasize that ATRA must be started immediately at the earliest clinical suspicion of APL without waiting for molecular confirmation, alongside aggressive platelet and cryoprecipitate transfusions to maintain fibrinogen > 150 mg/dL and platelets > 50,000/uL.

Differentiation syndrome (fever, dyspnea, pulmonary infiltrates, pleural effusions, peripheral edema) occurs in up to 25% of patients during ATRA/ATO therapy; immediate prompt initiation of intravenous dexamethasone (10 mg BID) halts progression without necessitating ATRA/ATO discontinuation unless severe multi-organ failure ensues.

page.standard_overview: Acute psychosis is characterized by hallucinations, delusions, thought disorganization, and loss of reality testing, precipitated by primary psychiatric disorders (schizophrenia, bipolar mania), substance intoxication/withdrawal, or underlying medical illness (encephalitis, endocrine disorders, systemic lupus). Initial management prioritizes safety, medical clearance, and calm, structured non-coercive verbal de-escalation. Pharmacotherapy with oral second-generation antipsychotics (e.g., olanzapine, risperidone, aripiprazole) represents the first-line evidence-based standard, while rapid tranquilization protocols are reserved for severe aggression threatening imminent injury.

standard_knowledge.claim: NICE clinical guideline CG178 recommends oral second-generation antipsychotics as first-line therapy for acute psychosis, advising individualized choice based on side-effect profiles (metabolic vs extrapyramidal vs hyperprolactinemia) in collaborative discussion with the patient.

A comprehensive Cochrane network meta-analysis of 402 randomized trials (Leucht et al., Lancet) established that all antipsychotics significantly reduce psychotic symptoms compared to placebo, with small differences in efficacy favoring clozapine, amisulpride, and olanzapine, but marked differences in weight gain, sedation, and extrapyramidal side effects.

The TREC randomized trials on rapid tranquilization in acute violent psychotic agitation demonstrated that intramuscular olanzapine or haloperidol combined with promethazine achieved rapid, safe tranquilization within 15-30 minutes with significantly fewer respiratory depressions than intramuscular benzodiazepines alone.

Physical restraints should be an absolute intervention of last resort, with continuous 1-to-1 nursing observation and regular vital sign/airway monitoring every 15 minutes to prevent restraint-related asphyxia and positional death.

page.standard_overview: Acute pulmonary edema secondary to decompensated heart failure represents an extreme emergency characterized by alveolar flooding, severe dyspnea, tachypnea, hypoxemia, and diaphoresis. Management requires immediate upright positioning, non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIV: CPAP or BiPAP), and aggressive peripheral vasodilatation with intravenous nitrates (nitroglycerin or isosorbide dinitrate) in hypertensive presentations. Historic routine administration of intravenous morphine is now strongly discouraged due to increased ICU admission, intubation, and mortality rates. Intravenous loop diuretics should be dosed dynamically, with ultrafiltration reserved for refractory diuretic resistance.

standard_knowledge.claim: The randomized multicenter 3CPO trial (1,069 patients) showed that non-invasive ventilation (either CPAP or BiPAP) induced rapid physiological improvements in dyspnea, acidosis, and hypercapnia compared to standard oxygen therapy, with CPAP being the simplest and most cost-effective initial modality.

A large-scale analysis from the ADHERE registry (147,362 patients) demonstrated that intravenous morphine administration in acute cardiogenic pulmonary edema was independently associated with a near-doubling of in-hospital mortality (OR 1.8), higher intubation rates, and prolonged ICU stay.

The UNLOAD trial showed that early venous ultrafiltration in hypervolemic heart failure produced greater weight loss and fluid removal with significantly lower 90-day heart failure rehospitalizations compared to continuous intravenous diuretics.

The 2021 ESC Heart Failure Guidelines emphasize high-dose intravenous vasodilators (nitrates) as first-line therapy in acute hypertensive pulmonary edema (systolic BP > 110 mmHg) to rapidly reduce cardiac preload and afterload, while restricting opioids to palliative end-of-life care.

page.standard_overview: Acute red eye is one of the most frequent ophthalmic presentations in primary care and emergency departments. Accurate differential diagnosis hinges on distinguishing benign, self-limiting superficial conditions (viral/bacterial conjunctivitis, episcleritis, subconjunctival hemorrhage) from sight-threatening emergencies requiring immediate ophthalmologic consultation: acute angle-closure glaucoma, acute anterior uveitis, bacterial/fungal keratitis, and endophthalmitis. The presence of 'red flag' symptoms—severe ocular pain, decreased visual acuity, photophobia, ciliary flush (perilimbal injection), corneal opacity, or a fixed mid-dilated pupil—mandates urgent specialist evaluation.

standard_knowledge.claim: American Academy of Ophthalmology (AAO) Preferred Practice Patterns emphasize identifying red flags: deep boring pain, photophobia, reduced visual acuity, ciliary flush, and corneal abnormalities, which rule out benign conjunctivitis and require immediate specialist care.

Acute angle-closure glaucoma presents with severe unilateral ocular pain, headache, nausea, steamy/hazy cornea, and a fixed mid-dilated pupil, requiring emergency medical lowering of intraocular pressure (timolol, apraclonidine, IV acetazolamide, and topical pilocarpine) followed by bilateral laser peripheral iridotomy.

Corneal fluorescein staining under cobalt blue light is essential in contact lens wearers presenting with acute red eye to detect Pseudomonas or Acanthamoeba keratitis; topical corticosteroids must never be prescribed empirically without slit-lamp examination due to catastrophic corneal melting or herpes simplex worsening.

Viral conjunctivitis (adenovirus) is characterized by watery discharge, preauricular lymphadenopathy, and follicular conjunctival response; it is self-limiting and requires strict hand hygiene rather than topical antibiotic therapy.

page.standard_overview: Acute respiratory failure is categorized into Type 1 (hypoxemic: PaO2 < 60 mmHg [8 kPa] with normal or low PaCO2) and Type 2 (hypercapnic: PaCO2 > 45-50 mmHg [6-6.5 kPa] with respiratory acidemia). Type 1 failure results from ventilation-perfusion mismatch, intrapulmonary shunt, or diffusion impairment (e.g., ARDS, pneumonia, pulmonary edema), while Type 2 failure reflects ventilatory pump failure, central hypoventilation, or neuromuscular weakness (e.g., severe COPD, myasthenia gravis, drug overdose). Conservative oxygenation targeting SpO2 92-96% (or 88-92% in patients at hypercapnic risk) avoids oxygen toxicity, while High-Flow Nasal Cannula (HFNC) and non-invasive ventilation provide first-line advanced support.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the landmark FLORALI trial (Frat et al., NEJM), high-flow nasal cannula (HFNC) oxygen therapy significantly reduced 90-day mortality (hazard ratio 0.42) and ventilator days compared to standard oxygen or non-invasive ventilation in patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (PaO2/FiO2 <= 300).

Multicenter randomized trials (LOCO2 and HOT-ICU) demonstrated that liberal oxygenation strategies targeting supranormal PaO2 levels do not improve survival and can increase mesenteric and myocardial ischemia, establishing a conservative oxygenation target (PaO2 55-80 mmHg or SpO2 92-96%).

British Thoracic Society (BTS) emergency oxygen guidelines recommend target SpO2 ranges of 94-98% for most acutely ill patients, but a restricted target of 88-92% for patients at risk of hypercapnic respiratory failure (COPD, neuromuscular disease, morbid obesity hypoventilation).

For acute hypercapnic respiratory failure secondary to COPD exacerbation (pH < 7.35 and PaCO2 > 45 mmHg), non-invasive positive pressure ventilation (NIV/BiPAP) reduces the need for intubation by > 60% and reduces hospital mortality by half.

page.standard_overview: Acute severe asthma is a life-threatening exacerbation defined clinically by peak expiratory flow (PEF) 33-50% of predicted/best, inability to complete sentences in one breath, respiratory rate >= 25 bpm, or heart rate >= 110 bpm. Life-threatening features ('silent chest', cyanosis, exhaustion, altered consciousness, PEF < 33%, or normal/elevated PaCO2) require immediate ICU escalation. First-line pharmacotherapy consists of high-dose inhaled short-acting beta-2 agonists (salbutamol) combined with ipratropium bromide via oxygen-driven nebulization, early systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone 40-50 mg or IV hydrocortisone), and intravenous magnesium sulfate.

standard_knowledge.claim: The multicenter 3Mg randomized trial demonstrated that a single infusion of intravenous magnesium sulfate (1.2 to 2 g over 20 minutes) produces rapid, clinically meaningful bronchodilation and reduces hospital admission in patients with acute severe asthma refractory to initial nebulized therapies.

British Thoracic Society (BTS/SIGN) and GINA guidelines classify asthma exacerbations into Moderate, Severe (PEF 33-50%, RR >= 25, HR >= 110, unable to complete sentences), and Life-threatening (PEF < 33%, SpO2 < 92%, silent chest, cyanosis, exhaustion, confusion, or normal/elevated PaCO2).

Early administration of systemic corticosteroids within 1 hour of emergency presentation significantly reduces hospital admission rates and prevents relapse; oral prednisolone (40-50 mg daily for 5 days) is as effective as intravenous corticosteroids unless the patient is unable to swallow or vomiting.

A 'normal' or rising PaCO2 (> 40-42 mmHg [5.3 kPa]) in an acutely tachypneic asthma patient indicates severe respiratory muscle exhaustion and imminent arrest, requiring immediate senior anesthesia consultation for endotracheal intubation.

page.standard_overview: Acute thrombolytic therapy with recombinant tissue plasminogen activators (alteplase, tenecteplase) offers rapid reperfusion in life-threatening thrombotic emergencies, but carries catastrophic intracranial hemorrhage risks requiring strict patient selection. In acute ischemic stroke, IV alteplase or tenecteplase within 4.5 hours of symptom onset preserves neurological functional independence (NINDS, ECASS-3). In massive pulmonary embolism with hemodynamic instability, systemic thrombolysis reduces all-cause mortality, whereas in intermediate-high risk PE (PEITHO trial), rescue thrombolysis is restricted to hemodynamic decompensation. In STEMI, thrombolysis is indicated within 12 hours when primary PCI cannot be achieved within 120 minutes (STREAM trial).

standard_knowledge.claim: The landmark NINDS rt-PA Stroke Study proved that intravenous alteplase administered within 3 hours of ischemic stroke onset resulted in a 30% absolute increase in patients achieving minimal or no disability at 3 months (OR 1.7) despite a 6.4% symptomatic intracranial hemorrhage rate.

The multinational PEITHO randomized trial (1,006 patients with intermediate-high-risk PE) showed that tenecteplase significantly prevented hemodynamic collapse (2.6% vs 5.6%) but tripled major extracranial bleeding and ten-folded hemorrhagic stroke (2.0% vs 0.2%), establishing that routine thrombolysis should be withheld in normotensive intermediate-risk PE until overt shock develops.

The STREAM randomized trial established that in STEMI patients presenting within 3 hours who cannot undergo primary PCI within 60-90 minutes, pre-hospital fibrinolysis with half-dose tenecteplase (in patients >= 75 years) followed by timely catheterization yielded equivalent clinical efficacy to primary PCI.

Absolute contraindications to systemic thrombolysis include prior intracranial hemorrhage, known structural cerebral vascular lesion or neoplasm, ischemic stroke within 3 months, active internal bleeding, and recent severe head/facial trauma within 3 months.

page.standard_overview: Acute allograft rejection presents as acute graft dysfunction categorized histologically under the international Banff classification into T cell-mediated rejection (TCMR) and antibody-mediated rejection (ABMR). Indication allograft biopsy is the definitive gold standard to differentiate rejection from calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity, BK polyomavirus nephropathy, or acute tubular necrosis. TCMR responds promptly to high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone pulses (500-1,000 mg daily for 3 days), with anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG) reserved for steroid-resistant or high-grade vascular rejection (Banff II/III). Conversely, ABMR—driven by donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies (DSA) and microvascular inflammation—requires multimodal desensitization combining therapeutic plasma exchange, intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and optimization of baseline immunosuppression.

standard_knowledge.claim: KDIGO clinical practice guidelines for kidney transplant recipients mandate prompt percutaneous core biopsy prior to treating acute allograft dysfunction to distinguish TCMR from ABMR and infection.

First-line therapy for acute TCMR consists of intravenous methylprednisolone (500-1000 mg/day for 3 days), which reverses > 80% of Grade IA/IB rejection episodes; steroid-resistant TCMR or vascular rejection (Banff II/III) warrants rabbit anti-thymocyte globulin (rATG).

Acute ABMR is diagnosed by the triad of graft dysfunction, histological microvascular inflammation (peritubular capillaritis/glomerulitis or C4d deposition), and circulating donor-specific anti-HLA antibodies (DSA).

Management of acute active ABMR centers on rapid removal and neutralization of donor-specific antibodies using therapeutic plasma exchange (PLEX) coupled with high-dose intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG 1-2 g/kg).

page.standard_overview: Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis—defined by localized colonic inflammation without perforation, abscess, fistula, or obstruction (modified Hinchey Stage 0 or Ia)—has undergone an evidence-based demedicalization. Landmark randomized clinical trials (AVOD and DIABOLO) demonstrated that observational management without antibiotics yields equivalent healing, symptom resolution, complication rates, and recurrence compared to routine antibiotic therapy in immunocompetent patients. Contemporary WSES and AGA guidelines recommend symptomatic outpatient care with paracetamol and clear liquids, reserving antibiotics strictly for patients with systemic sepsis, immunosuppression, severe comorbidities, or high-risk features.

standard_knowledge.claim: The landmark Swedish AVOD randomized trial (623 patients) demonstrated that antibiotic treatment for acute uncomplicated diverticulitis did not shorten hospital stay, decrease complications (1.0% vs 1.9%), or reduce 1-year recurrences (16% in both arms).

The Dutch DIABOLO trial confirmed that observational management without antibiotics resulted in identical 6-month recovery rates, complication rates, and healthcare costs compared to a 10-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate.

The 2020 World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) guidelines recommend an observational strategy without routine antibiotics for immunocompetent patients with uncomplicated diverticulitis (Stage 0/Ia) and no signs of systemic inflammatory response.

Antibiotic therapy (e.g., oral amoxicillin-clavulanate or ciprofloxacin plus metronidazole) should be strictly reserved for high-risk patients: immunosuppression, significant comorbidities (cirrhosis, CKD, uncontrolled diabetes), pregnancy, persistent fever, or CRP > 140 mg/L.

page.standard_overview: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) pharmacotherapy is guided by comprehensive comparative efficacy and tolerability data across pediatric and adult cohorts. In a landmark network meta-analysis of 133 randomized controlled trials (Cortese et al., Lancet Psychiatry), methylphenidate emerged as the first-choice medication in children and adolescents due to superior efficacy and favorable tolerability, whereas amphetamines (lisdexamfetamine) demonstrated superior efficacy in adults. Non-stimulant alternatives (atomoxetine, guanfacine, clonidine) represent valuable second-line options for patients with substance use disorders, intolerable stimulant-induced anxiety, or severe cardiovascular contraindications.

standard_knowledge.claim: A comprehensive network meta-analysis of 133 double-blind RCTs (Cortese et al., Lancet Psychiatry) established methylphenidate as the first-line medication for children/adolescents (highest balance of efficacy and tolerability), whereas amphetamines are the first-line pharmacotherapy in adults.

NICE Guideline NG87 recommends central nervous system stimulants (methylphenidate or lisdexamfetamine) as first-line pharmacological treatment for ADHD after environmental and behavioral modifications have been implemented.

Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug requiring enzymatic cleavage by red blood cell aminopeptidases to release active d-amphetamine, conferring a smoother pharmacokinetic profile and significantly reduced diversion/abuse potential compared to immediate-release stimulants.

Cardiovascular safety baseline monitoring requires blood pressure, heart rate, and routine personal/family cardiac history screening; routine pre-treatment ECG is indicated only if personal symptoms (syncope, palpitations) or family history of sudden unexplained cardiac death < 40 years are present.

page.standard_overview: Adhesional small bowel obstruction (ASBO) accounts for over 60-70% of mechanical bowel obstructions in patients with prior abdominopelvic surgery. Management requires distinguishing uncomplicated partial/complete obstruction from closed-loop obstruction, ischemia, or strangulation requiring emergency laparotomy. The World Society of Emergency Surgery (WSES) Bologna guidelines endorse conservative management (nasogastric tube decompression, intravenous fluids, and nil per os) combined with a water-soluble contrast (Gastrografin) challenge. Passage of Gastrografin into the colon within 24 hours on abdominal radiography confirms resolution of obstruction in over 90% of cases and reduces hospital stay.

standard_knowledge.claim: The Bologna guidelines of the WSES emphasize that contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen/pelvis is the diagnostic standard to differentiate simple adhesional SBO from closed-loop obstruction, strangulation, or bowel ischemia.
In the absence of peritonitis, strangulation, or ischemia, conservative management with nasogastric decompression and intravenous fluid resuscitation is successful in 70-80% of ASBO cases.

The water-soluble contrast medium (WSCM; Gastrografin) challenge is both diagnostic and therapeutic: transit of contrast into the cecum within 24 hours predicts successful non-operative resolution with > 95% sensitivity and reduces hospital length of stay by 2-3 days.

Failure of water-soluble contrast to reach the colon by 24 hours, persistent high-volume nasogastric output (> 500 mL/day at 48-72 hours), fever, localized peritonitis, or leukocytosis mandates prompt surgical exploration (laparoscopy or laparotomy) to prevent bowel gangrene.

page.standard_overview: Adrenal crisis is an acute life-threatening manifestation of severe absolute or relative glucocorticoid deficiency characterized by profound hypotension refractory to fluid resuscitation and vasopressors, hypovolemic shock, fever, hypoglycemia, and electrolyte derangements (hyponatremia, hyperkalemia). Management requires immediate administration of parenteral hydrocortisone (100 mg IV bolus followed by 200 mg/24h continuous infusion or 50 mg IV every 6 hours) and rapid isotonic saline resuscitation. Diagnostic testing must never delay steroid administration. Educating patients on 'sick-day rules'—doubling or tripling oral steroid doses during illness and carrying emergency intramuscular hydrocortisone kits—is life-saving.

standard_knowledge.claim: Endocrine Society clinical guidelines mandate immediate parenteral hydrocortisone (100 mg IV stat bolus followed by 200 mg over 24 hours) and isotonic saline fluid resuscitation without waiting for laboratory confirmation.

A large multicenter European study by Hahner et al. demonstrated that adrenal crises occur at an incidence of 6-8 per 100 patient-years, with gastrointestinal infections and fever being the leading precipitation triggers.

During active treatment of adrenal crisis with stress-dose hydrocortisone (>= 50 mg/day), mineralocorticoid (fludrocortisone) replacement is redundant and unnecessary because high-dose hydrocortisone provides maximal mineralocorticoid receptor saturation.

Sick day rules prevent crises: patients must double their oral maintenance hydrocortisone dose for fever > 38°C or moderate illness, triple the dose for fever > 39°C, and self-administer 100 mg intramuscular hydrocortisone immediately if vomiting or severe diarrhea prevents oral absorption.

page.standard_overview: An adrenal incidentaloma is an asymptomatic adrenal mass >= 1 cm discovered unexpectedly on abdominal imaging performed for an unrelated indication. Evaluation centers on two cardinal clinical questions: (1) Is the mass malignant (adrenocortical carcinoma or metastasis)? and (2) Is the mass hormonally active? Joint European Society of Endocrinology (ESE) and ENSAT clinical guidelines recommend unenhanced CT attenuation measurement as the primary imaging differentiator: homogeneous lesions with attenuation <= 10 Hounsfield Units (HU) are conclusively benign lipid-rich adenomas requiring no further imaging follow-up if non-functioning.

standard_knowledge.claim: ESE/ENSAT clinical guidelines recommend that all patients with an adrenal incidentaloma undergo initial biochemical testing: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test to exclude autonomous cortisol secretion, plasma or urinary metanephrines to exclude pheochromocytoma, and aldosterone-to-renin ratio in hypertensives.
Unenhanced CT attenuation <= 10 Hounsfield Units (HU) possesses near 100% sensitivity for lipid-rich benign adenomas; homogeneous lesions <= 4 cm with HU <= 10 require no repeated imaging follow-up.

Autonomous Cortisol Secretion (ACS; post-dexamethasone serum cortisol > 50 nmol/L [1.8 ug/dL] without overt Cushingoid features) is present in up to 15-20% of incidentalomas and is associated with increased hypertension, type 2 diabetes, vertebral fractures, and cardiovascular mortality.

Adrenalectomy is recommended for hormonally active tumors (pheochromocytoma, primary aldosteronism with unilateral disease, Cushing syndrome) and indeterminate masses > 4 cm with suspicious malignant features (heterogeneity, necrosis, HU > 20).

page.standard_overview: Comprehensive evaluation of adrenal incidentalomas balances meticulous identification of functional and malignant tumors against avoiding excessive follow-up for harmless benign lesions. Under the updated 2023 ESE/ENSAT guidelines, non-functioning, homogeneous adrenal adenomas < 4 cm with unenhanced attenuation <= 10 HU require neither repeated imaging nor repeated hormonal testing. For indeterminate lesions (unenhanced HU > 10), delayed contrast-enhanced CT with absolute percentage washout (> 60%) or chemical shift MRI is utilized to evaluate lipid content, and multidisciplinary adrenal tumor board review is indicated for lesions displaying malignant growth.

standard_knowledge.claim: The 2023 updated ESE/ENSAT guidelines reaffirm that if an adrenal lesion is < 4 cm, homogeneous, has unenhanced attenuation <= 10 HU, and is non-functional on 1 mg DST and metanephrine testing, no further imaging or endocrine surveillance is warranted.

For lipid-poor lesions (unenhanced HU > 10), delayed contrast-enhanced CT demonstrating an absolute percentage washout (APW) > 60% or relative percentage washout (RPW) > 40% at 15 minutes confirms a benign adenoma.

Biochemical re-evaluation for developing Autonomous Cortisol Secretion (MACS) is recommended annually only if the patient develops new or worsening hypertension, dyslipidemia, impaired glucose tolerance, or osteoporotic fractures.

Fine-needle aspiration (FNA) biopsy of an adrenal mass is contraindicated unless there is a known extra-adrenal primary malignancy, pheochromocytoma has been rigorously excluded by metanephrines, and confirmation of metastasis will directly alter systemic oncologic therapy.

page.standard_overview: Adrenal insufficiency encompasses primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease: adrenal cortex destruction, loss of both glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids, elevated ACTH) and secondary/tertiary adrenal insufficiency (hypothalamic-pituitary failure or exogenous steroid suppression, deficient ACTH, preserved mineralocorticoid secretion). Patients present insidiously with fatigue, weight loss, orthostatic hypotension, nausea, and in primary disease, cutaneous hyperpigmentation from pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) cleavage. Diagnosis requires morning serum cortisol and ACTH, followed by the standard short Synacthen (250 ug cosyntropin) stimulation test, where peak cortisol < 500 nmol/L (18 ug/dL) confirms the diagnosis.

standard_knowledge.claim: The standard 250 ug cosyntropin (short Synacthen) stimulation test is the diagnostic reference standard: peak serum cortisol < 500 nmol/L (18 ug/dL) at 30 or 60 minutes confirms adrenal insufficiency.

Plasma ACTH measured concurrently with morning cortisol differentiates primary (markedly elevated ACTH, usually > 2x upper limit of normal) from secondary/tertiary adrenal insufficiency (low or inappropriately normal ACTH).

In primary adrenal insufficiency, 21-hydroxylase autoantibodies confirm autoimmune adrenalitis (> 80-90% of cases in developed nations); adrenal CT is indicated if autoantibodies are negative to evaluate tuberculosis, hemorrhage, or infiltration.

Physiological glucocorticoid replacement consists of hydrocortisone 15-25 mg daily divided into 2-3 doses (highest dose upon waking) or oral cortisone acetate; primary disease additionally requires fludrocortisone (0.05-0.2 mg daily) titrated to seated/standing blood pressure and plasma renin activity.

page.standard_overview: Corticosteroid Insufficiency in Critical Illness (CIRCI) reflects dysregulated hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis signaling, altered cortisol metabolism, and systemic glucocorticoid tissue resistance during septic shock and critical illness. Landmark consensus guidelines from SCCM and ESICM advise against routine diagnostic cosyntropin stimulation testing to guide treatment. Instead, stress-dose hydrocortisone (200 mg/day administered as continuous IV infusion or 50 mg IV every 6 hours) is recommended strictly in septic shock patients who remain hemodynamically unstable despite adequate fluid resuscitation and escalating vasopressor therapy.

standard_knowledge.claim: Joint SCCM/ESICM consensus guidelines recommend against using the cosyntropin stimulation test (delta cortisol < 9 ug/dL) to identify CIRCI in septic shock, instead recommending empirical hydrocortisone based purely on clinical vasopressor refractoriness.

The landmark multicenter CORTICUS trial (Sprung et al., NEJM) demonstrated that hydrocortisone did not improve all-cause 28-day mortality in unselected septic shock patients, but significantly accelerated shock reversal compared to placebo.
Stress-dose hydrocortisone (200 mg/day) is recommended when norepinephrine or epinephrine requirements exceed 0.25 ug/kg/min for at least 4 hours despite adequate fluid resuscitation.

Continuous intravenous infusion of hydrocortisone (200 mg over 24 hours) results in better glycemic stability and fewer blood glucose fluctuations compared to repetitive intermittent intravenous boluses (50 mg every 6 hours).

page.standard_overview: Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) is a rare, aggressive malignancy carrying a 5-year survival of < 40-50%. Clinical presentation comprises symptoms of hormone excess (Cushing syndrome, virilization, feminization) in 60% of cases, abdominal pain/mass effect in 30%, or an incidental discovery. Staging utilizes the European Network for the Study of Adrenal Tumors (ENSAT) system (Stages I-IV). Complete surgical resection with negative margins (R0 en bloc adrenalectomy with lymphadenectomy) performed by high-volume endocrine surgeons is the sole curative modality. Adjuvant mitotane—an adrenocorticolytic oral agent—is recommended for patients at high risk of recurrence, while metastatic disease requires the EDP-M regimen.

standard_knowledge.claim: The international FIRM-ACT randomized phase 3 trial (Fassnacht et al., NEJM) established etoposide, doxorubicin, and cisplatin plus oral mitotane (EDP-M) as the first-line standard of care for advanced/metastatic ACC, demonstrating significantly superior response rates (23.2% vs 9.2%) and progression-free survival over streptozocin plus mitotane.

Complete macroscopic and microscopic surgical resection (R0 resection) by an experienced endocrine surgeon is the single most important factor determining long-term survival in localized ACC (ENSAT Stage I-III).
Adjuvant mitotane therapy for at least 2 years is recommended by ESE/ENSAT guidelines for patients at high risk of recurrence (ENSAT Stage III, R1 resection, or Ki-67 proliferation index > 10%).

Mitotane induces profound adrenal cortex destruction and CYP3A4 hepatic clearance, necessitating concurrent high-dose physiological glucocorticoid replacement (often 2-3x standard hydrocortisone doses) and close therapeutic drug monitoring to maintain target plasma levels (14-20 mg/L).

page.standard_overview: Eisenmenger syndrome represents the most extreme manifestation of pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) associated with adult congenital heart disease (ACHD), developing from a large uncorrected congenital systemic-to-pulmonary shunt (VSD, ASD, PDA). Sustained high pulmonary vascular flow leads to severe pulmonary vascular remodeling, elevated pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR), shunt reversal to right-to-left, chronic cyanosis, secondary erythrocytosis, and multi-organ sequelae. Primary corrective cardiac surgery is strictly contraindicated once irreversible Eisenmenger physiology is established. Management relies on pulmonary vasodilators (endothelin receptor antagonists, PDE-5 inhibitors), avoidance of dehydration or pregnancy, and restrictive phlebotomy indications.

standard_knowledge.claim: The landmark randomized BREATHE-5 trial demonstrated that oral bosentan (dual endothelin receptor antagonist) significantly reduced pulmonary vascular resistance and improved 6-minute walk distance without compromising systemic arterial oxygen saturation in Eisenmenger syndrome.

The 2020 ESC ACHD Guidelines emphasize that anatomical shunt repair or closure is absolute contraindicated in Eisenmenger syndrome, as the right-to-left shunt serves as an essential safety valve to preserve systemic cardiac output.

Secondary erythrocytosis in cyanotic ACHD is an adaptive physiological response to chronic tissue hypoxemia; routine prophylactic phlebotomy is contraindicated and induces severe iron-deficient microcytosis and hyperviscosity-related stroke.

Therapeutic phlebotomy (with isovolumetric isotonic saline replacement) is restricted strictly to patients with hematocrit > 65% presenting with severe hyperviscosity symptoms (headache, visual blurring, dizziness) in the absence of dehydration and iron deficiency.

page.standard_overview: Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD) is a rare systemic autoinflammatory disorder driven by dysregulated innate immunity, hyperactivation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, and massive overproduction of pro-inflammatory cytokines, specifically interleukin-1 (IL-1beta, IL-18) and interleukin-6 (IL-6). In patients with severe systemic features or steroid-refractory/steroid-dependent disease, targeted biologic inhibition with recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonists (anakinra, canakinumab) or IL-6 receptor antagonists (tocilizumab) produces rapid, profound clinical remission, normalizes hyperferritinemia, and halts progression to macrophage activation syndrome (MAS).

standard_knowledge.claim: A randomized placebo-controlled trial by Cavalli et al. proved that the IL-1 receptor antagonist anakinra (100 mg/day subcutaneously) achieved prompt, sustained clinical remission in over 70% of steroid-refractory AOSD patients, rapidly eliminating fever and systemic symptoms within 48-72 hours.

The randomized double-blind French trial by Puéchal et al. demonstrated that tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor antagonist) significantly improved systemic symptoms, lowered corticosteroid requirements, and controlled refractory polyarthritis in active AOSD.

International consensus guidelines recommend biologic initiation (IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitors) early in patients with inadequate response to corticosteroids (prednisone 0.5-1.0 mg/kg/day) or high-risk features (severe liver involvement, impending MAS) to avoid cumulative steroid toxicity.

Interleukin-1 blockade with anakinra is particularly effective for systemic manifestations (quotidian fevers, evanescent rash, serositis, hyperferritinemia), whereas IL-6 blockade with tocilizumab exhibits superior control over chronic erosive arthritis phenotypes.

page.standard_overview: Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD) is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring rigorous elimination of occult infections, hematologic malignancies (especially lymphoma), and other systemic autoimmune diseases. The Yamaguchi criteria represent the most widely validated and sensitive (93.5%) diagnostic framework, requiring at least five criteria with at least two major criteria: high quotidian fever (>= 39°C for >= 1 week), arthralgias/arthritis (>= 2 weeks), typical evanescent non-pruritic salmon-pink maculopapular rash, and leukocytosis (>= 10,000/uL with >= 80% granulocytes). Marked hyperferritinemia (> 5x ULN) with decreased glycosylated ferritin (< 20%) provides substantial corroborative diagnostic confirmation.

standard_knowledge.claim: Under the validated Yamaguchi criteria, diagnosis requires >= 5 criteria (with at least 2 major criteria): Major criteria include fever >= 39°C lasting >= 1 week, arthralgia/arthritis >= 2 weeks, typical salmon-pink maculopapular rash, and leukocytosis >= 10,000/uL (>= 80% neutrophils).
Minor Yamaguchi criteria include sore throat, lymphadenopathy and/or splenomegaly, abnormal liver enzymes (transaminitis), and negative antinuclear antibody (ANA) and rheumatoid factor (RF).

The Fautrel criteria introduced biological markers into diagnostic classification, incorporating extreme hyperferritinemia and glycosylated ferritin <= 20%, which provides high diagnostic specificity (98.5%) for AOSD.

A drop in the proportion of glycosylated ferritin (< 20%, normal 50-80%) in the setting of severe hyperferritinemia strongly supports AOSD and helps differentiate it from other systemic inflammatory or neoplastic disorders.

page.standard_overview: The clinical hallmark of Adult-Onset Still's Disease (AOSD) is the striking triad of high spiking quotidian fevers, an evanescent salmon-pink maculopapular rash that parallels febrile spikes, and extreme hyperferritinemia (frequently > 3,000 to > 50,000 ug/L). The most severe, life-threatening complication of AOSD is Macrophage Activation Syndrome (MAS), also known as secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (sHLH), characterized by uncontrolled cytokine storm, hemophagocytosis, paradoxical drop in ESR (due to consumptive hypofibrinogenemia), acute cytopenias, transaminitis, and coagulopathy, requiring emergency high-dose pulse corticosteroids and anakinra.

standard_knowledge.claim: The rash of AOSD is characteristically an evanescent, non-pruritic or mildly pruritic salmon-pink macular or maculopapular eruption, predominantly appearing on the trunk and proximal extremities during high evening fever spikes and disappearing as temperature normalizes.

Extreme hyperferritinemia (> 5-to-10-fold upper limit of normal, often exceeding 10,000 ug/L) reflects massive reticuloendothelial histiocyte activation and directly correlates with disease activity and response to treatment.

Macrophage Activation Syndrome (MAS/sHLH) develops in 10-15% of AOSD patients; laboratory clues include acute fall in erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) with rising CRP, sudden bicytopenia/pancytopenia, hypofibrinogenemia, elevated triglycerides, and hyperferritinemia > 10,000 ug/L.

Emergency management of AOSD-associated MAS mandates high-dose intravenous pulse methylprednisolone (1 g/day for 3 days) combined with high-dose intravenous or subcutaneous anakinra (100-200 mg every 6-8 hours) to arrest the fatal cytokine cascade.

page.standard_overview: The role of adjunctive corticosteroid therapy in adult septic shock was clarified by two landmark randomized controlled trials published simultaneously in 2018: the ADRENAL trial (3,800 patients) and the APROCCHSS trial (1,241 patients). While ADRENAL evaluated continuous intravenous hydrocortisone (200 mg/day) monotherapy and demonstrated faster shock resolution and shorter mechanical ventilation without 90-day mortality benefit, APROCCHSS evaluated hydrocortisone (50 mg IV q6h) plus oral fludrocortisone (50 ug daily) in severe shock and demonstrated a statistically significant 90-day all-cause mortality reduction (43.0% vs 49.1%). The 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines recommend low-dose corticosteroids in patients with persistent vasopressor dependency.

standard_knowledge.claim: The landmark ADRENAL trial (3,800 patients, Venkatesh et al., NEJM) showed that continuous hydrocortisone (200 mg/day for 7 days) significantly accelerated shock resolution (median 3 vs 4 days), shortened time to ICU discharge, and reduced blood transfusion requirements, though 90-day mortality was not significantly different (27.9% vs 28.8%).

The French APROCCHSS trial (1,241 patients with severe septic shock, Annane et al., NEJM) demonstrated that combined hydrocortisone (50 mg IV q6h) plus oral fludrocortisone (50 ug daily) significantly reduced 90-day all-cause mortality from 49.1% to 43.0% (hazard ratio 0.88, p=0.03).

The 2021 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines issue a weak recommendation for low-dose corticosteroid therapy (IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day) in adult septic shock patients who have an ongoing requirement for vasopressor therapy (norepinephrine or epinephrine >= 0.25 ug/kg/min) for at least 4 hours.

Neither trial reported an increase in secondary hospital-acquired infections or gastrointestinal bleeding with low-dose corticosteroids, although hydrocortisone was associated with higher rates of manageable hyperglycemia.

page.standard_overview: The therapeutic paradigm for advanced/metastatic melanoma has been revolutionized by immune checkpoint blockade targeting PD-1 and CTLA-4. In the benchmark CheckMate 067 trial, dual checkpoint inhibition with nivolumab plus ipilimumab achieved unprecedented durable 6.5-year overall survival (49% vs 42% for nivolumab alone and 23% for ipilimumab alone), with median overall survival reaching 72.1 months. While dual therapy yields the highest response rates (58%) and intracranial control, it induces severe Grade 3/4 immune-related adverse events (irAEs) in 59% of patients, necessitating proactive monitoring, prompt high-dose corticosteroid intervention, and careful risk-benefit stratification against anti-PD-1 monotherapy.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the landmark phase 3 CheckMate 067 trial (Wolchok et al., NEJM), nivolumab plus ipilimumab achieved a median overall survival of 72.1 months and a 6.5-year overall survival rate of 49%, establishing dual checkpoint blockade as the most potent frontline regimen.

Nivolumab monotherapy in CheckMate 067 demonstrated robust efficacy with a 6.5-year survival rate of 42% and a substantially lower rate of Grade 3/4 treatment-related adverse events (24%) compared to combination therapy (59%).

The randomized phase 3 KEYNOTE-006 trial established pembrolizumab (anti-PD-1) superiority over ipilimumab in both treatment-naive and previously treated advanced melanoma, prolonging progression-free and overall survival with significantly lower toxicity.

Immune-related adverse events (colitis, hepatitis, hypophysitis, pneumonitis, myocarditis) require protocolized grading and prompt high-dose systemic corticosteroids (prednisone 1-2 mg/kg/day or IV methylprednisolone); refractory colitis responds rapidly to infliximab or vedolizumab.

page.standard_overview: The treatment landscape of locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma has been fundamentally transformed by the antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) enfortumab vedotin paired with the anti-PD-1 inhibitor pembrolizumab. standard_knowledge.claim: In the global phase 3 EV-302 / KEYNOTE-A39 trial (Powles et al., NEJM), enfortumab vedotin combined with pembrolizumab nearly doubled median overall survival (31.5 vs 16.1 months; hazard ratio for death 0.47, p<0.001) compared with platinum-based chemotherapy.

page.standard_overview: Agitation in hospitalized adult medical and surgical patients represents a clinical emergency reflecting underlying delirium, substance intoxication or withdrawal, toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, or acute exacerbation of psychiatric illness. Systematic clinical evaluation utilizing the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS) objectively gauges severity. The initial approach prioritizes environmental optimization, de-escalation, addressing uncomfortable physical triggers (pain, urinary retention, hypoxia, constipation), and minimizing deliriogenic restraints. When severe aggression endangers the patient or staff, structured pharmacological calming (rapid tranquilization with oral or parenteral atypical antipsychotics) is implemented with continuous airway and vital sign monitoring.

standard_knowledge.claim: Structured bedside agitation scoring using validated tools such as the Richmond Agitation-Sedation Scale (RASS; ranging from +4 combative to -5 unarousable) allows objective titration of behavioral and pharmacological calming interventions.

NICE Guideline NG103 emphasizes that non-pharmacological interventions—reorientation, reassurance, family presence, lighting regulation, noise reduction, and pain control—are the mandatory first-line strategy for agitated delirium in hospital inpatients.

In the multicenter TREC randomized trials of rapid tranquilization in emergency settings, intramuscular olanzapine or haloperidol plus promethazine achieved rapid tranquility within 15-30 minutes with significantly lower risks of respiratory depression than parenteral benzodiazepines.

Physical restraints are an intervention of absolute last resort, carry high risks of strangulation, blunt trauma, and worsening agitation, and mandate continuous 1-on-1 nursing observation and regular vital sign checks every 15 minutes.

page.standard_overview: Vascular air embolism is a rare but catastrophic iatrogenic or barotraumatic event categorized into Venous Air Embolism (VAE; entrainment into systemic venous circulation or right heart) and Arterial Air Embolism (AAE; air entering pulmonary veins, left heart, or systemic arteries, leading to cerebral or coronary occlusions). VAE occurs during central venous catheter placement/removal, neurosurgical operations in the sitting position, or laparoscopic insufflation, precipitating right ventricular outflow tract 'air lock' and cardiovascular collapse. Immediate management requires stopping air ingress, 100% high-flow oxygen, Durant maneuver (left lateral decubitus and Trendelenburg positioning), and urgent hyperbaric oxygen (HBOT) therapy.

standard_knowledge.claim: Venous air embolism entering the right ventricle creates a mechanical 'air lock' obstructing the pulmonary artery, producing acute pulmonary hypertension, acute cor pulmonale, profound hypotension, and sudden drop in end-tidal CO2 (EtCO2).

Immediate bedside rescue positioning for suspected venous air embolism is the Durant maneuver: placing the patient in the left lateral decubitus and Trendelenburg position, which traps the air bubble at the apex of the right ventricle away from the pulmonary outflow tract.

Administration of 100% inspired oxygen accelerates bubble reabsorption by washing out systemic nitrogen, creating a steep nitrogen concentration gradient from the bubble into blood and reducing bubble volume.

Hyperbaric oxygen therapy (HBOT at 2.8 to 3.0 atmospheres absolute) is the definitive treatment of choice for arterial gas embolism and severe venous embolism with neurological or hemodynamic impairment, rapidly compressing bubble diameter (Boyle's law) and restoring microvascular tissue perfusion.

page.standard_overview: Systematic airway management requires structured pre-intubation difficult airway assessment and adherence to validated rescue algorithms to avoid the dreaded 'cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate' (CICO) scenario. The 4th National Audit Project (NAP4) in the United Kingdom revealed that poor airway assessment, failure to plan for difficult intubation, and persistent repeated laryngoscopy attempts are the leading causes of catastrophic airway brain damage and death. The 2015 Difficult Airway Society (DAS) guidelines structure unanticipated difficult tracheal intubation into four sequential plans: Plan A (facemask and video-laryngoscopy), Plan B (second-generation supraglottic airway device [SAD]), Plan C (facemask oxygenation and waking the patient), and Plan D (emergency front-of-neck access [FONA]).

standard_knowledge.claim: The NAP4 major airway complications audit demonstrated that unrecognized esophageal intubation, repeated blind attempts at laryngoscopy, and delay in performing surgical cricothyroidotomy were major causes of fatal airway outcomes.

The 2015 Difficult Airway Society (DAS) guidelines structure failed intubation into a strict sequential protocol: Plan A (tracheal intubation with video-laryngoscopy, maximum 3+1 attempts); Plan B (maintaining oxygenation with a 2nd generation supraglottic airway device); Plan C (facemask oxygenation); Plan D (emergency front-of-neck access).

Second-generation supraglottic airway devices (e.g., i-gel, ProSeal LMA) are superior to first-generation LMAs because of higher seal pressures (> 30 cmH2O) and a separate gastric drainage port that reduces pulmonary aspiration risk.

Plan D (Emergency Front-of-Neck Access / FONA) mandates a scalpel-bougie-tube cricothyroidotomy (stab incision through the cricothyroid membrane, coude-tip bougie insertion, and railroading a 6.0 mm cuffed endotracheal tube), which is faster and more reliable than needle/cannula techniques.

page.standard_overview: Endotracheal intubation in the intensive care unit is a high-risk procedure carrying a 10-to-20-fold higher incidence of life-threatening complications (severe hypoxemia, cardiovascular collapse, cardiac arrest) compared to elective operating room intubations. The landmark DEVICE trial (Prekker et al., NEJM) definitively established that video-laryngoscopy significantly improves first-pass intubation success (85.1% vs 70.8%) compared to direct laryngoscopy in critically ill adults. Structured ICU intubation bundles—comprising pre-oxygenation with HFNC or NIV, hemodynamic optimization, mandatory video-laryngoscopy, neuromuscular blockade, and capnography confirmation—mitigate peri-intubation morbidity.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the multicenter randomized DEVICE trial (1,417 critically ill patients, Prekker et al., NEJM), video-laryngoscopy resulted in a higher rate of successful intubation on the first attempt compared with direct laryngoscopy (85.1% vs 70.8%; absolute difference 14.2 percentage points, p<0.001).

The French MACMAN randomized trial demonstrated that video-laryngoscopy did not improve first-pass intubation when performed by highly experienced operators with standard Mac blades, highlighting that operator familiarity and blade geometry (hyperangulated vs standard) dictate performance.

DAS and Intensive Care Society (ICS) guidelines for management of the critically ill airway recommend mandatory pre-oxygenation with non-invasive ventilation (NIV) or high-flow nasal oxygen, aggressive fluid and vasopressor pre-loading, and continuous waveform capnography.

Peri-intubation cardiovascular collapse occurs in up to 30% of critically ill patients; prophylactic pre-induction initiation of peripheral norepinephrine or push-dose vasopressors significantly reduces severe hypotension and cardiac arrest during induction.

page.standard_overview: Malignant central airway obstruction (CAO) is a life-threatening complication occurring in up to 20-30% of advanced lung cancers and metastatic malignancies (esophagus, thyroid, melanoma, breast). Patients present with stridor, severe dyspnea, wheezing mistakenly treated as asthma, recurrent post-obstructive pneumonias, or hemoptysis. Emergency management requires high-dose corticosteroids, heliox (helium-oxygen mixture) to reduce airway resistance in laminar flow, and emergent multidisciplinary interventional pulmonology consultation. Rigid bronchoscopy is the optimal platform to secure the airway, de-bulk endobronchial tumor via ablative modalities (electrocautery, APC, cryotherapy), and deploy self-expanding metallic or silicone tracheobronchial stents.

standard_knowledge.claim: American College of Chest Physicians (CHEST) guidelines recommend rigid bronchoscopy under general anesthesia as the preferred diagnostic and therapeutic interventional modality for severe malignant central airway obstruction.

Immediate mechanical airway recanalization is achieved via rigid bronchoscope core-out debridement combined with immediate ablative thermal modalities (argon plasma coagulation [APC], electrocautery, or contact diode laser).

Airway stenting with silicone (Dumon) or self-expanding covered metallic stents (SEMS) provides immediate structural stabilization for extrinsic airway compression or mixed endobronchial/extrinsic obstruction, restoring airway lumen in > 90% of cases.

In the multicenter AQuIRE registry study (Ost et al., Chest), therapeutic bronchoscopy for malignant CAO resulted in immediate, statistically significant improvements in dyspnea, health-related quality of life, and lung function, with complication rates < 4% in experienced centers.

page.standard_overview: Acute kidney injury (AKI) diagnosis and management focuses on early detection, etiology identification, avoidance of compounding toxicities, and fluid stewardship. Under KDIGO recommendations, identifying AKI early via paired serum creatinine and hourly urine output monitoring mandates implementation of the KDIGO Stage-based Care Bundle. In resuscitating patients at risk of or suffering from AKI, the landmark SMART and SALT-ED randomized trials demonstrated that balanced crystalloids (Plasma-Lyte or Lactated Ringer's) significantly reduce Major Adverse Kidney Events at 30 days (MAKE30) compared to 0.9% normal saline, avoiding hyperchloremia-induced renal arteriolar vasoconstriction.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the landmark SMART trial of 15,802 critically ill adults (Semler et al., NEJM), intravenous resuscitation with balanced crystalloids significantly lowered the 30-day incidence of Major Adverse Kidney Events (MAKE30: death, new RRT, or persistent renal dysfunction) compared with 0.9% saline (14.3% vs 15.4%, p=0.04).

The companion SALT-ED trial in non-critically ill emergency department patients confirmed that balanced crystalloids reduced MAKE30 compared to saline (4.7% vs 5.6%), driven particularly by lower rates of acute renal replacement therapy in high-risk baseline subgroups.

KDIGO guidelines recommend discontinuing all potential nephrotoxic medications (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, amphotericin B, vancomycin where alternatives exist) and holding RAAS inhibitors during acute hypotension and volume depletion.

In severe AKI with fluid overload, diuretics (loop diuretics alone or combined with metolazone/acetazolamide) do not improve renal recovery or survival, but facilitate fluid balance and buy time while deciding on renal replacement therapy initiation.

page.standard_overview: Accurate diagnosis and staging of acute kidney injury under the KDIGO consensus criteria requires serial assessment of both serum creatinine and hourly urine output. Urine output criteria frequently detect AKI earlier than serum creatinine, which requires 24 to 48 hours of accumulation to cross diagnostic thresholds. The Acute Disease Quality Initiative (ADQI) consensus emphasizes that combining functional staging (creatinine and urine output) with structural injury biomarkers (TIMP-2, IGFBP7, NGAL) defines subclinical AKI, guiding risk-adapted monitoring and preventing secondary iatrogenic insult.

standard_knowledge.claim: KDIGO diagnostic criteria define AKI by any of the following: rise in serum creatinine by >= 0.3 mg/dL within 48 hours; rise in creatinine >= 1.5 times baseline within 7 days; or urine volume < 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 consecutive hours.

Oliguria criteria (< 0.5 mL/kg/h) provide earlier identification of AKI than creatinine in critically ill patients, and persistent oliguria beyond 12 hours independently predicts 30-day mortality even with minor creatinine increments.

KDIGO Stage 3 criteria include: serum creatinine >= 3.0 times baseline; serum creatinine >= 4.0 mg/dL (>= 353.6 umol/L); initiation of renal replacement therapy; or in patients < 18 years, a decrease in eGFR to < 35 mL/min/1.73m2.

The ADQI 23 consensus recommendations advocate incorporating damage biomarkers to refine staging: identifying 'biomarker positive / function negative' patients with subclinical AKI who carry elevated risks of prolonged hospitalization and progression.

Ascites and hepatic encephalopathy in acute alcoholic hepatitis require standard spironolactone/furosemide and lactulose/rifaximin titration.

standard_knowledge.claim: Wernicke encephalopathy is a clinical diagnosis requiring high-dose intravenous thiamine (500 mg IV three times daily for 3-5 days) before any enteral or parenteral carbohydrates.
Caine criteria diagnostic sensitivity for Wernicke encephalopathy requires 2 of: dietary deficiency, oculomotor abnormalities, cerebellar dysfunction, and altered mental state.
Alcohol-related cirrhosis requires systematic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) screening with ultrasound +/- AFP every 6 months and endoscopic variceal screening.
Sustained alcohol abstinence is the single most powerful determinant of survival and portal pressure reduction across all stages of alcohol-related liver disease.

page.standard_overview: Alcohol withdrawal syndrome (AWS) ranges from mild tremulousness to life-threatening delirium tremens and withdrawal seizures. Long-acting benzodiazepines (diazepam, chlordiazepoxide) are standard of care, administered preferably via symptom-triggered protocols (CIWA-Ar) rather than fixed schedules. In hepatic cirrhosis, short-acting agents without active metabolites (lorazepam, oxazepam) avoid drug accumulation.

standard_knowledge.claim: Symptom-triggered benzodiazepine administration guided by CIWA-Ar scores achieves equivalent clinical control with significantly lower total medication dose and shorter hospital stay.
Diazepam and chlordiazepoxide provide smoother withdrawal control due to long-acting active metabolites (desmethyldiazepam), reducing withdrawal seizure frequency.

In patients with severe liver failure or cirrhosis, lorazepam or oxazepam (LOT drugs: Lorazepam, Oxazepam, Temazepam) are preferred because they undergo direct glucuronidation without phase I hepatic metabolism.
Alcohol withdrawal seizures typically occur 12-48 hours after alcohol reduction, are generalized tonic-clonic, and are treated with benzodiazepines, not standard phenytoin.

page.standard_overview: Delirium tremens (DT) is a severe medical emergency characterized by profound delirium, hallucinations, agitation, fever, and severe autonomic instability, typically developing 48-96 hours after alcohol cessation.
