standard_knowledge.claim: Delirium tremens carries up to 5-15% mortality without intensive care; mortality is driven by hyperthermia, cardiac arrhythmias, and aspiration pneumonia.
Phenobarbital monotherapy or protocolized combination with benzodiazepines achieves faster symptom control, lower intubation rates, and decreased ICU length of stay in severe refractory withdrawal.
Dexmedetomidine reduces sympathetic overdrive and tachycardia as an adjunctive sedative, but does not prevent seizures or delirium and cannot substitute for GABAergic agents.
Severe hypomagnesemia and hypophosphatemia are common in severe withdrawal and must be corrected aggressively to prevent refractory seizures and refractory hypokalemia.

page.standard_overview: Allergic rhinitis is an IgE-mediated chronic inflammatory disease of the upper airway. Moderate-to-severe symptoms are managed first-line with intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) or combination INCS and intranasal antihistamines (e.g. fluticasone/azelastine). Allergen immunotherapy (SLIT or SCIT) is the only disease-modifying intervention for IgE-confirmed refractory disease.

standard_knowledge.claim: AAO-HNS guidelines recommend intranasal corticosteroids as first-line monotherapy for patients with clinically significant allergic rhinitis affecting quality of life.
Fixed-dose combination of intranasal corticosteroid and intranasal antihistamine (fluticasone propionate/azelastine) provides faster and superior symptom relief compared to either agent alone.
Oral first-generation sedating antihistamines (e.g. diphenhydramine, chlorpheniramine) should be avoided due to sedation, anticholinergic side effects, and cognitive impairment.

page.standard_overview: Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (AATD) is an autosomal codominant genetic disorder characterized by low circulating levels of AAT (a serine protease inhibitor protecting lung elastin). Homozygosity for the Z allele (Pi*ZZ) predisposes to early-onset panacinar emphysema (predominating in lower lung zones) and liver cirrhosis from misfolded polymer accumulation in hepatocytes.

standard_knowledge.claim: ATS/ERS guidelines recommend screening for AATD in all patients with COPD, unexplained liver disease, or persistent adult-onset asthma with incompletely reversible airflow obstruction.
Serum AAT concentration < 11 umol/L (< 57 mg/dL) combined with protein phenotyping (isoelectric focusing) or SERPINA1 genotyping confirms severe deficiency.
Intravenous AAT augmentation therapy (60 mg/kg weekly) significantly slows the loss of lung density assessed by chest computed tomography densitometry in patients with FEV1 35-70% (RAPID trial).

Hepatic disease in AATD results from toxic gain-of-function due to intracellular retention of Z-AAT protein polymers (PAS-positive, diastase-resistant globules) and is not corrected by IV augmentation.

page.standard_overview: Alport syndrome is an inherited progressive type IV collagen nephropathy caused by pathogenic variants in COL4A3, COL4A4, or COL4A5 genes. It presents with persistent microscopic hematuria in childhood, progressive proteinuria, hypertension, progressive renal failure, high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, and anterior lenticonus. Early ACE inhibitor therapy significantly delays progression to end-stage kidney disease.

standard_knowledge.claim: International consensus guidelines recommend early initiation of ACE inhibitors at the onset of persistent microalbuminuria (or at diagnosis in males with X-linked Alport syndrome) to delay end-stage kidney disease by decades.

X-linked inheritance due to COL4A5 mutations accounts for approximately 85% of cases; affected hemizygous males universally develop ESRD, whereas heterozygous females exhibit variable clinical phenotypes.
Renal biopsy electron microscopy demonstrates characteristic irregular thinning, thickening, and longitudinal splitting/lamellation ('basket-weave' appearance) of the glomerular basement membrane.
Post-transplant anti-GBM nephritis occurs in 3-5% of transplanted Alport patients due to alloimmunization against normal collagen alpha-3/4/5(IV) chains in the donor kidney.

page.standard_overview: Inherited collagen IV nephropathies span a continuum from benign familial hematuria (thin basement membrane nephropathy) to severe X-linked or autosomal recessive Alport syndrome. Genetic testing for COL4A3, COL4A4, and COL4A5 distinguishes benign non-progressive heterozygous carriers from individuals at high risk for progressive proteinuria, glomerulosclerosis, and extra-renal sensorineural deafness.

standard_knowledge.claim: Thin basement membrane nephropathy (TBMN), commonly caused by heterozygous COL4A3 or COL4A4 mutations, presents with isolated microscopic hematuria and a benign long-term renal prognosis in the absence of proteinuria.
Next-generation sequencing multigene panels have replaced routine renal biopsy as the preferred first-line diagnostic investigation for suspected inherited collagen IV disorders.
Heterozygous females with X-linked Alport syndrome (COL4A5) have a lifelong risk of developing proteinuria (up to 75%) and ESRD (up to 15-30% by age 60), requiring lifelong annual monitoring.
SGLT2 inhibitors confer additive antiproteinuric and renoprotective effects when added to maximum tolerated renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system blockade.

page.mentor_intro: The 2026 AHA/ASA acute stroke guideline updates reperfusion care. Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg is an effective alternative to alteplase, intra-arterial thrombolysis after successful thrombectomy may help selected patients, and early DOAC initiation after stroke with AF appears safe.

teaching_points.claim: The 2026 AHA/ASA guideline modifies the approach to thrombolysis contraindications and highlights remaining knowledge gaps.
Early DOAC initiation after acute ischaemic stroke with non-valvular AF appears safe and potentially more effective than delayed treatment.
Tenecteplase was superior for excellent functional outcomes and not inferior for major neurological improvement or death versus alteplase, with 0.25 mg/kg the optimal dose.
Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg gives better efficacy, while alteplase remains safer for symptomatic intracranial haemorrhage, so thrombolytic selection should be individualised.
A network meta-analysis found alteplase 0.6 mg/kg safer, and tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg and alteplase 0.6 mg/kg preferable beyond 4.5 hours with tissue window assessment.
Adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis after successful thrombectomy appears to benefit selected patients, such as those with higher NIHSS or cardioembolic aetiology.
Fibrinogen depletion was seen only after alteplase and tended to accompany more major haemorrhagic complications.

page.standard_overview: Intravenous thrombolysis with alteplase (0.9 mg/kg, max 90 mg; 10% bolus over 1 min, remainder over 60 min) or tenecteplase (0.25 mg/kg, max 25 mg) is the standard of care for acute ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours of symptom onset. Pre-treatment non-contrast head CT must exclude intracranial hemorrhage, and blood pressure must be safely lowered < 185/110 mmHg. Concurrently, patients with large vessel occlusion should be evaluated for endovascular thrombectomy.

standard_knowledge.claim: The landmark NINDS rt-PA Stroke Study demonstrated that patients treated with intravenous alteplase within 3 hours had a 30% higher likelihood of minimal or no disability at 3 months (mRS 0-1) despite a 6.4% symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage rate.

ECASS III trial demonstrated efficacy of alteplase extended to 4.5 hours from symptom onset in eligible patients without severe stroke (NIHSS > 25), age > 80 with previous stroke/diabetes, or oral anticoagulant use.
AHA/ASA guidelines require blood pressure to be maintained < 180/105 mmHg during and for 24 hours following intravenous thrombolysis to minimize hemorrhagic transformation.

In patients with acute large vessel occlusion (ICA or M1 segment MCA), mechanical thrombectomy is standard within 6 hours (and up to 24 hours selected by perfusion imaging via DAWN and DEFUSE-3 criteria), regardless of whether IV thrombolysis is given.

page.mentor_intro: Anti-amyloid antibodies slow decline in early Alzheimer disease but their effects are small, below the minimal clinically important difference in one analysis, and they carry meaningful harms including ARIA. MRI protocols to detect ARIA are recommended.

teaching_points.claim: Imaging recommendations for anti-amyloid therapies include implementing MRI protocols to detect ARIA in diverse practice settings.
FDA-approved anti-amyloid monoclonal antibodies slow disease progression on CDR-SB and other scales, at the cost of increased side effects.
Monoclonal antibodies targeting amyloid give small benefits on cognitive and functional scales that are far below the minimal clinically important difference, with clinically meaningful harms.
Aducanumab, lecanemab and donanemab do not appear to differ in effect on cognitive function, and low-dose lithium may be safer.

page.mentor_intro: Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia is a heterogeneous group, mainly due to MPL mutations, that can evolve to marrow failure. Management ranges from supportive care to transplantation, and acquired forms can respond to immunosuppression.

Reviews summarise the diagnostic features and clinical implications of inherited bone marrow failure syndromes including congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia.

page.standard_overview: Congenital amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia (CAMT) is a severe marrow failure disorder characterized by isolated severe thrombocytopenia and absent megakaryocytes on bone marrow biopsy. CAMT is caused by biallelic loss-of-function MPL mutations (TPO receptor), typically progressing to aplastic anemia or leukemia; allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation is the definitive curative treatment.

standard_knowledge.claim: Biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the MPL gene encoding the thrombopoietin receptor cause CAMT, leading to early marrow aplasia.
Bone marrow examination demonstrates selective absent or severely hypoplastic megakaryocytes with preserved erythroid and myeloid lineages in early stages.
Allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation performed prior to trilineage marrow failure or leukemic transformation achieves > 80% long-term cure.
In acquired amegakaryocytic thrombocytopenia (AAT), immunosuppressive therapy with cyclosporine, ATG, or rituximab achieves remissions in autoantibody-mediated cases.

page.standard_overview: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a neurodegenerative disorder causing progressive loss of upper and lower motor neurons. Diagnosis utilizes Revised El Escorial and Gold Coast criteria. Disease-modifying therapy includes riluzole (glutamate antagonist) and edaravone. page.standard_overview: Anaemia of chronic disease (ACD / anaemia of inflammation) is a cytokine-driven normocytic or mildly microcytic anaemia. Interleukin-6 stimulates hepatic production of hepcidin, which degrades ferroportin, trapping iron in reticuloendothelial macrophages and enterocytes. Laboratory hallmark is low serum iron, low TIBC/transferrin, normal to elevated ferritin (> 100 ng/mL), and elevated hepcidin.

standard_knowledge.claim: Hepcidin-mediated internalization and degradation of ferroportin-1 prevents intestinal iron absorption and macrophage iron release, causing hypoferremia.
Differentiating pure ACD from combined ACD + iron deficiency: TSAT < 20% with ferritin 30-100 ug/L indicates concurrent true iron deficiency responsive to IV iron.
Treating the underlying inflammatory, infectious, or rheumatologic condition remains the primary and most effective therapy for ACD.
Erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) or hypoxia-inducible factor prolyl hydroxylase inhibitors (HIF-PHIs) restore hemoglobin in chronic kidney disease ACD but require repletion of iron stores.

page.standard_overview: Squamous cell carcinoma of the anal canal is strongly associated with high-risk human papillomavirus (HPV types 16 and 18). Curative standard of care for localized disease (T1-T4, N0-N3) is definitive concurrent chemoradiotherapy (Nigro protocol: 5-fluorouracil or capecitabine + mitomycin C with external beam radiotherapy), preserving anal sphincter function in > 75% of patients.

standard_knowledge.claim: Definitive concurrent chemoradiation with 5-FU and mitomycin C provides 80% 5-year colostomy-free survival in localized anal squamous cell carcinoma.
ESMO and NCCN guidelines recommend IMRT (intensity-modulated radiation therapy) to minimize radiation dermatitis, proctitis, and pelvic bone marrow toxicity.
Abdominoperineal resection (APR) with permanent end colostomy is reserved strictly for persistent disease at 26 weeks post-CRT or biopsy-proven locoregional recurrence.

First-line systemic therapy for metastatic or unresectable recurrent anal carcinoma is carboplatin plus paclitaxel, with immune checkpoint inhibitors (retifanlimab, pembrolizumab) for refractory disease.

page.standard_overview: ANCA-associated vasculitis (AAV) encompasses Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA; PR3-ANCA), Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA; MPO-ANCA), and Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (EGPA). Remission induction for organ- or life-threatening disease combines high-dose glucocorticoids with rituximab or cyclophosphamide. Avacopan (C5a receptor antagonist) enables significant glucocorticoid-sparing induction.

standard_knowledge.claim: EULAR 2022 recommendations establish rituximab (375 mg/m2 weekly x 4 or 1000 mg x 2) as equivalent to cyclophosphamide for induction and superior for relapsing disease.
Avacopan (30 mg twice daily), an oral complement C5a receptor antagonist, produces sustained remission at 52 weeks while significantly reducing glucocorticoid-related toxicity (ADVOCATE trial).

PEXIVAS trial demonstrated that routine plasma exchange does not reduce end-stage kidney disease or all-cause mortality, and a reduced-dose glucocorticoid regimen is non-inferior with fewer severe infections.
Maintenance of remission is best achieved with scheduled low-dose rituximab (500 mg every 6 months for at least 24-48 months) compared to azathioprine (MAINRITSAN trial).

page.standard_overview: Angioedema is asymmetric swelling of the deep dermis and subcutaneous or submucosal tissues. It is critical to differentiate histamine-mediated angioedema (associated with urticaria/pruritus, responds to epinephrine, antihistamines, and steroids) from bradykinin-mediated angioedema (ACE-inhibitor induced or hereditary angioedema [HAE]). standard_knowledge.claim: WAO/EAACI guidelines recommend icatibant (bradykinin B2 receptor antagonist) or plasma-derived C1-inhibitor concentrate for acute attacks of hereditary angioedema.
ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema is caused by impaired bradykinin degradation; ACE inhibitors must be permanently discontinued, and ARBs should be avoided in acute severe airway presentation.
Hereditary angioedema (HAE) Type 1 (85%) has low C4 and low antigenic/functional C1-INH; Type 2 (15%) has low C4, normal antigenic but low functional C1-INH.
Emergent airway protection (fiberoptic intubation or cricothyroidotomy) takes precedence over pharmacotherapy in progressive laryngeal edema.

topic: angiotensin ii for catecholamine refractory vasodilatory shock

page.mentor_intro: Angiotensin II raises blood pressure and spares catecholamines in vasodilatory shock without clearly lowering mortality. It is a rescue (third-line) vasopressor, and patients with high renin may respond best.

teaching_points.claim: Expert consensus recognises angiotensin II as useful to reduce catecholamine requirements in vasopressor-resistant septic shock, while stressing the need for more trials.
A meta-analysis of distributive shock found angiotensin II did not reduce mortality but allowed significant adjunctive vasopressor reduction at 3 hours without more reported adverse events.
In vasoplegic shock, angiotensin II showed comparable in-hospital mortality to standard therapy but produced a significant mean arterial pressure rise.
A systematic review suggests angiotensin II may be a third-line vasopressor if the target MAP is not reached after noradrenaline above 200 ng/kg/min for more than 6 hours.
An exploratory analysis found a greater response in patients with elevated baseline plasma renin and a reduction in renal replacement therapy initiation.
Safety concerns include thromboembolism with angiotensin II, and in cardiogenic shock reported adverse events included hepatic injury, digital ischaemia and thrombotic events.

An overview of reviews found angiotensin II consistently improved MAP by more than 10 mmHg, with gaps in the definition of catecholamine-resistant shock, initiation thresholds and biomarker-guided treatment.

uncertainties: Optimal initiation threshold and renin-guided selection.
Effect on hard outcomes beyond MAP and catecholamine sparing.
mcq_angles: Thromboembolic risk as a key adverse effect.
case_hooks: Septic shock on noradrenaline 0.5 microgram/kg/min with MAP still 55.

page.standard_overview: Catecholamine-refractory vasodilatory shock is characterized by persistent severe hypotension and inadequate organ perfusion despite high-dose norepinephrine and vasopressin. Synthetic human angiotensin II acts through the AT1 receptor, providing a non-adrenergic vasoconstrictor mechanism. Management includes early hydrocortisone, vasopressin (0.03 units/min), and angiotensin II in refractory shock.

standard_knowledge.claim: ATHOS-3 randomized trial demonstrated that synthetic human angiotensin II significantly increased mean arterial pressure and reduced background catecholamine requirements in vasodilatory shock.
Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines recommend adding vasopressin (0.03 U/min) rather than escalating norepinephrine to high levels (> 0.25 mcg/kg/min).
Patients with high baseline serum renin concentrations or acute kidney injury receiving renal replacement therapy experience the greatest survival benefit from angiotensin II.
Thromboembolic events occur more frequently with angiotensin II, warranting mandatory concurrent pharmacological venous thromboembolism prophylaxis.

page.standard_overview: Ankylosing spondylitis (radiographic axial spondyloarthritis) is a chronic inflammatory arthritis predominantly affecting the axial skeleton and sacroiliac joints. It presents with inflammatory back pain (morning stiffness > 30 minutes, improvement with exercise, pain at night) in individuals < 45 years. First-line therapy is continuous full-dose NSAIDs; active disease refractory to NSAIDs is treated with TNF inhibitors or IL-17A inhibitors.

standard_knowledge.claim: ASAS/EULAR 2022 recommendations recommend continuous NSAIDs at maximum tolerated doses as first-line medical therapy for active axial spondyloarthritis.
TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, etanercept, infliximab, golimumab, certolizumab) or IL-17A inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab) achieve significant disease reduction (ASAS40) in active AS.
Conventional synthetic DMARDs (methotrexate, sulfasalazine) are ineffective for pure axial spinal disease, although sulfasalazine is useful for prominent peripheral arthritis.
JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib, tofacitinib) are approved oral options for active radiographic and non-radiographic axSpA refractory to bDMARDs.

page.standard_overview: Common benign anorectal disorders include hemorrhoidal disease, anal fissures, anorectal abscesses, and fistula-in-ano. Thrombosed external hemorrhoids present with acute severe pain and a bluish perianal lump (excised within 72h). Acute anal fissures present with tearing pain during defecation and bright red rectal bleeding (treated with topical nitroglycerin or diltiazem). Anorectal abscesses require prompt incision and drainage.

standard_knowledge.claim: ASCRS guidelines recommend dietary fiber supplementation (25-35g daily) and water intake as the cornerstone of conservative therapy for hemorrhoids.
Rubber band ligation is the most effective outpatient procedure for Grade I to III internal hemorrhoids that fail medical management.
Topical calcium channel blockers (2% diltiazem) or topical nitrates (0.4% nitroglycerin) are first-line for chronic anal fissure, healing 65-75% without fecal incontinence risk.
Anorectal abscesses require prompt surgical incision and drainage; routine antibiotics do not prevent fistula formation unless systemic sepsis or immunosuppression is present.

page.mentor_intro: Anterior mediastinal masses are mostly thymic epithelial tumours, managed by surgery with video-assisted or robotic approaches for suitable cases. Anaesthesia needs care because of airway and vascular compression risk.

teaching_points.claim: A China Anti-Cancer Association guideline provides integrative management for thymic epithelial tumours including systemic therapy for advanced disease and follow-up after resection.
Anaesthetic management of patients with an anterior mediastinal mass has evolved, with new approaches for safe induction and maintenance of general anaesthesia.
Robotic-assisted, video-assisted and open thymectomy for thymoma were compared, with robotic use constrained by cost, surgeon training and a lack of high-quality prospective data.
Thoracoscopic and robotic mediastinal tumour resection show insignificant differences in tumour size and operation time, with robotic surgery increasing hospitalisation costs.
In children, video-assisted resection of mediastinal tumours can be safe with low length of stay, while more complex tumours still need open surgery.
AI models for diagnosis and prognosis of thymic epithelial tumours are not yet ready for clinical implementation.

page.standard_overview: Anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity (doxorubicin, epirubicin) causes cumulative dose-dependent myocardial injury through topoisomerase II-beta inhibition, reactive oxygen species generation, and irreversible cardiomyocyte apoptosis. Surveillance relies on baseline and serial echocardiography with global longitudinal strain (GLS). Cardioprotection with dexrazoxane or neurohormonal blockade (ACEi/beta-blockers) is indicated in high-risk patients.

standard_knowledge.claim: ESC 2022 Cardio-Oncology guidelines define cancer therapy-related cardiac dysfunction (CTRCD) by a decrease in LVEF >= 10 percentage points to < 50%, or a relative reduction in global longitudinal strain (GLS) > 15%.
Cumulative lifetime doxorubicin dose is the strongest risk factor: heart failure incidence rises sharply above 400-500 mg/m2.
Dexrazoxane (iron-chelating topoisomerase II-beta inhibitor) significantly reduces anthracycline-induced cardiotoxicity without compromising oncological efficacy in high-risk patients.
Guideline-directed neurohormonal blockade (carvedilol, enalapril) initiated for early subclinical strain deterioration or asymptomatic LVEF drop prevents progression to clinical heart failure.

page.standard_overview: Antibiotic prophylaxis for infective endocarditis (IE) is restricted to patients at the highest risk of adverse outcomes undergoing high-risk dental procedures involving manipulation of the gingival tissue, periapical region of teeth, or perforation of oral mucosa. standard_knowledge.claim: ESC 2023 guidelines restrict antibiotic prophylaxis strictly to high-risk cardiac conditions undergoing dental procedures involving gingival or periapical manipulation.

Standard regimen: oral amoxicillin 2g (or ampicillin 2g IV) administered 30-60 minutes before the procedure; for severe penicillin allergy, cephalexin 2g, azithromycin 500mg, or doxycycline 100mg.
Prophylaxis is NOT recommended for gastrointestinal, urological, respiratory, or routine skin procedures in the absence of established local infection.

page.mentor_intro: Antibody-drug conjugate toxicity depends on linker cleavability and payload release. Trastuzumab deruxtecan can cause interstitial lung disease, sacituzumab govitecan causes neutropenia and diarrhoea, and HER2-low reporting needs structured pathology.

teaching_points.claim: A US Delphi consensus guides prevention and management of stomatitis with datopotamab deruxtecan.
International consensus recommends structured HER2 reporting that distinguishes IHC 0 (null), 0+ (ultralow) and HER2-low.
ADCs with cleavable linkers cause premature payload release, raising systemic free payload and associated toxicities.
A meta-analysis of ADC toxicity found more all-grade treatment-related adverse events, with no increase in high-grade events.
Trastuzumab deruxtecan adverse events mostly affect blood, lymphatic and gastrointestinal systems, with interstitial lung disease a notable and potentially serious event.
Sacituzumab govitecan toxicity includes neutropenia, nausea, diarrhoea and anaemia, supporting prophylactic protocols.
Caution is advised when irradiating intracranial sites concurrently with trastuzumab emtansine, and international guidance on combining T-DM1 with radiotherapy is needed.

page.standard_overview: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) deliver potent cytotoxic payloads directly to tumor cells expressing specific surface antigens using a targeted monoclonal antibody, cleavable or non-cleavable linker, and chemotherapeutic payload (e.g. topoisomerase I inhibitors, auristatins, calicheamicins). Landmark examples include trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) in HER2+ and HER2-low cancers, and enfortumab vedotin in urothelial cancer.

standard_knowledge.claim: Trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) demonstrated significant progression-free and overall survival improvements over standard therapy in HER2-low metastatic breast cancer (DESTINY-Breast04).
Enfortumab vedotin (targeting Nectin-4) combined with pembrolizumab established a new first-line standard of care in advanced urothelial carcinoma (EV-302 trial).

Drug-induced interstitial lung disease (ILD) / pneumonitis is a class-defining toxicity of topoisomerase I payload ADCs (T-DXd, sacituzumab govitecan), requiring routine CT surveillance and prompt steroid treatment.
The 'bystander killing effect' occurs when membrane-permeable cleaved cytotoxic payloads diffuse into adjacent antigen-negative tumor cells, overcoming intratumoral target heterogeneity.

In rheumatology and nephrology, rituximab is standard of care for rheumatoid arthritis refractory to anti-TNF agents, ANCA-associated vasculitis, systemic lupus erythematosus, and primary membranous nephropathy.

standard_knowledge.claim: ACR guidelines recommend rituximab in rheumatoid arthritis patients with inadequate response to TNF inhibitors, particularly in seropositive (RF/anti-CCP positive) disease.
Rituximab is standard first-line remission induction therapy for primary membranous nephropathy, demonstrating superior long-term remission rates compared to cyclosporine (MENTOR trial).
Universal screening for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) and anti-HBc total antibodies is mandatory prior to rituximab due to high risk of fatal hepatitis B reactivation.

topic: anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation in chronic kidney disease

page.mentor_intro: DOACs are as effective as and often safer than warfarin in AF, including CKD (CrCl 15 and above); evidence is weaker in dialysis. DOACs should be standard in low-risk AF needing anticoagulation, with correct dosing, and device-detected AF also benefits modestly.

teaching_points.claim: DOACs may increase efficacy and improve safety versus VKAs in AF with CKD (CrCl 15-90), with at least similar results in kidney failure.
In stage 5 CKD, DOACs showed a significant reduction in stroke and a non-significant trend to less major bleeding than VKAs.
In haemodialysis patients with AF, DOACs versus warfarin comparisons need validation by further prospective studies given thrombotic and bleeding risks.
DOACs should be standard of care in low-risk AF patients needing anticoagulation, with dabigatran showing the best balance of stroke prevention and bleeding reduction in one analysis.
A network meta-analysis found no difference in major bleeding, thromboembolism or mortality between DOACs and VKAs, and no DOAC clearly more favourable than others.
Anticoagulation with edoxaban or apixaban reduces stroke in device-detected AF and increases major bleeding.
Off-label underdosed DOACs, particularly rivaroxaban, were associated with increased ischaemic stroke without reduced bleeding, so on-label dosing should be emphasised.
DOACs may be a feasible option in AF with cirrhosis, pending validation.

uncertainties: Best strategy in dialysis patients.

page.standard_overview: Atrial fibrillation is highly prevalent in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), significantly increasing stroke and bleeding risks. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) provide superior or non-inferior stroke prevention compared to warfarin in mild-to-moderate CKD (CrCl 30-50 mL/min). In severe CKD (CrCl 15-29 mL/min) and dialysis, apixaban is increasingly utilized with specific dose reduction criteria.

standard_knowledge.claim: KDIGO 2023 guidelines recommend DOACs over vitamin K antagonists (warfarin) in patients with non-valvular AF and CKD Stages 1-3, and consider DOACs in Stage 4 (CrCl 15-29 mL/min).
Apixaban requires dose reduction to 2.5 mg BID if the patient meets at least two of the following criteria: age >= 80 years, body weight <= 60 kg, or serum creatinine >= 1.5 mg/dL (133 umol/L).
Warfarin in advanced CKD and dialysis accelerates vascular calcification and calcific uremic arteriolopathy (calciphylaxis) by inhibiting vitamin K-dependent matrix Gla protein.
Dabigatran is 80% renally eliminated and is contraindicated when CrCl < 30 mL/min in European guidelines.

page.mentor_intro: Warfarin remains the anticoagulant for mechanical valves; routine aspirin use beyond guideline indications adds bleeding. DOAC use in mechanical valves is under review, and low-dose vitamin K for supratherapeutic INR has not been shown to cause thromboembolism.

teaching_points.claim: A significant proportion of patients on warfarin for mechanical valves take guideline-discordant aspirin, and aspirin deprescribing in selected patients may safely reduce bleeding events.
A review compares direct-acting oral anticoagulants versus warfarin in mechanical valve patients, with findings needing exploration in specific subgroups.
Portable coagulometers with internet connectivity offer a new model of warfarin management after mechanical valve replacement, improving follow-up and compliance.
In pregnancy with a mechanical valve on non-warfarin anticoagulation, valve thrombosis may present as acute heart failure, and surgery should be prompt if needed.
In mechanical aortic valve patients with warfarin hypersensitivity due to an F9 variant, factor Xa or thrombin inhibitors deserve further investigation.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of vitamin K in mechanical valve patients with supratherapeutic INR addressed the thromboembolism risk of low-dose vitamin K, and more well-designed studies are needed.

uncertainties: DOACs in mechanical valves remain unproven.

Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are strictly contraindicated based on the RE-ALIGN trial, which demonstrated significantly higher thromboembolic and bleeding events with dabigatran.

standard_knowledge.claim: AHA/ACC and ESC guidelines establish vitamin K antagonists (warfarin) as the only approved anticoagulation for mechanical heart valves; DOACs are absolutely contraindicated.
The RE-ALIGN trial testing dabigatran in mechanical heart valves was halted early due to an excess of ischemic strokes, valve thrombosis, and major bleeding.
Target INR for mechanical aortic valves without thromboembolic risk factors is 2.5 (range 2.0-3.0); target INR for mechanical mitral valves or aortic valves with risk factors is 3.0 (range 2.5-3.5).
Low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg daily) is recommended in addition to warfarin only if there is a concomitant clinical indication (e.g. established atherosclerotic disease).

page.standard_overview: Pregnancy is a prothrombotic state with a 4- to 5-fold increased risk of venous thromboembolism. Low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH: enoxaparin, dalteparin) is the anticoagulant of choice throughout pregnancy and the postpartum period because it does not cross the placenta. Warfarin is teratogenic in the first trimester (warfarin embryopathy), and DOACs cross the placenta and are strictly contraindicated.

standard_knowledge.claim: ACOG and RCOG guidelines mandate LMWH as the anticoagulant of choice for prevention and treatment of VTE in pregnancy and lactation.
Warfarin crosses the placental barrier and causes warfarin embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses, CNS defects) when taken between 6 and 12 weeks gestation.
Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) cross the placenta, have documented embryofetal toxicities in animal models, and are strictly contraindicated in pregnancy.
Peripartum management: therapeutic LMWH must be held at least 24 hours (and prophylactic LMWH held 12 hours) prior to planned induction or neuraxial anesthesia.

page.standard_overview: Management of acute life-threatening bleeding or urgent surgery in anticoagulated patients requires specific reversal agents and supportive hemostatic resuscitation. Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran; andexanet alfa reverses apixaban and rivaroxaban; 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) combined with IV vitamin K reverses warfarin (target INR < 1.5). Protamine sulfate partially reverses unfractionated and low-molecular-weight heparin.

standard_knowledge.claim: AHA/ACC and CHEST guidelines recommend 4-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (4F-PCC) over fresh frozen plasma for emergent warfarin reversal due to faster INR normalization and lower volume overload.
Idarucizumab (5g IV in two divided doses) produces immediate, complete, and sustained reversal of dabigatran anticoagulation within minutes (RE-VERSE AD trial).
Andexanet alfa reverses factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban and rivaroxaban), achieving rapid reduction in anti-factor Xa activity and effective hemostasis in acute major bleeding (ANNEXA-4 trial).
Intravenous vitamin K (5-10 mg by slow infusion) must always be co-administered with 4F-PCC to sustain vitamin K-dependent clotting factor synthesis once PCC factors clear.

teaching_points.claim: A meta-analysis of relative effectiveness in treatment-resistant depression identified treatments with clear benefit, including ketamine and neurostimulation, with others (minocycline, aripiprazole) promising for some outcomes.
The number needed to treat for ketamine in adults with treatment-resistant depression was below 10 across observation intervals.
Deep TMS is an effective and safe strategy for treatment-resistant depression with similar adverse event rates to sham.
Ketamine and esketamine failed to reduce suicidal ideation in patients with treatment-resistant depression in one meta-analysis.
Deep brain stimulation for treatment-resistant depression has limited sham-controlled data and does not show significant improvement over placebo.
Esketamine carries abuse potential and unknown long-term effects, with signals regarding deaths and suicidality in testing.
Psilocybin shows a time-dependent therapeutic effect in major depressive disorder in a dose-response network meta-analysis.
Psychedelic-induced psychosis evidence is of low quality, and a conservative approach is recommended until more data are available.

page.standard_overview: Major depressive disorder (MDD) requires systematic stepwise pharmacotherapy guided by measurement-based care (e.g. PHQ-9). The landmark STAR*D trial demonstrated that approximately 33% of patients achieve remission with initial SSRI monotherapy (Step 1). Subsequent steps—switching classes (to bupropion, venlafaxine) or augmenting with bupropion, buspirone, lithium, or second-generation antipsychotics—achieve cumulative remission rates up to 67%.

standard_knowledge.claim: The STAR*D trial established that sequential treatment steps for treatment-resistant depression produce cumulative remission rates approaching 67%.
APA practice guidelines recommend evaluating antidepressant response at 4-8 weeks before modifying therapy (switching vs augmenting).
Augmentation of an SSRI/SNRI with an atypical antipsychotic (aripiprazole, quetiapine) or bupropion produces higher response rates than switching monotherapy in partial responders.
Ketamine and esketamine nasal spray provide rapid-onset antidepressant effects in treatment-resistant depression with acute suicidal ideation.

page.mentor_intro: Antiseizure medication choice is shaped by pregnancy risk, drug interactions and adverse effects. Folic acid of at least 0.4 mg daily is advised for people with epilepsy of child-bearing potential on ASMs, carbamazepine should not be co-prescribed with clozapine, and cannabidiol can cause liver injury.

teaching_points.claim: Clinicians should prescribe at least 0.4 mg of folic acid daily before and during pregnancy to people with epilepsy of child-bearing potential treated with an antiseizure medication, to reduce neural tube defects and possibly improve neurodevelopmental outcomes.
Carbamazepine should not be co-prescribed with clozapine because of agranulocytosis risk and induction of clozapine metabolism.
ILAE-linked guidance on neonatal seizures recommends a standardised pathway for managing neonatal seizures in each neonatal unit.
A national Delphi consensus in Egypt adapts epilepsy management to resource-limited settings.
Women with epilepsy have worse perinatal outcomes and should receive pregnancy counselling from an epilepsy specialist who can optimise their antiseizure regimen.
Cannabidiol-associated liver enzyme elevations and drug-induced liver injury are common adverse events, so liver function should be monitored.
After paediatric epilepsy surgery with seizure freedom, ASM cessation allows optimisation of intellectual and developmental trajectories.

page.standard_overview: Antiseizure medication (ASM) selection is determined by seizure classification (focal vs generalized vs unclassified), patient demographics (age, childbearing potential), comorbidity profiles, and potential drug-drug interactions. Broad-spectrum ASMs (levetiracetam, lamotrigine, valproate, topiramate) are effective for both focal and generalized seizures. Sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, phenytoin) treat focal seizures but can aggravate generalized absence or myoclonic seizures.

standard_knowledge.claim: SANAD II trials established lamotrigine as first-line for focal epilepsy, and valproate as superior to levetiracetam for generalized epilepsy in males.
Sodium valproate is strictly contraindicated in women of childbearing potential due to high teratogenicity (neural tube defects) and neurodevelopmental delays.
Narrow-spectrum sodium channel blockers (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin) can exacerbate generalized absence and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy.
Levetiracetam has low drug interaction potential and broad efficacy, but requires monitoring for behavioral changes, agitation, and depressive mood swings.

page.standard_overview: Systemic antifungal therapy is organized into three major classes: polyenes (amphotericin B), azoles (fluconazole, voriconazole, posaconazole, isavuconazole), and echinocandins (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin). Echinocandins are first-line for invasive candidiasis; voriconazole or isavuconazole is first-line for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis; liposomal amphotericin B is standard for mucormycosis and cryptococcal meningitis.

standard_knowledge.claim: IDSA guidelines recommend an echinocandin (caspofungin, micafungin, anidulafungin) as initial first-line therapy for candidemia and invasive candidiasis.
Voriconazole is the treatment of choice for invasive pulmonary aspergillosis, but requires therapeutic drug monitoring (target trough 1.5-5.0 ug/mL) and visual/hepatic monitoring.
Isavuconazole provides equivalent efficacy to voriconazole for invasive aspergillosis with significantly fewer drug-related adverse events and drug discontinuations (SECURE trial).
Liposomal amphotericin B (5-10 mg/kg daily) combined with urgent surgical debridement is the cornerstone of management for invasive mucormycosis.

page.mentor_intro: Anti-GBM disease is rare with high renal risk. KDIGO 2021 covers glomerular disease management, double-positive ANCA/anti-GBM cases are difficult to treat, and kidney transplant should wait for 6 months of anti-GBM antibody negativity.

Kidney transplantation in anti-GBM disease should be performed 6 months after absence of anti-GBM antibodies.
An international consensus recommends indirect immunofluorescence for ANCA testing beyond systemic vasculitis.
A core curriculum on therapeutic plasma exchange discusses its use from a nephrologist's perspective given limited supporting evidence.
Anti-GBM antibodies show high sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing anti-GBM disease, with cohort studies needed to compare immunoassays.
ANCA and anti-GBM double-positive patients are difficult to treat, supporting simultaneous antibody testing and systematic renal biopsy in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
A meta-analysis of anti-GBM disease provides epidemiology, clinical features, risk factors and outcomes, with caution due to observational design.
About one in four children with crescentic glomerulonephritis progress to kidney failure.

page.standard_overview: Anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) disease (Goodpasture disease) is a rare, severe autoimmune vasculitis mediated by pathogenic autoantibodies against the non-collagenous-1 (NC1) domain of the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen. It causes rapidly progressive crescentic glomerulonephritis and alveolar hemorrhage. Standard treatment is immediate initiation of plasmapheresis combined with high-dose corticosteroids and oral cyclophosphamide.

standard_knowledge.claim: KDIGO guidelines mandate immediate daily plasma exchange (for 14 days or until anti-GBM antibodies are undetectable) plus high-dose steroids and cyclophosphamide.
Renal prognosis is directly correlated with serum creatinine at presentation; patients presenting with dialysis-dependence and 100% cellular crescents rarely recover native kidney function.
Renal biopsy immunofluorescence demonstrates pathognomonic bright linear deposition of IgG (and often C3) along the glomerular capillary basement membrane.
Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole is mandatory during cyclophosphamide immunosuppression.

page.mentor_intro: IL-6 receptor blockade is effective in difficult-to-treat RA (tocilizumab 8 mg/4 weeks may be first choice), giant cell arteritis and refractory uveitis, and in hospitalised moderate-to-severe COVID-19. teaching_points.claim: A systematic review informing EULAR PMR/GCA recommendations found multiple trials supporting IL-6, IL-17 and JAK inhibition and B-cell depletion in GCA and PMR, though robust Takayasu trials are lacking.
French recommendations standardise use of immunosuppressants and biologics in giant cell arteritis.
Turkish recommendations note upadacitinib seems promising in GCA but needs more real-life safety data in the elderly with high cardiovascular risk.
A systematic review supports the 2026 JCS guideline on large-vessel vasculitis, with comparable adverse event rates between treatment groups.
Several pharmacological interventions are efficacious and generally safe for managing fatigue in inflammatory rheumatic diseases.
Tocilizumab and rituximab have better efficacy and safety in difficult-to-treat RA, with tocilizumab 8 mg every 4 weeks possibly first choice for remission.
Tocilizumab is a therapeutic option for refractory non-infectious uveitis after failure of conventional immunosuppressants and anti-TNF agents.

page.standard_overview: Interleukin-6 receptor (IL-6R) antagonist monoclonal antibodies (tocilizumab, sarilumab) block both soluble and membrane-bound IL-6 signaling. In rheumatology and immunology, anti-IL-6 therapy is standard of care for rheumatoid arthritis, giant cell arteritis (GiACTA trial), systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis, cytokine release syndrome (CRS) after CAR-T cell therapy, and severe hospitalized COVID-19.

standard_knowledge.claim: The GiACTA trial demonstrated that tocilizumab combined with a 26-week prednisone taper achieved 56% sustained remission at 52 weeks in giant cell arteritis compared to 14% with placebo.
Tocilizumab is the FDA-approved first-line therapy for severe or life-threatening chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell-induced cytokine release syndrome.
In hospitalized patients with severe COVID-19 hypoxia and systemic inflammation, tocilizumab significantly reduces 28-day mortality and progression to mechanical ventilation (RECOVERY trial).
Anti-IL-6 therapy completely suppresses hepatic C-reactive protein (CRP) synthesis; serum CRP cannot be used as an inflammatory marker to detect intercurrent bacterial infection.

page.standard_overview: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a top-tier global public health threat driven by the selective pressure of overuse and inappropriate antimicrobial prescribing in human health and agriculture. Pathogens of highest clinical priority ('ESKAPE': Enterococcus faecium, Staphylococcus aureus, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Enterobacter species) cause severe hospital-acquired infections with limited therapeutic options.

standard_knowledge.claim: The WHO Global Antimicrobial Resistance Report identifies carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) and Acinetobacter baumannii as critical priority pathogens.
Gram-negative resistance mechanisms include carbapenemases (KPC, NDM, VIM, OXA-48), extended-spectrum beta-lactamases (ESBLs), and porin loss / efflux pumps.
Novel beta-lactamase inhibitor combinations (ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, imipenem-relebactam, cefiderocol) provide targeted coverage for specific CRE classes.
Comprehensive infection prevention and control (hand hygiene, contact precautions, environmental disinfection) reduces horizontal nosocomial transmission of multidrug-resistant organisms.

page.standard_overview: Antimicrobial stewardship programs (ASPs) optimize clinical outcomes while minimizing unintended consequences of antimicrobial use, including toxicity, selection of pathogenic organisms (such as Clostridioides difficile), and the emergence of antimicrobial resistance. Core strategies include pre-authorization, prospective audit with feedback, evidence-based guidelines, and diagnostic stewardship.

standard_knowledge.claim: CDC and IDSA guidelines emphasize prospective audit and feedback as the most effective stewardship intervention to optimize antibiotic prescribing.
Implementing hospital-based ASPs significantly reduces overall antibiotic consumption, hospital-onset Clostridioides difficile infection, and institutional resistance rates.
Diagnostic stewardship ensures appropriate collection of microbiological cultures before antimicrobial initiation, preventing contaminated or unindicated blood and urine cultures.
Facility-specific antibiograms updated annually guide empirical therapy based on local pathogen susceptibility patterns rather than national estimates.

page.mentor_intro: In antiphospholipid syndrome, DOACs carry increased arterial thrombosis risk versus VKAs, so warfarin remains standard. Triple positivity and lupus anticoagulant predict adverse pregnancy outcomes, and aPS/PT antibodies are common in APS.

teaching_points.claim: For recurrent VTE on anticoagulation, evidence is minimal and expert-based, with options to switch or intensify anticoagulant therapy.
The RCOG guideline on recurrent miscarriage includes supportive care and treatments such as progesterone for bleeding in early pregnancy.
The Canadian recurrent pregnancy loss guideline stresses trauma-informed care and shared decision-making.
Patients with antiphospholipid syndrome randomised to DOACs compared with VKAs have increased risk of arterial thrombosis, with no significant difference in subsequent VTE or major bleeding.
Triple positivity, lupus anticoagulant positivity and laboratory category I are the most important predictors of adverse pregnancy outcomes in APS.
In SLE, predictors of adverse pregnancy outcomes include disease activity at conception and secondary antiphospholipid syndrome.
Phosphatidylserine/prothrombin antibodies are frequently positive in APS, especially in lupus anticoagulant positive patients, but their classification role needs study.

uncertainties: Optimal anticoagulation after recurrent VTE in APS.

page.standard_overview: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is a systemic autoimmune thrombophilia characterized by vascular thrombosis (arterial, venous, or microvascular) and/or pregnancy morbidity in the presence of persistent antiphospholipid antibodies (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, and anti-beta-2 glycoprotein I). Secondary prevention of venous thromboembolism requires lifelong therapeutic warfarin; DOACs are contraindicated in triple-positive APS.

standard_knowledge.claim: 2023 ACR/EULAR APS Classification Criteria incorporate modern weighted scoring across clinical domains (macrovascular, obstetric, microvascular) and laboratory antibody titers.
The TRAPS trial demonstrated that oral rivaroxaban was associated with an excess of arterial thrombotic events (mainly stroke) compared to warfarin in triple-positive APS.
Long-term therapeutic anticoagulation with warfarin targeting an INR of 2.0-3.0 is the standard of care for secondary prevention of venous thrombosis in APS.
Obstetric APS management requires combination low-dose aspirin (75-100 mg daily) and prophylactic-to-therapeutic LMWH throughout pregnancy and 6 weeks postpartum.

page.mentor_intro: Metformin is recommended for preventing and treating antipsychotic-induced weight gain, with consensus guidelines for co-commencement. GLP-1 agonists are promising, and second-generation antipsychotics differ in weight-gain propensity and dose-response.

teaching_points.claim: A consensus-validated guideline recommends metformin for preventing antipsychotic-induced weight gain, including co-commencement.
The BAP guideline covers management of weight gain, metabolic disturbance and cardiovascular risk associated with psychotropic drugs.
UK recommendations support optimised use of metformin when managing antipsychotic-induced weight gain.
Metformin is effective for treating antipsychotic-induced weight gain in schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder, but not for fasting glucose in one analysis.
Second-generation antipsychotics differ in propensity to produce weight gain and in the shapes of their dose-response curves.
GLP-1 agonists such as semaglutide and liraglutide are promising for antipsychotic-induced weight gain, with acceptable adverse effects and no worsening of psychopathology.
Antipsychotic-related weight gain is polygenic and associated with variants in genes coding for pharmacodynamic targets.
A meta-analysis described metabolic risk changes with second-generation antipsychotics from start of treatment to end of follow-up.

page.standard_overview: Second-generation (atypical) antipsychotics are effective for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and treatment-resistant depression, but carry significant cardiometabolic liabilities (weight gain, dyslipidemia, insulin resistance, type 2 diabetes, and accelerated cardiovascular mortality). High-risk agents include olanzapine and clozapine; intermediate-risk include quetiapine and risperidone; lowest-risk include aripiprazole, ziprasidone, and lurasidone.

standard_knowledge.claim: ADA/APA consensus guidelines mandate structured baseline and periodic metabolic monitoring: BMI and blood pressure at every visit; fasting glucose and lipid profile at 12 weeks, then annually.
Olanzapine and clozapine cause the greatest increases in adiposity, visceral fat, triglyceride levels, and incident diabetes through 5-HT2C, H1, and M3 receptor antagonism.
Metformin initiated early in antipsychotic treatment significantly attenuates drug-induced weight gain and improves insulin sensitivity.

Switching to a metabolic-neutral atypical antipsychotic (aripiprazole, lurasidone) or adding GLP-1 receptor agonists provides effective weight and glycemic reduction in established metabolic syndrome.

page.standard_overview: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) mandates antithrombotic therapy to balance the risks of leaflet thrombosis, thromboembolic stroke, and major bleeding. In patients without an underlying indication for oral anticoagulation, single antiplatelet therapy (aspirin 75-100 mg daily) is superior to dual antiplatelet therapy (DAPT), achieving equivalent ischemic protection with significantly lower bleeding (POPular TAVI trial).

standard_knowledge.claim: The POPular TAVI trial (Cohort A) demonstrated that aspirin monotherapy significantly reduced bleeding without increasing stroke or thromboembolic events compared to DAPT after TAVR.
In patients with pre-existing indications for oral anticoagulation, oral anticoagulation alone without antiplatelet therapy reduces major bleeding (POPular TAVI Cohort B).
Subclinical leaflet thrombosis (hypoattenuating leaflet thickening, HALT) occurs in 10-15% of bioprosthetic valves on four-dimensional cardiac CT, and is resolved with oral anticoagulation.
ESC/EACTS and ACC/AHA guidelines recommend single antiplatelet therapy (aspirin) as the standard default antithrombotic strategy in patients without OAC indications.

First-line evidence-based treatments are cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) and SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram) or SNRIs (venlafaxine, duloxetine). Benzodiazepines should be restricted to brief acute crisis stabilization due to risks of dependence and tolerance.

standard_knowledge.claim: NICE Guideline CG113 recommends CBT and SSRIs (sertraline as first-line) as the most effective long-term treatments for GAD and panic disorder.
Benzodiazepines are not recommended for long-term treatment of anxiety disorders due to tolerance, cognitive impairment, withdrawal rebound, and dependence.
Initial 'jitteriness / paradoxical anxiety' syndrome occurs during the first 1-2 weeks of SSRI initiation; start at half the standard starting dose and titrate gradually.
Pregabalin (alpha-2-delta ligand) is an approved non-benzodiazepine second-line option for generalized anxiety disorder with rapid onset of anxiolysis.

page.mentor_intro: Retrieved evidence centres on outcomes rather than the diagnostic pathway: type A dissection carries organ-specific malperfusion risk that predicts in-hospital death, and for type B the question is whether and when to add TEVAR to medical therapy. Guideline-level recommendations were not in the retrieved set.

teaching_points.claim: In acute type A aortic dissection, in-hospital survival varies with the type of malperfusion; mesenteric, coronary and cerebral malperfusion carried the highest in-hospital mortality, so organ-specific malperfusion should inform perioperative risk and surgical planning.
Women with type A dissection more often had pericardial effusion or tamponade, while in-hospital surgical mortality did not differ by sex (RR 1.02), suggesting a personalised approach.

A meta-analysis found TEVAR was associated with lower mortality than best medical therapy in type B dissection, especially in patients aged 65 or older, at the cost of longer hospital and ICU stays, with randomised trials still needed.

For uncomplicated type B dissection, the role of TEVAR remains debated: it improves aortic remodelling but there is no definitive survival evidence, and trials and guidelines that include high-risk features are needed.
Meta-analyses of TEVAR timing found the subacute phase (14-90 days from onset) associated with better long-term outcomes, including lower aortic-related death and reintervention.
Retrograde type A dissection after TEVAR is rare but carries high mortality (about 42%), especially in the first month and with proximal bare-stent grafts.
The GERAADA score showed better calibration than EuroSCORE II for 30-day mortality after surgery for acute type A dissection, though discrimination of both was moderate.
AI tools can feasibly detect aortic dissection on CT but do not yet demonstrate clinical applicability, and most studies were low quality.

uncertainties: Whether pre-emptive TEVAR improves survival in uncomplicated type B dissection.

page.standard_overview: Acute aortic dissection is a life-threatening cardiovascular emergency resulting from an intimal tear that creates a false lumen in the aortic media. Stanford Type A involves the ascending aorta (mandates emergent open surgical repair). Stanford Type B involves only the descending aorta distal to the left subclavian artery (managed with medical anti-impulse therapy using IV beta-blockers, reserving TEVAR for complicated Type B).

standard_knowledge.claim: ESC and AHA/ACC guidelines mandate emergent cardiothoracic surgical repair for Stanford Type A aortic dissection to prevent fatal tamponade, rupture, or coronary malperfusion.

Initial medical management requires anti-impulse therapy: IV beta-blockers (esmolol, labetalol) to reduce heart rate < 60 bpm and shear stress (dP/dt), followed by vasodilators to achieve SBP 100-120 mmHg.
Vasodilators (nitroprusside, nicardipine) must NEVER be started before beta-blockade, as reflex sympathetic tachycardia increases aortic wall shear stress and propagates the tear.
Thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) is indicated for complicated Stanford Type B dissection (refractory pain, rapid expansion, organ malperfusion, rupture).

page.standard_overview: Severe aortic stenosis (AS) is defined on transthoracic echocardiography by an aortic valve area (AVA) <= 1.0 cm2 (or indexed AVA <= 0.6 cm2/m2), mean transvalvular gradient >= 40 mmHg, or peak jet velocity >= 4.0 m/s. Once symptoms (angina, syncope, dyspnea) develop, 2-year mortality exceeds 50% without valve intervention. Low-flow low-gradient AS requires dobutamine stress echocardiography or non-contrast cardiac CT calcium scoring.

standard_knowledge.claim: ESC and AHA/ACC guidelines define severe aortic stenosis by AVA <= 1.0 cm2, mean gradient >= 40 mmHg, or peak velocity >= 4.0 m/s.
Low-dose dobutamine stress echocardiography differentiates true severe AS from pseudo-severe AS in low-flow low-gradient AS with reduced LVEF.
In paradoxical low-flow low-gradient AS with preserved LVEF, non-contrast cardiac CT aortic valve calcium scoring confirms severity (threshold >= 2,000 in men, >= 1,200 in women).
Aortic valve replacement (SAVR or TAVR) is indicated in all symptomatic patients with severe AS, and in asymptomatic patients with LVEF < 50% or abnormal exercise testing.

page.standard_overview: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) has transformed the treatment of severe symptomatic aortic stenosis across all surgical risk categories (high, intermediate, and low surgical risk). Valve selection between transfemoral TAVR and surgical aortic valve replacement (SAVR) is made by the Heart Team, considering patient age (TAVR favored in age >= 75; SAVR favored in age < 65), life expectancy, anatomical suitability, and vascular access.

standard_knowledge.claim: The PARTNER 3 and Evolut Low Risk trials demonstrated that transfemoral TAVR was non-inferior or superior to surgical aortic valve replacement in low-risk elderly patients.
ESC/EACTS guidelines recommend TAVR in older patients (age >= 75 years) or those who are inoperable or high surgical risk (STS/EuroSCORE II > 8%).
Complications of TAVR include complete heart block requiring permanent pacemaker implantation (higher with self-expanding valves), vascular access site injury, paravalvular leak, and stroke.
Pre-procedural planning requires ECG-gated multislice cardiac CT of the aortic root and iliofemoral vasculature for valve sizing and access evaluation.

page.mentor_intro: DOACs are as effective as and often safer than warfarin in AF, including CKD (CrCl 15 and above); evidence is weaker in dialysis. DOACs should be standard in low-risk AF needing anticoagulation, with correct dosing, and device-detected AF also benefits modestly.

teaching_points.claim: DOACs may increase efficacy and improve safety versus VKAs in AF with CKD (CrCl 15-90), with at least similar results in kidney failure.
In stage 5 CKD, DOACs showed a significant reduction in stroke and a non-significant trend to less major bleeding than VKAs.
In haemodialysis patients with AF, DOACs versus warfarin comparisons need validation by further prospective studies given thrombotic and bleeding risks.
DOACs should be standard of care in low-risk AF patients needing anticoagulation, with dabigatran showing the best balance of stroke prevention and bleeding reduction in one analysis.
A network meta-analysis found no difference in major bleeding, thromboembolism or mortality between DOACs and VKAs, and no DOAC clearly more favourable than others.
Anticoagulation with edoxaban or apixaban reduces stroke in device-detected AF and increases major bleeding.
Off-label underdosed DOACs, particularly rivaroxaban, were associated with increased ischaemic stroke without reduced bleeding, so on-label dosing should be emphasised.
DOACs may be a feasible option in AF with cirrhosis, pending validation.

uncertainties: Best strategy in dialysis patients.

page.standard_overview: Apixaban and rivaroxaban are direct factor Xa inhibitors widely prescribed for stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation and treatment of venous thromboembolism. Apixaban is administered twice daily (12-hour half-life) and has the lowest renal elimination (~27%) among DOACs. Rivaroxaban is administered once daily with food (to ensure absorption of 15 mg and 20 mg doses) and is 35% renally cleared. Large observational comparative studies show lower gastrointestinal bleeding and mortality with apixaban.

standard_knowledge.claim: Large real-world observational comparative effectiveness studies consistently associate apixaban with lower rates of major bleeding and gastrointestinal hemorrhage compared to rivaroxaban.
Rivaroxaban 15 mg and 20 mg tablets must strictly be taken with food to achieve predictable oral bioavailability (bioavailability falls to 66% in the fasting state).
Apixaban requires twice-daily dosing to maintain steady-state anticoagulation, reducing peak-to-trough plasma fluctuations compared to once-daily rivaroxaban.
Both agents are substrate of CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein, requiring dose adjustment or avoidance with strong dual inhibitors (ketoconazole, ritonavir) or inducers (rifampin, carbamazepine).

page.standard_overview: Severe aplastic anaemia (SAA) is an immune-mediated bone marrow failure disorder characterized by profound pancytopenia and hypocellular bone marrow (cellularity < 25-30%) without dysplasia or fibrosis. In young, fit patients (< 40-50 years) with an HLA-matched sibling donor, upfront allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation is curative. For older patients or those lacking a matched sibling, immunosuppressive therapy (IST) with horse anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG), cyclosporine, and the thrombopoietin receptor agonist eltrombopag achieves > 80% response rates.

standard_knowledge.claim: British Society for Haematology guidelines define SAA by bone marrow cellularity < 25% and at least two of: neutrophils < 0.5 x 10^9/L, platelets < 20 x 10^9/L, or reticulocytes < 60 x 10^9/L (Camitta criteria).
First-line allogeneic HCT from an HLA-matched sibling donor cures > 85-90% of children and young adults with severe aplastic anaemia.
Adding eltrombopag to horse ATG and cyclosporine significantly increases complete and overall hematologic response rates (87% vs 66%) in treatment-naive SAA (RACE trial).
Horse ATG (ATGAM) is clinically superior to rabbit ATG (Thymoglobulin) for initial immunosuppressive therapy in SAA.

page.standard_overview: Acute appendicitis is the most common surgical abdominal emergency, caused by luminal obstruction (fecalith, lymphoid hyperplasia) leading to distension, bacterial invasion, ischemia, and perforation. Diagnosis is supported by clinical decision rules (Alvarado, AIR scores) and confirmed by ultrasound in children/young females or contrast-enhanced CT in adults. Laparoscopic appendectomy remains the definitive standard of care, though selected uncomplicated cases can be managed with antibiotics.

standard_knowledge.claim: WSES guidelines recommend laparoscopic appendectomy as the gold-standard treatment for acute appendicitis, offering lower surgical site infection and faster recovery.

Antibiotic-first non-operative management (CODA trial) is successful in ~70% of uncomplicated appendicitis at 90 days, but is associated with a 29% appendectomy recurrence rate at 1 year.
Presence of an appendicolith on CT is strongly associated with non-operative antibiotic failure, recurrent appendicitis, and early perforation.

page.standard_overview: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is an acute diffuse inflammatory lung injury characterized by increased pulmonary vascular permeability, alveolar flooding, and severe refractory hypoxemia. The Berlin definition requires onset within 1 week of clinical insult, bilateral radiographic opacities not fully explained by heart failure, and PaO2/FiO2 <= 300 with PEEP >= 5 cmH2O. Core management relies on lung-protective ventilation (low tidal volumes, low driving pressure) and early prone positioning.

standard_knowledge.claim: The Berlin definition stages ARDS into mild (PaO2/FiO2 201-300), moderate (101-200), and severe (<= 100 mmHg) with minimum PEEP >= 5 cmH2O.
Lung-protective ventilation with low tidal volumes (4-8 mL/kg predicted body weight) and plateau pressure < 30 cmH2O significantly reduces 28-day mortality (ARMA trial).
Prone positioning for at least 16 consecutive hours daily reduces 28-day and 90-day mortality in severe ARDS with PaO2/FiO2 < 150 mmHg (PROSEVA trial).
Conservative fluid management strategy increases ventilator-free days and ICU-free days without increasing non-pulmonary organ failure (FACTT trial).

page.standard_overview: Arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis is a foundational diagnostic tool in critical care and emergency medicine. A systematic 6-step interpretation approach evaluates: 1) PaO2 and SaO2 for oxygenation, 2) pH for acidemia (< 7.35) or alkalemia (> 7.45), 3) PaCO2 for respiratory disturbances, 4) HCO3- and Base Excess for metabolic disturbances, 5) Serum anion gap (Na - [Cl + HCO3-], normal 10-12 mEq/L), and 6) Delta ratio (Delta AG / Delta HCO3-) to identify mixed metabolic disorders.

standard_knowledge.claim: A systematic 6-step algorithmic approach prevents overlooking hidden mixed acid-base disorders in critically ill ICU patients.
Anion gap calculation must be corrected for hypoalbuminemia: adjusted AG = observed AG + 2.5 * (4.0 - serum albumin in g/dL).
Winter's formula determines appropriate respiratory compensation in metabolic acidosis: expected PaCO2 = 1.5 * [HCO3-] + 8 (+/- 2).
Delta ratio (Delta AG / Delta HCO3-): < 0.4-0.8 indicates mixed high AG and normal AG metabolic acidosis; > 1.6-2.0 indicates concurrent metabolic alkalosis.

page.standard_overview: Arterial leg ulcers are painful, ischemic, non-healing lower extremity wounds resulting from peripheral artery disease (PAD) and microvascular insufficiency. They are typically deep, punched-out, painful (worse with elevation, relieved by hanging leg over bed), located on distally perfused sites (toes, lateral malleolus, heels), with pale/cyanotic skin and absent pulses. Diagnostic evaluation requires Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI), duplex ultrasound, and vascular surgery revascularization.

standard_knowledge.claim: AHA/ACC and ESVS guidelines establish that compression bandaging is strictly contraindicated in severe arterial ulcers with ABI < 0.5 or ankle pressure < 50 mmHg.
Ankle-Brachial Index (ABI) <= 0.90 is diagnostic of peripheral artery disease; values > 1.40 indicate non-compressible, calcified arteries warranting Toe-Brachial Index (TBI < 0.70).
Endovascular or surgical revascularization is the essential cornerstone of limb salvage in chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI / Rutherford stage 5-6).
Comprehensive medical therapy includes high-intensity statin, single antiplatelet therapy (clopidogrel 75 mg or low-dose rivaroxaban + aspirin [COMPASS trial]), and smoking cessation.

page.standard_overview: Asbestosis is a chronic interstitial pneumonitis and progressive pulmonary fibrosis caused by the inhalation of microscopic asbestos fibers. It typically manifests 20-30 years following substantial occupational exposure (shipyards, construction, insulation). Clinical features include exertional dyspnea, dry bibasilar inspiratory crackles, finger clubbing, and restrictive spirometry with reduced DLCO. HRCT shows subpleural curvilinear lines, parenchymal bands, and calcified pleural plaques.

standard_knowledge.claim: ATS criteria establish diagnosis based on documented history of significant asbestos exposure, latency > 20 years, restrictive lung defect with reduced DLCO, and characteristic HRCT fibrosis.
High-resolution chest CT demonstrates bilateral, predominantly subpleural and basilar fibrosis, accompanied by bilateral calcified parietal pleural plaques along ribs and diaphragm.
Pleural plaques indicate prior asbestos exposure but do not themselves cause significant functional lung impairment or undergo malignant transformation.

page.standard_overview: Ascites in cirrhosis results from sinusoidal portal hypertension, splanchnic arterial vasodilation, neurohumoral activation (RAAS, sympathetic nervous system), and avid renal sodium/water retention. Diagnostic paracentesis is mandatory at admission to calculate the serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) and exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (neutrophils >= 250/uL). First-line medical therapy combines dietary sodium restriction (< 2 g/day) with dual diuretic therapy (spironolactone plus furosemide).

standard_knowledge.claim: AASLD and EASL guidelines mandate diagnostic paracentesis in all patients hospitalized with new-onset or worsening cirrhotic ascites to rule out SBP.
Serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG = serum albumin - ascites albumin) >= 1.1 g/dL confirms portal hypertension with 97% accuracy.
First-line diuretic therapy uses a 100:40 mg ratio of spironolactone to furosemide, maintaining normokalemia while titrating to a maximum of 400:160 mg daily.
Large-volume paracentesis (> 5 L) requires concurrent intravenous albumin infusion (6-8 g per liter of ascites removed) to prevent paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunction (PICD).

page.standard_overview: Aspiration pneumonia occurs when colonized oropharyngeal or gastric secretions are inhaled into the lower respiratory tract, triggering acute bacterial infection. It must be distinguished from chemical aspiration pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome: acute gastric acid-induced chemical lung injury without initial bacterial infection). First-line antibiotic therapy for community-acquired aspiration pneumonia is ampicillin-sulbactam, amoxicillin-clavulanate, or moxifloxacin. Dedicated anaerobic coverage is reserved for lung abscess, empyema, or severe periodontal disease.

standard_knowledge.claim: IDSA/ATS guidelines recommend ampicillin-sulbactam or amoxicillin-clavulanate as preferred first-line therapy for community-acquired aspiration pneumonia.
Routine addition of specific anaerobic coverage (e.g. clindamycin or metronidazole) is no longer recommended for uncomplicated aspiration pneumonia unless lung abscess or empyema is present.
Aspiration pneumonitis (sterile acid chemical burn) presents hyperacutely with bronchospasm and infiltrates within 2-4 hours, typically resolving with supportive care without antibiotics.
Formal speech and language pathology swallowing assessment and post-pyloric feeding or thickened liquids reduce recurrent aspiration risk in post-stroke dysphagia.

page.standard_overview: Aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD / Samter triad) is a non-IgE-mediated pseudoallergic syndrome characterized by adult-onset asthma, recurrent chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP), and severe acute upper and lower respiratory reactions following the ingestion of aspirin or other COX-1-inhibiting NSAIDs. Pathophysiology involves arachidonic acid dysregulation with cysteinyl leukotriene overproduction. Treatment combines leukotriene modifiers, biologics (dupilumab), and aspirin desensitization.

standard_knowledge.claim: AERD is triggered by pharmacologic inhibition of cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), diverting arachidonic acid metabolism to the 5-lipoxygenase pathway and causing massive leukotriene release.
Selective COX-2 inhibitors (celecoxib, etoricoxib) do not trigger bronchospasm and are safe alternatives for analgesia in verified AERD.
Dupilumab (anti-IL-4Ralpha) and omalizumab (anti-IgE) achieve significant sinus polyp regression, asthma symptom control, and reduction in leukotriene production in AERD.
Aspirin desensitization followed by high-dose aspirin maintenance therapy (325-650 mg twice daily) provides disease-modifying reduction in nasal polyp recurrence.

page.mentor_intro: Modern asthma care favours inhaled corticosteroid-containing regimens, with as-needed ICS-formoterol or maintenance-and-reliever therapy rather than SABA alone. Severe asthma needs phenotyping and consideration of biologics, macrolides or triple inhaler therapy.

teaching_points.claim: The 2025 VA/DoD guideline strongly recommends inhaled corticosteroids and suggests ICS combined with a rapid-onset long-acting beta-agonist as both reliever and controller, with step-up by increasing ICS or adding a long-acting anticholinergic.
The ERS/ATS severe asthma guideline suggests a trial of chronic macrolide therapy for persistent symptoms at GINA step 5 and anti-IL-4/13 for severe eosinophilic or corticosteroid-dependent asthma.

The ACCP 2026 guideline gives seven recommendations on choosing a biologic, based on quality of life, lung function, exacerbation frequency, oral steroid use, endotype, biomarkers and comorbidities, while noting no comparative effectiveness trials.
A Spanish study found most guideline quality indicators of asthma care are not followed in practice.

In poorly controlled asthma at GINA step 3 or 4, budesonide-formoterol maintenance and reliever therapy lengthened time to first severe exacerbation compared with stepping up or continuing maintenance ICS-LABA with SABA reliever.
Triple versus dual inhaler therapy in moderate to severe asthma was associated with fewer severe exacerbations and modest control gains, without differences in quality of life or mortality.
Licensed asthma biologics reduce exacerbations and hospitalisations, improve lung function, control and quality of life, and limit systemic corticosteroid use, with greater effect in T2 inflammation.
Clinical remission is achievable for a minority on biologics, with lower rates in those with worse FEV1, longer disease, maintenance oral corticosteroids, depression or obesity.

uncertainties: Head-to-head comparative efficacy of biologics.

page.standard_overview: Asthma is a heterogeneous chronic inflammatory airway disease characterized by variable respiratory symptoms and variable expiratory airflow limitation. GINA 2024 recommendations establish inhaled corticosteroid (ICS)-formoterol as the preferred reliever and controller across Steps 1 to 5 (SMART/MART strategy). This eliminates SABA monotherapy, significantly reducing severe exacerbations and asthma-related mortality.

standard_knowledge.claim: GINA guidelines recommend as-needed low-dose ICS-formoterol as the preferred reliever across all asthma severities, eliminating short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA) monotherapy.
Single maintenance and reliever therapy (SMART / MART) with ICS-formoterol reduces severe exacerbations by 30-40% compared to fixed-dose ICS-LABA with SABA reliever.
Severe asthma requiring Step 5 care requires phenotyping for Type 2 inflammation: blood eosinophils >= 150-300 cells/uL, FeNO >= 20-25 ppb, or allergen sensitization.
Targeted biologic therapies (omalizumab, mepolizumab, benralizumab, dupilumab, tezepelumab) dramatically reduce exacerbations, oral steroid dependence, and hospitalizations.

page.mentor_intro: Licensed asthma biologics reduce exacerbations and hospitalisations, improve lung function, control and quality of life, and spare oral steroids, especially in T2 inflammation. Choice rests on endotype, biomarkers and comorbidities because head-to-head trials are lacking; clinical remission is achievable for a minority.

teaching_points.claim: The ACCP 2026 guideline gives seven recommendations on choosing a biologic based on quality of life, lung function, exacerbation frequency, oral steroid use, endotype, biomarkers and comorbidities, but no comparative effectiveness trials exist.

The EAACI systematic review found high certainty that benralizumab, dupilumab, mepolizumab and omalizumab reduce severe exacerbation rates, and benralizumab, dupilumab and mepolizumab reduce oral corticosteroid use.
The ERS/ATS guideline suggests anti-IL-4/13 for severe eosinophilic asthma and for corticosteroid-dependent asthma regardless of eosinophils.

Licensed asthma biologics reduce exacerbations and hospitalisations, improve lung function, asthma control and quality of life, and limit systemic corticosteroid use, with greater effect in T2 inflammation.
Head-to-head comparisons show small effect size differences with wide confidence interval overlap, and direct pragmatic trials assessing remission are needed.
Clinical remission is achievable for a minority treated with biologics, with lower rates in worse FEV1, longer disease, maintenance oral steroids, depression and obesity.
Real-world anti-IL5 biologics improve outcomes with effect sizes similar to RCTs, though data are largely retrospective.

uncertainties: Comparative efficacy of biologics.
