page.standard_overview: Acute severe asthma exacerbation is a life-threatening medical emergency. Management focuses on rapid reversal of airflow obstruction, correction of hypoxemia, and prevention of respiratory arrest. First-line therapy includes repetitive inhaled SABA (albuterol/salbutamol) combined with ipratropium bromide, early systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone 40-50 mg daily for 5-7 days), controlled oxygen targeting SpO2 93-95%, and IV magnesium sulfate for severe or refractory cases.

standard_knowledge.claim: GINA and BTS/SIGN guidelines mandate early systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone 40-50 mg daily) within 1 hour of ED presentation to accelerate resolution and prevent relapse.
Combining inhaled ipratropium bromide with albuterol in acute moderate-to-severe exacerbations significantly reduces hospital admission rates and improves FEV1.
Single-dose intravenous magnesium sulfate (2g IV over 20 minutes) reduces hospital admissions in severe exacerbations with FEV1 < 50% or poor initial response.
A 'normal' or rising PaCO2 (>= 40-45 mmHg) in a severely tachypneic patient signifies impending respiratory muscle fatigue and catastrophic arrest.

page.mentor_intro: Modern asthma care favours inhaled corticosteroid-containing regimens, with as-needed ICS-formoterol or maintenance-and-reliever therapy rather than SABA alone. Severe asthma needs phenotyping and consideration of biologics, macrolides or triple inhaler therapy.

teaching_points.claim: The 2025 VA/DoD guideline strongly recommends inhaled corticosteroids and suggests ICS combined with a rapid-onset long-acting beta-agonist as both reliever and controller, with step-up by increasing ICS or adding a long-acting anticholinergic.
The ERS/ATS severe asthma guideline suggests a trial of chronic macrolide therapy for persistent symptoms at GINA step 5 and anti-IL-4/13 for severe eosinophilic or corticosteroid-dependent asthma.

The ACCP 2026 guideline gives seven recommendations on choosing a biologic, based on quality of life, lung function, exacerbation frequency, oral steroid use, endotype, biomarkers and comorbidities, while noting no comparative effectiveness trials.
A Spanish study found most guideline quality indicators of asthma care are not followed in practice.

In poorly controlled asthma at GINA step 3 or 4, budesonide-formoterol maintenance and reliever therapy lengthened time to first severe exacerbation compared with stepping up or continuing maintenance ICS-LABA with SABA reliever.
Triple versus dual inhaler therapy in moderate to severe asthma was associated with fewer severe exacerbations and modest control gains, without differences in quality of life or mortality.
Licensed asthma biologics reduce exacerbations and hospitalisations, improve lung function, control and quality of life, and limit systemic corticosteroid use, with greater effect in T2 inflammation.
Clinical remission is achievable for a minority on biologics, with lower rates in those with worse FEV1, longer disease, maintenance oral corticosteroids, depression or obesity.

uncertainties: Head-to-head comparative efficacy of biologics.
Definition of clinical remission.

page.standard_overview: Asthma affects approximately 8-10% of pregnant women. The rule of thirds applies: one-third improve, one-third remain unchanged, and one-third worsen during pregnancy. Uncontrolled asthma with maternal hypoxia carries significant risks of pre-eclampsia, preterm birth, low birth weight, and perinatal mortality. Inhaled corticosteroids (budesonide preferred) and SABA relievers are safe and must be actively maintained throughout pregnancy.

standard_knowledge.claim: ACOG and GINA guidelines emphasize that it is far safer for pregnant women to take asthma medications than to experience asthma exacerbations or hypoxia.
Inhaled budesonide is the preferred maintenance inhaled corticosteroid in pregnancy due to the largest volume of human safety data.
Acute asthma exacerbations in pregnancy require aggressive treatment: controlled oxygen targeting maternal SpO2 >= 95% to maintain adequate fetal oxygenation.
Systemic corticosteroids (oral prednisolone) should never be withheld in acute severe asthma exacerbations, as maternal hypoxia poses immediate fetal risk.

page.standard_overview: Atherosclerotic renal artery stenosis (ARAS) is common in elderly patients with generalized vascular disease. Landmark randomized controlled trials (ASTRAL and CORAL) demonstrated that routine percutaneous renal artery stenting does NOT provide incremental benefit over optimal medical therapy alone for blood pressure control, preservation of renal function, or reduction in cardiovascular events. Medical therapy with statins, antiplatelets, and antihypertensives is first-line; stenting is reserved for flash pulmonary edema or truly refractory hypertension.

standard_knowledge.claim: The CORAL trial demonstrated that renal-artery stenting added to medical therapy did not reduce cardiovascular or renal events in atherosclerotic renal-artery stenosis.
The ASTRAL trial showed no evidence of clinically meaningful benefit of renal-artery revascularization on renal function or survival compared to medical therapy.

AHA/ACC and ESC guidelines restrict renal artery stenting to high-risk clinical presentations: recurrent unexplained flash pulmonary edema (Pickering syndrome) or refractory hypertension resistant to >= 4 medications.
ACE inhibitors and ARBs are safe and reduce cardiovascular mortality in unilateral ARAS, but can cause acute reversible decline in GFR (> 30%) in bilateral high-grade stenosis.

Dupilumab may unmask or exacerbate cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, particularly mycosis fungoides and Sezary syndrome, so consensus recommendations guide patient selection and reassessment.

The ACG evidence-to-recommendation framework for mild and moderate atopic dermatitis weighs benefits, certainty, patient preferences and feasibility.
Real-world effectiveness and safety of JAK inhibitors in atopic dermatitis are comparable to clinical trials.
Increased pollutants and temperature extremes are associated with a higher population burden of atopic dermatitis.

page.standard_overview: Atopic dermatitis (eczema) is a chronic, relapsing, pruritic inflammatory skin disease characterized by epidermal barrier dysfunction (often associated with filaggrin mutations) and immune dysregulation with prominent Th2 cytokine activation (IL-4, IL-13). Management follows a stepwise approach: daily bland emollients, topical corticosteroids or topical calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus) for flares, and targeted systemic biologics (dupilumab, tralokinumab) or oral JAK inhibitors for moderate-to-severe refractory disease.

standard_knowledge.claim: AAD guidelines recommend proactive twice-weekly application of topical calcineurin inhibitors or low-potency steroids to previously affected sites to prevent recurrent flares.
Dupilumab (monoclonal antibody blocking IL-4Ralpha, inhibiting IL-4 and IL-13 signaling) achieves 75% reduction in EASI score in over 50-60% of patients without organ toxicity (SOLO 1 and 2 trials).
Oral JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib, abrocitinib, baricitinib) provide rapid pruritus relief and cutaneous clearance in moderate-to-severe atopic dermatitis.
Eczema herpeticum (disseminated cutaneous herpes simplex virus infection) is a dermatological emergency requiring immediate oral or intravenous acyclovir.

page.mentor_intro: Catheter ablation reduces mortality, stroke and heart failure hospitalisation compared with medical therapy in AF, including in AF with heart failure and in HFpEF. A 4-week blanking period may be optimal, and uninterrupted NOACs cut major bleeding periprocedurally.

teaching_points.claim: A review compares guidelines and consensus documents on AF catheter ablation.
In AF with heart failure, catheter ablation reduces mortality and heart failure hospitalisation compared with medical therapy (RR 0.60 for hospitalisation).
Catheter ablation of AF significantly reduces death, stroke and hospitalisation compared with medical therapy alone.
In HFpEF with AF, catheter ablation showed cardiovascular morbidity and mortality benefits compared with standard medical therapy, and lower AF recurrence.
A 4-week blanking period may be the optimal cutoff after AF ablation, supporting revision of the current 3-month period.
Uninterrupted periprocedural NOACs are associated with low stroke or TIA and significantly less major bleeding than uninterrupted VKAs during AF ablation.
Most oesophageal injuries after AF ablation resolved conservatively, while a small percentage of type 2b lesions progressed to perforation or fistula.

page.standard_overview: Stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation is guided by the CHA2DS2-VASc risk score. Oral anticoagulation is recommended for men with score >= 2 and women with score >= 3, and should be considered for men with score 1 and women with score 2. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban) are preferred over warfarin due to a 50% reduction in intracranial hemorrhage.

standard_knowledge.claim: ESC 2024 guidelines recommend DOACs over warfarin as first-line stroke prevention for non-valvular atrial fibrillation (Class I, Level A).
CHA2DS2-VASc score assigns points: CHF (1), HTN (1), Age >= 75 (2), Diabetes (1), Stroke/TIA/thromboembolism (2), Vascular disease (1), Age 65-74 (1), Sex female (1).
Female sex is a risk modifier rather than an independent risk factor; a female with no other risk factors (CHA2DS2-VASc = 1) does NOT require anticoagulation.
Meta-analysis of landmark DOAC trials demonstrates a 19% relative reduction in stroke/systemic embolism and a 51% reduction in hemorrhagic stroke compared to warfarin.

page.mentor_intro: DOACs are as effective as and often safer than warfarin in AF, including CKD (CrCl 15 and above); evidence is weaker in dialysis. DOACs should be standard in low-risk AF needing anticoagulation, with correct dosing, and device-detected AF also benefits modestly.

teaching_points.claim: DOACs may increase efficacy and improve safety versus VKAs in AF with CKD (CrCl 15-90), with at least similar results in kidney failure.
In stage 5 CKD, DOACs showed a significant reduction in stroke and a non-significant trend to less major bleeding than VKAs.
In haemodialysis patients with AF, DOACs versus warfarin comparisons need validation by further prospective studies given thrombotic and bleeding risks.
DOACs should be standard of care in low-risk AF patients needing anticoagulation, with dabigatran showing the best balance of stroke prevention and bleeding reduction in one analysis.
A network meta-analysis found no difference in major bleeding, thromboembolism or mortality between DOACs and VKAs, and no DOAC clearly more favourable than others.
Anticoagulation with edoxaban or apixaban reduces stroke in device-detected AF and increases major bleeding.
Off-label underdosed DOACs, particularly rivaroxaban, were associated with increased ischaemic stroke without reduced bleeding, so on-label dosing should be emphasised.
DOACs may be a feasible option in AF with cirrhosis, pending validation.

uncertainties: Best strategy in dialysis patients.

page.standard_overview: Atrial fibrillation is highly prevalent in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD), significantly increasing stroke and bleeding risks. Direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban, edoxaban, dabigatran) provide superior or non-inferior stroke prevention compared to warfarin in mild-to-moderate CKD (CrCl 30-50 mL/min). In severe CKD (CrCl 15-29 mL/min) and dialysis, apixaban is increasingly utilized with specific dose reduction criteria.

standard_knowledge.claim: KDIGO 2023 guidelines recommend DOACs over vitamin K antagonists (warfarin) in patients with non-valvular AF and CKD Stages 1-3, and consider DOACs in Stage 4 (CrCl 15-29 mL/min).
Apixaban requires dose reduction to 2.5 mg BID if the patient meets at least two of the following criteria: age >= 80 years, body weight <= 60 kg, or serum creatinine >= 1.5 mg/dL (133 umol/L).
Warfarin in advanced CKD and dialysis accelerates vascular calcification and calcific uremic arteriolopathy (calciphylaxis) by inhibiting vitamin K-dependent matrix Gla protein.
Dabigatran is 80% renally eliminated and is contraindicated when CrCl < 30 mL/min in European guidelines.

page.standard_overview: Atypical pneumonia is caused by organisms that lack a peptidoglycan cell wall (Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae) or are obligate/facultative intracellular pathogens (Legionella pneumophila, Coxiella burnetii [Q fever]). Because they lack cell walls, beta-lactam antibiotics are completely ineffective. Diagnostic workup uses urinary antigen testing (for Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1) and respiratory multiplex PCR. First-line therapy relies on macrolides (azithromycin), respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin), or tetracyclines (doxycycline).

standard_knowledge.claim: Beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins) are inherently inactive against Mycoplasma and Chlamydia due to the absence of a bacterial peptidoglycan cell wall.
Legionella urinary antigen testing is rapid, specific (> 95%), and detects Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1 (responsible for 70-80% of community-acquired legionellosis).
IDSA/ATS guidelines recommend respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) or azithromycin as first-line treatment for Legionnaires' disease.

Extrapulmonary manifestations: Mycoplasma is associated with cold agglutinin autoimmune hemolytic anemia, erythema multiforme, and bullous myringitis; Legionella causes hyponatremia, diarrhea, and confusion.

page.standard_overview: Autoantibody panels are essential diagnostic instruments in systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases (SARD), but must be interpreted strictly within the pre-test clinical context to avoid false-positive misdiagnoses. Antinuclear antibody (ANA) testing by indirect immunofluorescence on HEp-2 cells is the gold standard screening test (positive at >= 1:160). Downstream extractable nuclear antigen (ENA) testing differentiates specific diseases: anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm (SLE), anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB (Sjögren/SLE/congenital heart block), anti-Scl-70 (diffuse systemic sclerosis), anti-centromere (limited systemic sclerosis), anti-Jo-1 (myositis), anti-CCP and RF (rheumatoid arthritis), and ANCA (systemic vasculitis).

standard_knowledge.claim: EULAR/ACR 2019 criteria mandate positive ANA by HEp-2 immunofluorescence at a titer >= 1:80 as the required entry criterion for the classification of SLE.
Anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies have high diagnostic specificity (> 96%) for rheumatoid arthritis and predict progressive radiographic erosive joint damage.
Anti-dsDNA antibody titers correlate with disease activity and active lupus nephritis; falling complement (C3, C4) alongside rising anti-dsDNA signals an impending clinical flare.
Anti-Ro/SSA antibodies in pregnant women cross the placenta and carry a 2% risk of causing neonatal lupus erythematosus and irreversible congenital complete heart block in the fetus.

page.standard_overview: Autoimmune encephalitis (AIE) is a rapidly progressive inflammatory brain disease caused by autoantibodies directed against neuronal cell-surface synaptic antigens (e.g. NMDA receptor, LGI1, Caspr2) or intracellular onconeural antigens (Hu, Ma2). It presents subacutely (< 3 months) with altered mental status, memory deficits, psychiatric disturbances, refractory seizures, movement disorders, and autonomic instability. First-line immunotherapy consists of high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, IVIG, or plasma exchange, alongside screening for occult systemic tumors (e.g. ovarian teratoma in anti-NMDAR).

page.standard_overview: Autoimmune gastritis (AIG) is a chronic, immune-mediated, organ-specific gastritis directed against gastric parietal cells and their secretory products (H+/K+-ATPase and intrinsic factor). standard_knowledge.claim: Destruction of gastric parietal cells leads to achlorhydria, high fasting serum gastrin, and lack of intrinsic factor causing vitamin B12 deficiency (pernicious anemia).

page.standard_overview: Autoimmune hepatitis (AIH) is a chronic, progressive necroinflammatory liver disease characterized by circulating autoantibodies, hypergammaglobulinemia (elevated IgG), and interface hepatitis on liver biopsy. page.standard_overview: Autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP) is a unique form of chronic fibroinflammatory pancreatitis. Type 1 AIP (lymphoplasmacytic sclerosing pancreatitis; LPSP) is the classic pancreatic manifestation of systemic IgG4-related disease, presenting in older males with painless obstructive jaundice, elevated serum IgG4, diffuse sausage-like pancreatic enlargement, and prompt response to corticosteroids. Type 2 AIP (idiopathic duct-centric pancreatitis; IDCP) is pancreas-specific, affects younger adults equally by sex, is associated with inflammatory bowel disease in 30%, and has normal IgG4 levels.

standard_knowledge.claim: International Consensus Diagnostic Criteria (ICDC) classify AIP into Type 1 (systemic IgG4-related) and Type 2 (pancreas-specific, associated with IBD) using five cardinal features (HISORt criteria).
Type 1 AIP is characterized by elevated serum IgG4 (> 1-2x upper limit of normal), storiform fibrosis, obliterative phlebitis, and abundant IgG4-positive plasma cells (> 10 per HPF).
Oral corticosteroids (prednisone 0.6-0.8 mg/kg daily, typically 30-40 mg daily for 2-4 weeks, then tapered) achieve rapid clinical and radiological remission in > 90% of AIP patients.
Rituximab (anti-CD20) is highly effective for inducing and maintaining remission in steroid-dependent or relapsing Type 1 IgG4-related AIP.

page.standard_overview: Autoimmune polyglandular syndromes (APS) are clusters of multiple endocrine gland deficiencies combined with non-endocrine autoimmune diseases. APS-1 (APECED) is a rare monogenic autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations in the autoimmune regulator (AIRE) gene, presenting in childhood with the classic triad of chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease). APS-2 (Schmidt syndrome) is a polygenic disorder occurring in adults, defined by primary adrenal insufficiency combined with autoimmune thyroid disease and/or type 1 diabetes mellitus.

standard_knowledge.claim: APS-1 is diagnosed clinically by the presence of at least 2 of the 3 cardinal features: chronic mucocutaneous candidiasis, hypoparathyroidism, and Addison disease.
APS-1 is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the AIRE gene on chromosome 21q22.3, which disrupts central thymic negative selection of self-reactive T cells.
APS-2 is strongly associated with HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4 haplotypes; primary adrenal insufficiency is the mandatory component, accompanied by autoimmune thyroiditis or type 1 diabetes.

page.standard_overview: Cardiovascular autonomic dysfunction encompasses disorders of autonomic blood pressure and heart rate regulation, primarily Postural Orthostatic Tachycardia Syndrome (POTS), Neurogenic Orthostatic Hypotension (nOH), and Vasovagal (neurocardiogenic) Syncope. POTS is defined as a sustained heart rate increase >= 30 bpm (or >= 40 bpm in individuals aged 12-19) within 10 minutes of standing or head-up tilt, in the absence of orthostatic hypotension. Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a sustained drop in SBP >= 20 mmHg or DBP >= 10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing. Management emphasizes non-pharmacological volume expansion, compression garments, exercise conditioning, and targeted pharmacotherapy (midodrine, fludrocortisone, droxidopa, pyridostigmine, ivabradine).

standard_knowledge.claim: AHA/ACC and HRS guidelines define POTS as sustained HR increase >= 30 bpm within 10 min of standing without orthostatic hypotension, accompanied by chronic orthostatic symptoms for >= 3 months.

First-line non-pharmacological management for POTS and orthostatic hypotension includes oral fluid loading (2-3 L/day), dietary sodium (8-10 g/day), waist-high compression garments, and recumbent aerobic exercise training.
Neurogenic orthostatic hypotension (nOH) is caused by impaired norepinephrine release in neurodegenerative synucleinopathies (Parkinson disease, Multiple System Atrophy, Pure Autonomic Failure).

Pharmacological therapies: fludrocortisone expands plasma volume; midodrine (alpha-1 agonist) and droxidopa (norepinephrine prodrug) increase peripheral vascular resistance; ivabradine lowers sinus tachycardia without causing hypotension.

page.standard_overview: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) is the most common monogenic kidney disease, primarily caused by PKD1 (~78%) and PKD2 (~15%) mutations. Tolvaptan, an oral selective vasopressin V2 receptor antagonist, slows kidney cyst growth and decelerates the rate of eGFR decline in rapidly progressing ADPKD (TEMPO 3:4 and REPRISE trials). Candidates are stratified by Mayo Imaging Classification (Classes 1C, 1D, 1E) or rapid eGFR decline (>= 3.0 mL/min/1.73 m2/year). Due to idiosyncratic hepatotoxicity, mandatory monthly liver function monitoring is required for the first 18 months and quarterly thereafter.

standard_knowledge.claim: Tolvaptan slowed total kidney volume growth by 49% and reduced annual eGFR decline by ~1.0 mL/min/1.73 m2 in rapid progressors (TEMPO 3:4 trial).
In later-stage ADPKD (CKD G2-G4, eGFR 25-65 mL/min/1.73 m2), tolvaptan sustained a significant slowing of eGFR loss by 1.27 mL/min/1.73 m2/year (REPRISE trial).
KDIGO/ERA-EDTA consensus recommends tolvaptan specifically for adult ADPKD patients with evidence of rapid disease progression (Mayo Class 1C-1E or eGFR decline >= 3.0 mL/min/1.73 m2/year).

Tolvaptan causes severe aquaresis (polyuria 5-7 L/day, thirst, nocturia) and carries a black-box warning for drug-induced liver injury, necessitating monthly hepatic transaminase monitoring for 18 months.

page.standard_overview: Avascular necrosis (AVN, osteonecrosis) of bone results from compromised microvascular blood supply leading to osteocyte death, subchondral microfractures, and eventual structural joint collapse, predominantly affecting the femoral head. Major etiologies include high-dose systemic corticosteroid therapy, chronic excess alcohol use, sickle cell disease, trauma (femoral neck fracture), and systemic lupus erythematosus. Early pre-collapse diagnosis is achieved using MRI (pathognomonic 'double-line sign' on T2-weighted sequences). Pre-collapse stages (Ficat I-II) are managed with core decompression +/- bone marrow aspirate concentrate, whereas post-collapse stages (Ficat III-IV) necessitate total joint arthroplasty.

standard_knowledge.claim: MRI is the most sensitive and specific diagnostic imaging modality, detecting early pre-collapse osteonecrosis (T1 low-signal band, T2 double-line sign) when radiographs are normal.
High-dose corticosteroid exposure (> 20 mg/day prednisone equivalent for prolonged duration) and chronic alcohol use account for > 70-80% of non-traumatic AVN cases.

Ficat and Arlet staging guides surgical management: Stage I-II (pre-collapse) candidates for joint-preserving core decompression; Stage III-IV (crescent sign, subchondral collapse, osteoarthritis) require total hip arthroplasty (THA).

In sickle cell disease, repeated microvascular sickling and marrow expansion drive bilateral femoral and humeral head osteonecrosis requiring early multidisciplinary hematology-orthopedic intervention.

page.standard_overview: Axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA) is a chronic inflammatory rheumatologic disease characterized by involvement of the axial skeleton, enthesitis, and extra-articular manifestations (uveitis, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease). The ASAS classification criteria define two arms for patients with chronic back pain >= 3 months starting before age 45: the Imaging Arm (sacroiliitis on MRI showing active bone marrow edema or definite radiographic sacroiliitis by modified New York criteria, plus >= 1 SpA feature) and the Clinical Arm (HLA-B27 positivity plus >= 2 SpA features). Non-radiographic axSpA (nr-axSpA) shares identical symptom severity and disease burden with radiographic ankylosing spondylitis (AS).

standard_knowledge.claim: The ASAS classification criteria provide > 82% sensitivity and specificity for axSpA, encompassing both radiographic AS and non-radiographic axSpA (nr-axSpA).
MRI is the imaging gold standard for early disease: ASAS consensus requires active subchondral bone marrow edema (osteitis) on STIR/T2-weighted images adjacent to the sacroiliac joints.
Non-radiographic axSpA (nr-axSpA) exhibits similar symptom burden, inflammatory pain, functional impairment, and response to biologic therapy compared to radiographic ankylosing spondylitis.
First-line pharmacotherapy for both nr-axSpA and AS is full-dose continuous or on-demand Nonsteroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drugs (NSAIDs) with physical therapy.

page.standard_overview: Biologic and targeted synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (b/tsDMARDs) are indicated in axial spondyloarthritis with persistently high disease activity (ASDAS >= 2.1 or BASDAI >= 4) despite trials of at least two different full-dose NSAIDs. Approved classes include TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept, golimumab, certolizumab pegol), IL-17A inhibitors (secukinumab, ixekizumab), dual IL-17A/F inhibitors (bimekizumab), and oral JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib, tofacitinib). In patients with concomitant active inflammatory bowel disease or recurrent anterior uveitis, monoclonal anti-TNF antibodies (adalimumab, infliximab, certolizumab) are preferred over etanercept and IL-17 inhibitors.

standard_knowledge.claim: ACR/EULAR guidelines recommend initiating a TNF inhibitor or IL-17A inhibitor when axSpA remains active despite adequate trials of >= 2 NSAIDs over 4 weeks.
Secukinumab (MEASURE trials) and ixekizumab (COAST trials) demonstrate significant and sustained reductions in ASDAS, spinal inflammation, and physical disability.

In axSpA with comorbid recurrent uveitis or inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease or ulcerative colitis), anti-TNF monoclonal antibodies are preferred; etanercept lacks efficacy for uveitis/IBD, and IL-17 inhibitors can exacerbate IBD.
Oral JAK inhibitors (upadacitinib [SELECT-AXIS trials], tofacitinib) are approved for active axSpA non-responsive to NSAIDs or biologics.

page.mentor_intro: Bacterial meningitis is time-critical: antibiotics later than two hours after presentation roughly double mortality. Case fatality has fallen over eighty years but remains high; molecular and host-marker tests may help when cultures are negative.

teaching_points.claim: In community-acquired bacterial meningitis, odds of mortality increase markedly when antibiotics are given later than two hours after presentation, and delay raised the odds of neurological impairment (aOR 1.79).

page.standard_overview: Acute community-acquired bacterial meningitis is a life-threatening neurologic emergency requiring immediate empiric parenteral bactericidal antibiotics and adjuvant dexamethasone. Most common pathogens are Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and in adults >= 50 or immunocompromised hosts, Listeria monocytogenes. Standard empiric therapy in adults < 50 is IV ceftriaxone (2 g q12h) plus IV vancomycin (15-20 mg/kg q8-12h); adults >= 50 or immunocompromised require the addition of IV ampicillin (2 g q4h) to cover Listeria. Adjuvant dexamethasone (10 mg IV) must be administered prior to or with the first dose of antibiotics to attenuate inflammatory mortality and sensorineural hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis.

standard_knowledge.claim: Adjuvant intravenous dexamethasone (10 mg q6h for 4 days) initiated prior to or concurrently with the first antibiotic dose reduces mortality and hearing loss in pneumococcal meningitis.
Empiric therapy for adults < 50: ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) plus vancomycin; adults >= 50, alcoholics, or immunocompromised patients must receive ampicillin to cover Listeria monocytogenes.

Lumbar puncture should NOT be delayed for neuroimaging unless specific indications exist: focal neurological deficit, new-onset seizures, papilledema, severely altered consciousness (GCS < 10), or immunocompromised state.
If neuroimaging is required prior to LP, blood cultures must be drawn immediately and empiric antibiotics plus dexamethasone administered without waiting for the CT scan.

page.standard_overview: Metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) is the most effective and durable intervention for severe obesity and related cardiometabolic comorbidities. The ASMBS/IFSO 2022 guidelines recommend MBS for individuals with BMI >= 35 kg/m2 regardless of comorbidities, and BMI 30-34.9 kg/m2 with obesity-related conditions (e.g. type 2 diabetes). The landmark STAMPEDE trial demonstrated that Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) and sleeve gastrectomy (SG) achieve superior glycemic control, diabetes remission, and reduction in cardiovascular medications compared to intensive medical therapy out to 5 years. RYGB has higher rates of internal hernia, marginal ulcers, and micronutrient malabsorption (iron, calcium, vitamin B12, copper), whereas sleeve gastrectomy has higher risks of de novo or worsening gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

standard_knowledge.claim: ASMBS/IFSO 2022 guidelines expand indications for bariatric surgery to BMI >= 35 kg/m2 regardless of comorbidities and BMI >= 30 kg/m2 with metabolic disease (lowered to 27.5 for Asian populations).

The 5-year STAMPEDE trial proved bariatric surgery combined with medical therapy is significantly more effective than intensive medical therapy alone in achieving glycemic control (HbA1c <= 6.0%) and reducing cardiovascular risk in type 2 diabetes.
Nutritional deficiencies are common: lifelong supplementation is mandatory for vitamin B12, vitamin D, calcium citrate, iron, and multivitamin with minerals.

Major complications: RYGB predisposes to internal Petersen hernia, marginal anastomotic ulcers, and dumping syndrome (early vasomotor vs late hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia); SG can cause severe reflux and gastric stenosis.

page.standard_overview: Metabolic and bariatric surgery (MBS) is the most effective and durable intervention for severe obesity and related cardiometabolic comorbidities. The ASMBS/IFSO 2022 guidelines recommend MBS for individuals with BMI >= 35 kg/m2 regardless of comorbidities, and BMI 30-34.9 kg/m2 with obesity-related conditions (e.g. type 2 diabetes). The landmark STAMPEDE trial demonstrated that Roux-en-Y gastric bypass (RYGB) and sleeve gastrectomy (SG) achieve superior glycemic control, diabetes remission, and reduction in cardiovascular medications compared to intensive medical therapy out to 5 years. RYGB has higher rates of internal hernia, marginal ulcers, and micronutrient malabsorption (iron, calcium, vitamin B12, copper), whereas sleeve gastrectomy has higher risks of de novo or worsening gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD).

standard_knowledge.claim: ASMBS/IFSO 2022 guidelines expand indications for bariatric surgery to BMI >= 35 kg/m2 regardless of comorbidities and BMI >= 30 kg/m2 with metabolic disease (lowered to 27.5 for Asian populations).

The 5-year STAMPEDE trial proved bariatric surgery combined with medical therapy is significantly more effective than intensive medical therapy alone in achieving glycemic control (HbA1c <= 6.0%) and reducing cardiovascular risk in type 2 diabetes.
Nutritional deficiencies are common: lifelong supplementation is mandatory for vitamin B12, vitamin D, calcium citrate, iron, and multivitamin with minerals.

Major complications: RYGB predisposes to internal Petersen hernia, marginal anastomotic ulcers, and dumping syndrome (early vasomotor vs late hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia); SG can cause severe reflux and gastric stenosis.

teaching_points.claim: A Joint British guideline recommends specialist diabetes follow-up and inpatient diabetes care for people undergoing metabolic-bariatric surgery.

GLP-1 receptor agonists after bariatric surgery give significant weight loss and cardiometabolic improvements versus placebo or lifestyle.
Erector spinae plane block reduces opioid consumption and middle and late postoperative pain after bariatric surgery compared with TAP block.

page.standard_overview: Barrett's esophagus (BE) is the replacement of normal stratified squamous esophageal epithelium by specialized intestinal metaplasia with goblet cells, predisposing to esophageal adenocarcinoma. Diagnosis requires endoscopically visible columnar epithelium >= 1 cm proximal to the gastroesophageal junction (Prague C & M criteria) and histological confirmation of intestinal metaplasia. ACG guidelines recommend endoscopic surveillance every 3-5 years for non-dysplastic BE. For confirmed low-grade dysplasia (LGD), endoscopic eradication therapy (EET) via endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) for visible nodular lesions followed by radiofrequency ablation (RFA) is preferred over surveillance; high-grade dysplasia (HGD) and intramucosal carcinoma mandate immediate EET.

standard_knowledge.claim: ACG and BSG guidelines define Barrett's esophagus as salmon-colored columnar mucosa extending >= 1 cm proximal to GEJ with intestinal metaplasia (goblet cells) on histology.

Endoscopic eradication therapy (visible lesion EMR + radiofrequency ablation) is the standard of care for high-grade dysplasia and intramucosal adenocarcinoma, eradicating dysplasia in > 90% (SURF and AIM-Dysplasia trials).

For confirmed low-grade dysplasia (verified by an expert gastrointestinal pathologist), endoscopic ablation significantly reduces 3-year progression to HGD/adenocarcinoma from 26.5% to 1.5% compared to surveillance.
Non-dysplastic Barrett's esophagus carries a low annual risk of cancer progression (0.2-0.3% per year), warranting surveillance endoscopy every 3-5 years rather than ablative eradication.

page.standard_overview: Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is the most common human malignancy, driven by ultraviolet radiation-induced oncogenic mutations activating the Hedgehog (PTCH1/SMO) signaling pathway. Clinical subtypes include nodular (pearly papule with telangiectasias and rolled borders), superficial (erythematous scaly plaque), and infiltrative/morpheaform (firm scar-like plaque). Treatment is risk-stratified: low-risk lesions are treated with standard surgical excision (4 mm margins) or electrodessication and curettage (ED&C); high-risk lesions (central face 'H-zone', infiltrative histology, recurrent, perineural invasion) require Mohs micrographic surgery. Advanced or metastatic BCC refractory to surgery/radiation is treated with oral Hedgehog pathway inhibitors (vismodegib, sonidegib) or cemiplimab (anti-PD-1).

standard_knowledge.claim: Mohs micrographic surgery provides complete microscopic peripheral and deep margin examination, achieving the lowest 5-year recurrence rate (< 1-2%) for high-risk facial BCC.

NCCN guidelines categorize BCC into low-risk and high-risk based on location (Area H: face, eyelids, nose, lips, ears is high-risk), size (>= 6 mm in Area H, >= 10 mm in Area M), and histological subtype (morpheaform, sclerosing, infiltrative are high-risk).

Vismodegib and sonidegib inhibit the smoothened (SMO) receptor in the Sonic Hedgehog pathway, producing objective response rates > 40-60% in locally advanced or metastatic BCC (ERIVANCE and BOLT trials).
Cemiplimab (anti-PD-1) is approved for locally advanced or metastatic BCC in patients who progressed on or are intolerant to Hedgehog pathway inhibitors.

page.standard_overview: Basic calcium phosphate (BCP) crystal deposition encompasses carbonate-substituted hydroxyapatite, octacalcium phosphate, and tricalcium phosphate. BCP crystals deposit in periarticular structures (calcific tendinitis of the rotator cuff) or cause destructive arthropathy, most notably Milwaukee shoulder syndrome (rapidly destructive cuff-tear arthropathy). Milwaukee shoulder predominantly affects elderly women, presenting with large, cool, non-inflammatory hemorrhagic joint effusions, extensive rotator cuff tearing, and severe glenohumeral osteolysis. Synovial fluid is non-inflammatory (< 2,000 WBC/uL) with negative polarizing microscopy (BCP crystals are submicroscopic and non-birefringent, requiring Alizarin Red S staining or electron microscopy). Management consists of joint aspiration, intra-articular corticosteroids, NSAIDs, and reverse total shoulder arthroplasty.

standard_knowledge.claim: BCP crystals (hydroxyapatite) are submicroscopic and non-birefringent under compensated polarized light, distinguishing them from birefringent monosodium urate and CPPD crystals.
Alizarin Red S staining demonstrates characteristic bright red-orange crystal clumps under light microscopy, facilitating rapid identification of BCP deposition.
Milwaukee shoulder syndrome is characterized by rapid destructive arthropathy of the glenohumeral joint, massive rotator cuff disruption, and large non-inflammatory serosanguinous joint effusions.
Surgical management of advanced Milwaukee shoulder requires reverse total shoulder arthroplasty (rTSA) to restore shoulder kinematics in the absence of an intact rotator cuff.

page.standard_overview: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) - including agitation, aggression, psychosis, depression, apathy, and wandering - occur in > 80-90% of dementia patients over the course of illness. First-line management is strictly non-pharmacological: identifying and treating underlying medical triggers (pain, urinary tract infection, constipation, delirium, sensory deficits) and deploying individualized behavioral strategies (DICE approach: Describe, Investigate, Create, Evaluate). Pharmacotherapy with atypical antipsychotics (risperidone, olanzapine) should be restricted to patients with severe, distressing, or dangerous aggression/psychosis where non-pharmacological interventions fail, due to an increased risk of stroke and mortality (black-box warning). Brexpiprazole is the first FDA-approved medication specifically for agitation associated with Alzheimer's dementia.

standard_knowledge.claim: APA and AGS guidelines mandate non-pharmacological interventions (DICE approach, pain management, sensory adaptation) as first-line therapy before considering psychotropic medications.
Antipsychotic medications carry an FDA black-box warning for a 1.6- to 1.7-fold increase in all-cause mortality and increased cerebrovascular adverse events in elderly dementia patients.

When indicated for refractory severe agitation or dangerous psychosis, oral risperidone (0.25-1 mg/day) or olanzapine should be used at the lowest effective dose with a planned tapering attempt within 3-4 months.
Brexpiprazole (1-3 mg daily) demonstrated significant reductions in agitation scores compared to placebo in agitation associated with Alzheimer's dementia.

page.standard_overview: Behçet's disease is a systemic variable-vessel vasculitis characterized by recurrent painful oral aphthous ulcers, genital ulcers, inflammatory ocular disease (relapsing panuveitis, retinal vasculitis), and cutaneous lesions (erythema nodosum, pseudofolliculitis). The pathergy test (development of a pustule 24-48 hours after sterile needle prick) is highly specific. Venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis, Budd-Chiari, dural venous sinus thrombosis) and pulmonary artery aneurysms are classic severe vascular complications. EULAR guidelines recommend colchicine for mucocutaneous manifestations, topical corticosteroids for aphthous ulcers, azathioprine or TNF inhibitors (adalimumab, infliximab) for sight-threatening uveitis and vascular disease, and high-dose glucocorticoids + cyclophosphamide for pulmonary artery aneurysms. Anticoagulation alone is contraindicated for venous thrombosis driven by active vasculitis due to risk of fatal rupture of occult pulmonary aneurysms.

standard_knowledge.claim: EULAR 2018 recommendations specify colchicine as first-line therapy for the prevention of recurrent mucocutaneous lesions and erythema nodosum.
Sight-threatening uveitis and retinal vasculitis require immunosuppression with azathioprine, cyclosporine, or monoclonal anti-TNF antibodies (adalimumab, infliximab) to prevent permanent blindness.

Pulmonary artery aneurysms carry high mortality from fatal hemoptysis; treatment requires high-dose corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide (or infliximab), with transcatheter embolization for active rupture.

Venous thrombosis in Behçet's is driven by severe vascular inflammation (endothelial dysfunction) rather than hypercoagulability; immunosuppressive therapy is the cornerstone, and anticoagulation alone without immunosuppressants is contraindicated.

page.standard_overview: Targeted biologics have transformed the management of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with active disease refractory to standard-of-care antimalarials (hydroxychloroquine) and corticosteroids. Belimumab is a human monoclonal antibody that neutralizes soluble B-lymphocyte stimulator (BLyS/BAFF), inhibiting autoreactive B-cell survival. Belimumab demonstrated significant reductions in SLE disease activity (SRI-4 response), flare rates, and corticosteroid dependence (BLISS-52, BLISS-76), and achieved superior renal responses when added to standard induction for active lupus nephritis (BLISS-LN trial). Anifrolumab is a human monoclonal antibody against the type I interferon receptor subunit 1 (IFNAR1), blocking interferon-alpha, -beta, and -omega signaling. In the TULIP-1 and TULIP-2 trials, anifrolumab significantly improved BICLA composite disease activity and skin manifestations in moderate-to-severe SLE.

standard_knowledge.claim: Belimumab added to standard therapy significantly improves SRI-4 composite response, reduces severe lupus flare frequency, and facilitates steroid sparing in active SLE (BLISS trials).

The BLISS-LN trial demonstrated that adding belimumab to standard therapy (mycophenolate or cyclophosphamide) significantly improved primary efficacy renal response (43% vs 32%) in active lupus nephritis.
Anifrolumab blocks type I interferon receptor subunit 1 (IFNAR1), achieving significant BICLA response and skin clearance in patients with high type I interferon gene signatures (TULIP-2 trial).
EULAR 2023 updated guidelines recommend considering belimumab or anifrolumab as add-on therapy in patients with non-renal SLE not adequately controlled on hydroxychloroquine and glucocorticoids.

page.standard_overview: Targeted biologics have transformed the management of systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) with active disease refractory to standard-of-care antimalarials (hydroxychloroquine) and corticosteroids. page.standard_overview: Bell's palsy is an acute, unilateral peripheral facial nerve (CN VII) paresis of idiopathic etiology, frequently linked to reactivation of herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) within the geniculate ganglion. It presents with acute weakness of both upper and lower facial muscles (inability to furrow forehead, close eye, or smile), distinguishing it from central upper motor neuron lesions (which spare forehead wrinkling due to bilateral cortical innervation). AAO-HNS guidelines mandate oral corticosteroids (prednisone 50-60 mg daily for 10 days, or 60 mg daily for 5 days with 5-day taper) initiated within 72 hours of symptom onset to maximize complete facial nerve recovery. Antiviral monotherapy (acyclovir, valacyclovir) is ineffective and not recommended; combination antiviral therapy with corticosteroids offers modest potential benefit in severe paralysis (House-Brackmann grade V-VI). Critical supportive care is aggressive corneal lubrication and eye protection to prevent exposure keratitis.

standard_knowledge.claim: Oral corticosteroids initiated within 72 hours of onset significantly increase the probability of complete facial nerve recovery at 9-12 months (NNT ~6-8).

Aggressive eye care is mandatory to prevent permanent corneal ulceration and visual loss: preservative-free artificial tears by day, ophthalmic ointment at night, and tape patching or moisture chambers.

page.standard_overview: Bempedoic acid is an oral non-statin lipid-lowering prodrug that inhibits ATP citrate lyase (ACL), acting upstream of HMG-CoA reductase in the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway in hepatocytes. Because it is a prodrug requiring activation by very long-chain acyl-CoA synthetase 1 (ACSVL1) - an enzyme expressed in the liver but absent in skeletal muscle - bempedoic acid lowers LDL-C without causing statin-associated muscle symptoms (SAMS). In the landmark CLEAR Outcomes trial involving 13,970 statin-intolerant patients, bempedoic acid (180 mg daily) significantly reduced 4-point MACE (cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke, or coronary revascularization) by 13% and fatal/nonfatal MI by 23%. Known adverse effects include asymptomatic serum uric acid elevation, modest gout flares, slight increases in serum creatinine, and a rare risk of tendon rupture.

page.standard_overview: Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (BPPV) is the most common peripheral vestibular disorder, caused by free-floating otoconia (calcium carbonate crystals) detached from the utricle that enter the semicircular canals (canalithiasis, > 90% posterior canal). It presents with brief recurrent episodes of spinning vertigo (< 60 seconds) triggered by head position changes (rolling over in bed, looking upward). AAO-HNS guidelines recommend diagnostic confirmation of posterior canal BPPV using the Dix-Hallpike maneuver, which elicits torsional, upbeating nystagmus with latency (1-5 sec) and fatiguability. Posterior canal BPPV is treated definitively with the Epley canalith repositioning maneuver, achieving > 85-90% resolution without vestibular suppressant medications (meclizine, dimenhydrinate), which are ineffective and cause unnecessary sedation.

standard_knowledge.claim: AAO-HNS guidelines recommend diagnosing posterior canal BPPV when the Dix-Hallpike maneuver produces torsional, upbeating positional nystagmus with a latency of several seconds.
The Epley canalith repositioning maneuver is the treatment of choice for posterior canal BPPV, achieving complete symptomatic resolution in > 85-90% after 1-2 sessions.
Vestibular suppressant medications (meclizine, benzodiazepines, antihistamines) are NOT recommended for routine treatment of BPPV, as they do not resolve canalithiasis and delay central compensation.
Horizontal canal BPPV (5-15% of cases) is diagnosed via the Supine Roll test (horizontal geotropic or apogeotropic nystagmus) and treated with the Lempert (BBQ roll) or Gufoni maneuvers.

page.standard_overview: Benign pleural diseases associated with environmental or occupational asbestos exposure include pleural plaques, benign asbestos pleural effusion (BAPE), diffuse pleural thickening (DPT), and rounded atelectasis (Blesovsky syndrome). Pleural plaques are the most common manifestation (occurring 20-30 years post-exposure), characterized by well-circumscribed, bilateral fibrocalcific plaques on the parietal pleura (posterolateral chest wall and diaphragm) that are asymptomatic and do not undergo malignant degeneration into mesothelioma. In contrast, diffuse pleural thickening (DPT) involves visceral-parietal pleural symphysis over > 25% of the hemithorax, causing restrictive ventilatory impairment and dyspnea. BAPE is an exudative, often hemorrhagic pleural effusion that presents early (latency < 10-20 years) and resolves spontaneously.

standard_knowledge.claim: ATS guidelines emphasize that benign pleural plaques are markers of asbestos exposure but are NOT premalignant and do not undergo malignant transformation into mesothelioma.
Pleural plaques typically spare the lung apices and costophrenic angles, presenting radiographically as 'holly-leaf' calcifications along the diaphragmatic domes and posterolateral ribs.
Diffuse pleural thickening (DPT) causes blunting of costophrenic angles, extensive visceral pleural fibrosis, and progressive restrictive lung defect on pulmonary function testing.
Rounded atelectasis presents as a peripheral, pleural-based pulmonary mass with the 'comet-tail sign' of converging bronchovascular bundles, mimicking bronchogenic carcinoma on imaging.

page.standard_overview: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) is an age-dependent, non-malignant adenomatous proliferation of the prostatic transitional zone leading to lower urinary tract symptoms (LUTS: storage symptoms [urgency, frequency, nocturia] and voiding symptoms [hesitancy, weak stream, intermittency, straining]). Initial evaluation requires the International Prostate Symptom Score (IPSS), urinalysis, post-void residual (PVR) volume, and serum PSA in appropriate candidates. First-line medical therapy for moderate-to-severe symptoms includes alpha-1 blockers (tamsulosin, alfuzosin, silodosin) for rapid symptom relief, and 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (5-ARIs: finasteride, dutasteride) for enlarged prostates (> 30 mL) to reduce prostate volume, prevent acute urinary retention, and reduce the need for surgery. Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors (tadalafil 5 mg daily) are indicated for concurrent LUTS and erectile dysfunction.

standard_knowledge.claim: AUA/EAU guidelines recommend alpha-1 blockers as first-line therapy for rapid improvement in LUTS and peak urinary flow rate (Qmax).

5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride) inhibit conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT), reducing prostate volume by ~20-25% and halving the risk of acute urinary retention in prostates > 30 mL.
Combination therapy with an alpha-blocker plus a 5-ARI (MTOPS and CombAT trials) is superior to monotherapy in preventing long-term clinical progression of BPH.

page.standard_overview: Long-term benzodiazepine and 'Z-drug' (zolpidem, zopiclone) receptor agonist use in older adults is associated with substantial harms, including cognitive impairment, delirium, falls, fractures, motor vehicle accidents, physical dependence, and all-cause mortality. AGS Beers Criteria strongly recommend avoiding benzodiazepines in older adults for insomnia or anxiety. Deprescribing requires patient engagement, structured shared decision-making, and a gradual dose reduction schedule (typically decreasing 10-25% of the baseline dose every 2-4 weeks over months to over a year) to prevent withdrawal syndromes (rebound insomnia, autonomic instability, delirium, seizures). Switching to a longer-acting agent (diazepam) may facilitate smooth tapering in difficult cases. Cognitive Behavioral Therapy for Insomnia (CBT-I) is the recommended first-line substitute therapy for chronic insomnia.

standard_knowledge.claim: AGS Beers Criteria and Deprescribing Guidelines strongly recommend tapering and discontinuing benzodiazepines and Z-drugs in older adults due to elevated risks of falls, fractures, delirium, and cognitive decline.

page.standard_overview: Chronic Beryllium Disease (CBD, berylliosis) is an occupational granulomatous lung disease caused by a cell-mediated hypersensitivity reaction to inhaled beryllium dust or fumes, primarily in aerospace, telecommunications, electronics, nuclear defense, and dental alloy manufacturing. It is strongly linked to genetic susceptibility conferred by the HLA-DPB1 allele containing a glutamic acid at position 69 (Glu69). Pathologically, CBD is characterized by non-caseating granulomas and interstitial fibrosis that are clinically and radiologically indistinguishable from sarcoidosis. Diagnosis requires demonstration of beryllium-specific sensitization via the Beryllium Lymphocyte Proliferation Test (BeLPT) in blood or bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid, coupled with biopsy evidence of non-caseating granulomas. Management includes cessation of beryllium exposure and systemic corticosteroids.

standard_knowledge.claim: The Beryllium Lymphocyte Proliferation Test (BeLPT) is the gold standard diagnostic test, measuring in vitro proliferation of memory T-cells exposed to beryllium salts in blood or BAL fluid.
Genetic susceptibility: the HLA-DPB1 Glu69 allele confers up to a 30-fold increased risk of developing beryllium sensitization and progression to CBD.
ATS criteria for definite CBD require: 1) documented occupational exposure, 2) positive blood or BAL BeLPT, and 3) lung biopsy demonstrating non-caseating granulomas.
First-line therapy for symptomatic or progressive CBD is oral corticosteroids (prednisone 0.5 mg/kg daily tapered over months), with methotrexate or azathioprine as steroid-sparing alternatives.

page.standard_overview: The diagnostic evaluation of suspected acute pulmonary embolism (PE) in a hemodynamically stable patient relies on sequential pre-test clinical probability assessment, age-adjusted D-dimer testing, and definitive imaging to minimize unnecessary radiation. Validated prediction rules (Wells score or revised Geneva score) stratify patients into low, intermediate, or high probability. In low-risk patients, the Pulmonary Embolism Rule-out Criteria (PERC rule: age < 50, HR < 100, SpO2 >= 95%, no prior DVT/PE, no recent surgery/trauma, no hemoptysis, no estrogen use, no unilateral leg swelling) safely excludes PE without laboratory testing (PROPER trial). For non-low risk or PERC-positive patients, high-sensitivity D-dimer with age-adjusted cutoffs (age x 10 ug/L for patients > 50) rules out PE (ADJUST-PE trial). When imaging is required, Computed Tomography Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is the diagnostic gold standard; Ventilation/Perfusion (V/Q) planar/SPECT scintigraphy is preferred in severe renal impairment or severe contrast allergy.

standard_knowledge.claim: In low-risk patients by Wells or Geneva criteria, fulfilling all 8 PERC criteria safely rules out PE without D-dimer testing (PROPER trial).
The ADJUST-PE trial proved that using an age-adjusted D-dimer cutoff (age x 10 ug/L in patients aged > 50 years) increases diagnostic specificity without missing PE events.
Computed Tomography Pulmonary Angiography (CTPA) is the imaging modality of choice, providing high sensitivity (> 96%) and alternative diagnostic evaluation of thoracic pathology.

Ventilation/perfusion (V/Q) scintigraphy is the preferred diagnostic modality in patients with severe renal impairment (eGFR < 30 mL/min), iodinated contrast anaphylaxis, or pregnancy with normal chest radiograph.

page.standard_overview: Evidence-based beta-blockers constitute one of the four foundational pillars of guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT) in heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF; LVEF <= 40%). Landmark randomized trials proved that only three specific beta-blockers reduce all-cause mortality and hospitalizations: bisoprolol (CIBIS-II), carvedilol (COPERNICUS, US Carvedilol), and sustained-release metoprolol succinate (MERIT-HF). Atenolol, immediate-release metoprolol tartrate, and nebivolol have not shown equivalent mortality reduction in HFrEF. Initiation should begin at low doses in clinically stable, euvolemic patients and be titrated slowly (doubling dose every 2-4 weeks) toward target clinical trial doses (carvedilol 25-50 mg BID, bisoprolol 10 mg daily, metoprolol succinate 200 mg daily). Beta-blockers should NOT be abruptly discontinued during mild-to-moderate decompensation unless cardiogenic shock or profound bradycardia is present.

standard_knowledge.claim: Only three beta-blockers have proven mortality benefit in HFrEF: bisoprolol (CIBIS-II: 34% mortality reduction), carvedilol (COPERNICUS: 35% reduction), and metoprolol succinate (MERIT-HF: 34% reduction).
Short-acting metoprolol tartrate was inferior to carvedilol in reducing all-cause mortality in the COMET trial and should not be used for HFrEF.

Titration must be gradual, doubling doses every 2-4 weeks in euvolemic patients toward target doses: carvedilol 25 mg BID (50 mg BID if > 85 kg), bisoprolol 10 mg daily, or metoprolol succinate 200 mg daily.

During acute decompensated heart failure, continuation of beta-blocker therapy (at current or slightly halved dose) is associated with lower post-discharge mortality compared to withdrawal, unless cardiogenic shock is present.

page.standard_overview: Approximately 10% of the population reports a penicillin allergy, yet > 90-95% are not truly allergic when formally evaluated with skin testing or direct oral challenge. Inappropriate penicillin allergy labels lead to the use of broader-spectrum, less effective, and more toxic alternative antibiotics (fluoroquinolones, vancomycin, carbapenems), driving increased risks of Clostridioides difficile infection, surgical site infections, antimicrobial resistance, prolonged hospitalizations, and higher healthcare costs. Validated risk stratification algorithms (such as the PEN-FAST score: Penicillin allergy < 5 years = 2 pts, Anaphylaxis/Angioedema = 2 pts, Severe cutaneous adverse reaction = 3 pts, Treatment required for allergy = 1 pt) accurately identify low-risk patients (PEN-FAST score < 3) who can safely undergo direct oral challenge without preceding skin testing (PALACE trial).

standard_knowledge.claim: Over 90-95% of patients with a self-reported penicillin allergy tolerate penicillins upon formal testing due to misattribution of non-allergic symptoms or natural waning of IgE over time.
The PALACE randomized trial proved that direct oral amoxicillin challenge in low-risk patients (PEN-FAST score < 3) is non-inferior to traditional skin testing followed by oral challenge.

Cross-reactivity between penicillins and modern 3rd/4th/5th generation cephalosporins is extremely low (< 1-2%) because cross-reactivity is driven by R1 side-chain similarities rather than the shared beta-lactam ring.
Direct oral challenge and skin testing are strictly contraindicated in patients with a history of severe cutaneous adverse reactions (SCAR: SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP) or organ damage.

page.standard_overview: Biliary strictures represent narrowing of the extrahepatic or intrahepatic bile ducts resulting from benign (iatrogenic post-cholecystectomy, chronic pancreatitis, primary sclerosing cholangitis [PSC], IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis, anastomotic post-liver transplant) or malignant (cholangiocarcinoma, pancreatic adenocarcinoma, gallbladder cancer) etiologies. Diagnostic evaluation begins with magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) to non-invasively map stricture anatomy. Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) allows direct therapeutic stenting and tissue acquisition via brush cytology and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), although routine cytology has low sensitivity (30-40%). Digital single-operator cholangioscopy (SpyGlass) enables direct visualization and targeted intraductal biopsy, boosting diagnostic sensitivity for malignancy to > 80-85%. Benign strictures are managed with progressive balloon dilation and serial insertion of multiple plastic stents or fully covered self-expandable metal stents (FCSEMS).

standard_knowledge.claim: MRCP is the non-invasive imaging modality of choice, providing superior anatomical mapping of the biliary tree and differentiating high vs low stricture level.
Routine ERCP brush cytology has high specificity (> 95%) but poor diagnostic sensitivity (30-40%) for detecting malignant biliary strictures.
Single-operator cholangioscopy (SpyGlass) with targeted biopsies significantly improves diagnostic sensitivity for indeterminate strictures to > 80-88% compared to fluoroscopy-guided brushings.
ASGE guidelines recommend serial placement of multiple plastic stents or fully covered self-expandable metal stents (FCSEMS) for benign postoperative or chronic pancreatitis biliary strictures.

page.standard_overview: Biliary tract cancers (BTCs) encompass intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCCA), extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (perihilar [Klatskin] and distal), and gallbladder carcinoma. Surgical resection with negative margins (R0) and regional lymphadenectomy offers the only potentially curative option. The landmark phase 3 BILCAP trial established adjuvant oral capecitabine (1,250 mg/m2 BID, days 1-14 q3w for 8 cycles) as the global standard of care post-resection, demonstrating a median overall survival of 53 months vs 36 months for observation. In unresectable, locally advanced, or metastatic disease, the phase 3 TOPAZ-1 trial established first-line systemic chemoimmunotherapy with durvalumab (anti-PD-L1) plus gemcitabine and cisplatin as standard of care, significantly improving overall survival (median OS 12.8 vs 11.5 months; 2-year OS 24% vs 10%). Comprehensive molecular profiling is mandatory in all advanced BTCs (especially iCCA) to detect actionable genomic alterations, including FGFR2 fusions (pemigatinib, futibatinib), IDH1 mutations (ivosidenib), HER2 amplification, BRAF V600E, and NTRK fusions.

standard_knowledge.claim: The BILCAP randomized phase 3 trial established adjuvant oral capecitabine for 6 months as the global standard of care following curative-intent surgical resection of BTC.
The TOPAZ-1 trial proved that adding durvalumab (anti-PD-L1) to gemcitabine and cisplatin significantly improves overall survival in advanced/metastatic biliary tract cancer.
Comprehensive next-generation sequencing (NGS) is mandatory in advanced cholangiocarcinoma to detect actionable FGFR2 fusions (pemigatinib, futibatinib) and IDH1 mutations (ivosidenib).
The KEYNOTE-966 trial confirmed that adding pembrolizumab to gemcitabine and cisplatin also provides statistically significant overall survival benefit in advanced BTC.

page.standard_overview: Biofilm-associated infections involving prosthetic joints, vascular grafts, chronic wounds, and indwelling central catheters are characterized by bacterial communities encased in an extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) matrix. Bacteria within biofilms enter a low-metabolic 'persister' phenotype conferring extreme tolerance to standard cell wall-active antibiotics. In staphylococcal prosthetic joint infections (PJI), the landmark Zimmerli trials established that debridement, antibiotics, and implant retention (DAIR) requires combination bactericidal biofilm-active therapy—specifically oral rifampicin paired with a companion agent (fluoroquinolone, cotrimoxazole, or fusidic acid)—to eradicate adherent surface biofilms. Rifampicin monotherapy is strictly contraindicated due to rapid emergence of single-step rpoB point mutation resistance.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the landmark randomized trial by Zimmerli et al. (NEJM), adding oral rifampicin to ciprofloxacin in early staphylococcal orthopedic implant infections treated with surgical debridement and implant retention achieved a 100% cure rate compared with 58% for ciprofloxacin alone.

Rifampicin should never be initiated until the bacterial bioburden has been surgically debrided and blood cultures cleared, and must never be administered as monotherapy to avoid rapid selection of resistant rpoB mutants.

In chronic non-healing wounds, bacterial biofilms delay re-epithelialization by maintaining chronic non-resolving inflammation; repeated sharp physical debridement remains the cornerstone of biofilm disruption because topical antimicrobials cannot penetrate mature EPS matrices.
IDSA prosthetic joint infection guidelines recommend 3 months of oral rifampicin-based combination therapy for total hip arthroplasties and 6 months for total knee arthroplasties managed with DAIR.

page.standard_overview: Targeted biological therapy has transformed the management of severe, uncontrolled asthma refractory to maximal inhaled corticosteroid and long-acting bronchodilator (ICS-LABA) regimens. Contemporary GINA guidelines recommend phenotyping patients into Type 2 (T2)-high inflammation (characterized by blood eosinophils >= 150-300 cells/uL, fractional exhaled nitric oxide [FeNO] >= 20-25 ppb, or allergen-driven IgE) versus non-T2 asthma. Five distinct monoclonal antibody pathways are approved: anti-IgE (omalizumab), anti-IL-5 (mepolizumab, reslizumab), anti-IL-5 receptor alpha (benralizumab), anti-IL-4 receptor alpha (dupilumab), and the epithelial alarmin inhibitor anti-TSLP (tezepelumab), which also benefits non-T2 severe asthma.

standard_knowledge.claim: The NAVIGATOR randomized phase 3 trial (Castro et al., NEJM) proved that tezepelumab (anti-TSLP) significantly reduced annualized asthma exacerbation rates by 56% across all patients, maintaining efficacy in patients with low baseline blood eosinophils (< 300 cells/uL) and FeNO.

The landmark LIBERTY ASTHMA QUEST trial demonstrated that dupilumab (blocking IL-4 and IL-13 signaling via IL-4R alpha) reduced exacerbation rates by nearly 50% and improved FEV1 by 200 mL in patients with elevated eosinophils or FeNO.

The MENSA trial established that mepolizumab (anti-IL-5) halved severe asthma exacerbations (53% reduction) and reduced emergency department visits in patients with blood eosinophils >= 150 cells/uL at screening.

GINA guidelines mandate a minimum 4-month trial of biologic therapy before evaluating clinical response (reduction in oral corticosteroid use, lower exacerbation frequency, improved spirometry and symptom scores).

page.standard_overview: The potential association between biological disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (bDMARDs)—particularly TNF-alpha inhibitors—and de novo or recurrent malignancy has been evaluated extensively across large prospective nationwide registries. Rigorous long-term registry data (such as the French RATIO, Swedish ARTIS, and British BSRBR registries) have definitively shown that TNF inhibitors do not increase the overall risk of solid tumors or lymphomas beyond the baseline elevation inherent to active, severe rheumatoid arthritis. However, TNF inhibitor therapy is associated with a modest but statistically significant 30-40% increase in the risk of non-melanoma skin cancer (NMSC: basal cell and squamous cell carcinoma), mandating routine dermatologic skin surveillance.

standard_knowledge.claim: The Swedish ARTIS registry study (Askling et al.) of over 6,000 RA patients treated with TNF inhibitors demonstrated no increased risk of overall solid cancers or non-Hodgkin lymphoma compared with biologic-naive RA controls with similar inflammatory disease activity.

The French RATIO prospective registry (Mariette et al.) showed that the observed lymphoma risk in RA patients on anti-TNF therapy is primarily driven by high chronic inflammatory activity rather than the biologic agent itself.

In the British Society for Rheumatology Biologics Register (BSRBR; Mercer et al.), anti-TNF therapy was associated with a statistically significant increased hazard (HR 1.3-1.4) of non-melanoma skin cancer, supporting annual skin cancer screening.

EULAR and ACR recommendations indicate that in patients with a history of successfully treated solid malignancy in remission for >= 5 years, biologic therapy (particularly rituximab or non-TNF biologics) may be considered when conventional DMARDs fail.

page.standard_overview: When patients with rheumatoid arthritis experience treatment failure on their first biological DMARD, determining whether to rotate within the same mechanism of action (cycling to a second TNF inhibitor) or switch to an alternate class with a distinct mechanism (anti-IL-6 receptor tocilizumab, T-cell costimulation blocker abatacept, B-cell depleter rituximab, or JAK inhibitors) is a fundamental decision. The randomized ROC trial conclusively established that switching to a non-TNF targeted mechanism yields significantly higher clinical response rates (EULAR good/moderate response) and disease low activity than cycling to a second anti-TNF, particularly after primary lack of efficacy.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the multicenter randomized ROC trial (Gottenberg et al., JAMA), patients with active RA failing an initial anti-TNF who were switched to a non-TNF biologic (abatacept, rituximab, or tocilizumab) achieved significantly higher EULAR good or moderate response rates at 6 months (69% vs 52%, p=0.003) than those cycled to a second anti-TNF.

EULAR 2022 management recommendations recommend switching to a medication with an alternate mode of action (IL-6 inhibitor, abatacept, rituximab, or JAK inhibitor) or another anti-TNF agent after biologic failure.
In primary non-responders (no initial disease suppression by 3 months), mechanism switching to a non-TNF agent is vastly superior, as non-response reflects TNF-independent inflammatory biology.

In secondary failure (initial good response followed by loss of efficacy over time), detection of anti-drug antibodies (ADAs) identifies patients who can respond successfully to cycling to an alternate TNF inhibitor.

topic: Biologic therapies in severe eosinophilic asthma

page.mentor_intro: Licensed asthma biologics reduce exacerbations and hospitalisations, improve lung function, control and quality of life, and spare oral steroids, especially in T2 inflammation. Choice rests on endotype, biomarkers and comorbidities because head-to-head trials are lacking; clinical remission is achievable for a minority.

teaching_points.claim: The ACCP 2026 guideline gives seven recommendations on choosing a biologic based on quality of life, lung function, exacerbation frequency, oral steroid use, endotype, biomarkers and comorbidities, but no comparative effectiveness trials exist.

The EAACI systematic review found high certainty that benralizumab, dupilumab, mepolizumab and omalizumab reduce severe exacerbation rates, and benralizumab, dupilumab and mepolizumab reduce oral corticosteroid use.
The ERS/ATS guideline suggests anti-IL-4/13 for severe eosinophilic asthma and for corticosteroid-dependent asthma regardless of eosinophils.

Licensed asthma biologics reduce exacerbations and hospitalisations, improve lung function, asthma control and quality of life, and limit systemic corticosteroid use, with greater effect in T2 inflammation.
Head-to-head comparisons show small effect size differences with wide confidence interval overlap, and direct pragmatic trials assessing remission are needed.
Clinical remission is achievable for a minority treated with biologics, with lower rates in worse FEV1, longer disease, maintenance oral steroids, depression and obesity.
Real-world anti-IL5 biologics improve outcomes with effect sizes similar to RCTs, though data are largely retrospective.

uncertainties: Comparative efficacy of biologics.
case_hooks: Eosinophilic asthma with frequent exacerbations despite high-dose ICS-LABA.

page.standard_overview: Severe eosinophilic asthma (SEA) represents a distinct, adult-onset Type 2-high inflammatory endotype driven by interleukin-5 (IL-5), the master cytokine governing eosinophil differentiation, activation, and survival. Monoclonal antibodies targeting either the soluble IL-5 ligand (mepolizumab, reslizumab) or the IL-5 receptor alpha chain on eosinophils and basophils (benralizumab) have demonstrated profound clinical efficacy in randomized clinical trials (MENSA, SIROCCO, CALIMA, and SIRIUS). In addition to halving asthma exacerbations and improving lung function, IL-5/IL-5R blockade achieves remarkable oral corticosteroid (OCS)-sparing effects, allowing up to 50-75% of previously steroid-dependent patients to completely discontinue maintenance oral prednisone.

standard_knowledge.claim: The landmark MENSA trial (Ortega et al., NEJM) proved that mepolizumab (100 mg SC every 4 weeks) reduced severe exacerbations by 53% and significantly improved asthma quality-of-life scores in patients with recurrent exacerbations and blood eosinophils >= 150/uL.

In the randomized double-blind SIROCCO and CALIMA phase 3 trials, benralizumab (30 mg SC every 8 weeks) reduced annual exacerbation rates by up to 51% and rapidly induced near-complete depletion of circulating blood eosinophils via antibody-dependent cell-mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC).

The SIRIUS trial established that mepolizumab enabled a median 50% reduction in daily oral corticosteroid dose while maintaining asthma symptom control, with 14% of patients achieving complete prednisone cessation compared with placebo.

Selection of anti-IL-5 therapy requires documented peripheral blood eosinophilia (>= 150 cells/uL at presentation or >= 300 cells/uL within the preceding 12 months); baseline eosinophil count directly predicts the magnitude of exacerbation reduction.

page.standard_overview: Prior to the initiation of biologic or targeted synthetic DMARDs (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6, anti-IL-17, anti-IL-23, anti-CD20, and JAK inhibitors), rigorous standardized pre-treatment screening for latent and active infections is legally and clinically mandatory. Immunosuppressive biologic therapies significantly increase the risk of reactivation of latent tuberculosis (LTBI) and chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV). American College of Rheumatology (ACR) and European consensus guidelines mandate baseline screening with interferon-gamma release assays (IGRA) or tuberculin skin testing (TST), chest radiography, and comprehensive hepatitis B serologies (HBsAg, anti-HBc total, anti-HBs) and hepatitis C antibodies (anti-HCV).

standard_knowledge.claim: ACR guidelines for rheumatoid arthritis mandate screening for latent tuberculosis with an IGRA or TST and chest radiograph prior to initiating any biologic or targeted synthetic DMARD.

In patients testing positive for latent tuberculosis (positive IGRA without active symptoms or radiographic disease), prophylactic LTBI therapy (e.g., 3-4 months of rifampin or 3 months of weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine) must be initiated, and biologic therapy should be delayed for at least 1 month of completed prophylactic treatment.

Hepatitis B screening must include both HBsAg and anti-HBc; in patients with resolved hepatitis B (HBsAg negative, anti-HBc positive), B-cell depleting therapies (rituximab) carry a high (> 10-20%) risk of fatal viral reactivation, requiring mandatory prophylactic antiviral therapy (entecavir).

European consensus guidelines emphasize assessing serological status for HIV, hepatitis C, and varicella zoster virus (VZV) prior to biologic initiation, ensuring completion of indicated non-live vaccines.

page.standard_overview: Beyond tuberculosis and hepatitis, comprehensive pre-treatment evaluation before initiating biological or targeted synthetic therapies requires assessing endemic fungal risks, screening for latent parasitic infections (Strongyloides in exposed populations), and updating the patient's vaccination schedule. EULAR and ACR consensus guidelines recommend administering all indicated non-live vaccines (pneumococcal conjugate PCV20, recombinant zoster vaccine Shingrix, influenza, COVID-19, and hepatitis B) prior to immunosuppression. Live-attenuated vaccines (e.g., MMR, yellow fever, oral polio) are strictly contraindicated during active biologic therapy and must be completed at least 4 weeks prior to biologic initiation.

standard_knowledge.claim: EULAR recommendations on vaccination in adult patients with autoimmune inflammatory rheumatic diseases advise administering all indicated vaccines during stable disease, ideally prior to commencing biologic DMARD therapy, to ensure optimal humoral immune responses.

Live-attenuated vaccines are strictly contraindicated during therapy with biologic DMARDs; if indicated, live vaccines must be administered at least 4 weeks before the initiation of biologic treatment.

Recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix, a non-live adjuvant subunit vaccine) is safe, highly immunogenic, and strongly recommended in patients >= 19-50 years of age initiating biologic or targeted synthetic DMARDs (including JAK inhibitors) to prevent herpes zoster reactivation.

In patients originating from or traveling to endemic areas, screening for Strongyloides stercoralis (with serology) is recommended prior to high-dose immunosuppression, as biologic and corticosteroid therapy can trigger catastrophic Strongyloides hyperinfection syndrome.

page.standard_overview: Treating acute bipolar depression is one of the most challenging areas in psychiatric medicine because antidepressant monotherapy (SSRIs, SNRIs, tricyclics) carries minimal proven efficacy and poses a substantial risk of precipitating manic switch, cycle acceleration, or mixed states. Evidence-based guidelines (CANMAT and ISBD) endorse atypical antipsychotics with proven antimanic and antidepressant properties as first-line monotherapy: quetiapine (BOLDER trials), lurasidone (PREVAIL trials), lumateperone, cariprazine, or the olanzapine-fluoxetine combination (OFC). Lamotrigine and lithium provide valuable mood-stabilizing maintenance, but are slower-acting for severe acute depressive crises.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled BOLDER trials (Calabrese et al., Am J Psychiatry), quetiapine monotherapy (300 mg or 600 mg daily) demonstrated rapid and statistically significant reductions in depressive symptoms (MADRS score) in both bipolar I and bipolar II depression.

The PREVAIL randomized trial (Suppes et al.) proved that lurasidone monotherapy (20-120 mg daily, taken with >= 350 calories) achieved significant depressive symptom improvement with minimal metabolic liabilities (weight neutral) compared to placebo.

The Canadian Network for Mood and Anxiety Treatments (CANMAT) and ISBD guidelines recommend quetiapine, lurasidone, cariprazine, and lithium as first-line treatments for acute bipolar I depression, and strongly recommend against antidepressant monotherapy.

Antidepressants (specifically bupropion or SSRIs) should only ever be considered as adjuncts to a therapeutic mood stabilizer (lithium, valproate, or second-generation antipsychotic) in bipolar I depression, and should be tapered once depressive remission is achieved.

page.standard_overview: Maintenance pharmacotherapy is essential for individuals with bipolar disorder to prevent affective relapse (both manic and depressive poles), attenuate subthreshold mood instability, and reduce completed suicide rates. Lithium remains the gold standard, first-line mood stabilizer, demonstrating unmatched long-term evidence in preventing relapse and reducing suicide risk by > 60-80%. In the landmark BALANCE trial, lithium monotherapy and combined lithium plus valproate were both significantly superior to valproate monotherapy in preventing relapse. Lamotrigine provides preferential protection against recurrent depressive episodes, while second-generation antipsychotics (quetiapine, aripiprazole, olanzapine) prevent predominantly manic recurrences.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the open-label randomized BALANCE trial (Geddes et al., Lancet), lithium monotherapy and combined lithium plus valproate were both significantly more effective at preventing relapse to any mood episode than valproate monotherapy in bipolar I disorder.

Lithium possesses proven, unique anti-suicidal properties independent of its mood-stabilizing effects, reducing suicides and suicide attempts by over 60-80% compared with other mood stabilizers and placebo.

Lamotrigine demonstrates preferential efficacy in preventing depressive relapses rather than manic relapses; slow upward dose titration (25 mg daily for 2 weeks, doubling every 2 weeks) is mandatory to prevent life-threatening Stevens-Johnson syndrome.

Therapeutic drug monitoring is essential for lithium maintenance, targeting serum trough concentrations of 0.6 to 0.8 mmol/L (up to 1.0 mmol/L during acute stabilization), with regular 6-month surveillance of renal function (eGFR) and thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH).
