page.standard_overview: The cardiovascular toxicity associated with selective cyclooxygenase-2 (COX-2) inhibitors (coxibs) represents a classic paradigm in molecular pharmacology and drug safety. Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs exert analgesic and anti-inflammatory effects by inhibiting COX-2, whereas classical GI toxicity is mediated by inhibiting gastroprotective COX-1. However, selective COX-2 inhibition creates an atherothrombotic imbalance: it suppresses endothelial prostacyclin (PGI2, a potent vasodilator and endogenous inhibitor of platelet aggregation) without inhibiting platelet COX-1, leaving platelet thromboxane A2 (TXA2, a potent vasoconstrictor and platelet activator) unopposed. This biological mechanism precipitated the withdrawal of rofecoxib following the APPROVe and VIGOR trials. The landmark PRECISION trial (24,081 patients) established that moderate-dose celecoxib (100-200 mg daily) is non-inferior to naproxen or ibuprofen regarding composite cardiovascular safety, though all NSAIDs carry dose-dependent cardiovascular risk.

standard_knowledge.claim: Selective COX-2 inhibition suppresses vascular endothelial prostacyclin (PGI2) production while leaving platelet COX-1-derived thromboxane A2 (TXA2) intact, disrupting the physiological balance and predisposing to platelet aggregation, arterial vasoconstriction, hypertension, and acute myocardial infarction.

In the landmark PRECISION randomized trial (24,081 patients with osteoarthritis or rheumatoid arthritis and established CVD or high CV risk), moderate-dose celecoxib (100-200 mg daily) was non-inferior to prescription-dose naproxen (375-500 mg BID) and ibuprofen (600-800 mg TID) for the composite primary cardiovascular outcome (death, MI, or stroke).

The randomized APPROVe trial (2,587 patients with adenomatous polyps) demonstrated a doubled relative risk of adjudicated serious thrombotic cardiovascular events (relative risk 1.92) with rofecoxib (25 mg daily) compared to placebo, leading to its worldwide voluntary market withdrawal in 2004.

Naproxen exhibits the most favorable cardiovascular safety profile among traditional NSAIDs due to its sustained 24-hour platelet COX-1 inhibition mimicking aspirin, making it the preferred NSAID in patients with high baseline cardiovascular risk when an NSAID is unavoidable.

page.standard_overview: Craniopharyngiomas are histologically benign (WHO Grade I) but biologically aggressive neuroepithelial neoplasms arising from embryonic remnants of Rathke's pouch along the craniopharyngeal duct in the sellar and suprasellar cistern. Two distinct clinicopathological subtypes exist: adamantinomatous craniopharyngiomas (predominantly pediatric, driven by CTNNB1/beta-catenin somatic mutations, characterized by cystic components with viscous 'machinery oil' cholesterol-rich fluid and calcification) and papillary craniopharyngiomas (almost exclusively in adults, driven by BRAF V600E mutations, solid without calcification). Clinical presentation is governed by mass effect on adjacent neurovascular structures: bitemporal hemianopsia from chiasmal compression, panhypopituitarism and central diabetes insipidus, and catastrophic hypothalamic syndrome (intractable hypothalamic obesity, hyperphagia, poikilothermia, and memory loss). Surgical gross total resection carries substantial risk of hypothalamic damage; thus, organ-sparing subtotal resection combined with stereotactic proton/photon radiotherapy is increasingly preferred. For BRAF-mutant papillary tumors, targeted therapy with dabrafenib-trametinib produces dramatic non-surgical tumor regression.

standard_knowledge.claim: Craniopharyngiomas are divided into adamantinomatous variants (pediatric/bimodal, driven by CTNNB1/beta-catenin mutations, featuring cystic 'machinery oil' fluid and calcification on CT) and papillary variants (adult, driven by BRAF V600E mutations, predominantly solid, non-calcified).

Hypothalamic syndrome—resulting from direct tumor invasion or surgical manipulation of the ventromedial hypothalamus and arcuate nucleus—causes devastating hypothalamic obesity resistant to caloric restriction, hyperphagia, loss of satiety, poikilothermia, and central hypersomnolence.

Endocrine evaluation demonstrates anterior pituitary hormone deficiencies in >80% of patients (growth hormone, gonadotropins, TSH, ACTH) and central diabetes insipidus (arginine vasopressin deficiency) in up to 50%, mandating thorough hormone replacement prior to surgical intervention.

In adults with BRAF V600E-mutated papillary craniopharyngioma, neoadjuvant or salvage targeted therapy with the BRAF/MEK inhibitors dabrafenib and trametinib achieves dramatic objective tumor volume reductions (>90% reduction in >90% of patients, NEJM 2023), establishing a non-surgical targeted treatment paradigm.

page.standard_overview: Creutzfeldt-Jakob Disease (CJD) is a transmissible, rapidly progressive, and uniformly fatal neurodegenerative prion encephalopathy caused by the post-translational conformational conversion of normal cellular prion protein (PrPC) into a misfolded, beta-sheet-rich, protease-resistant scrapie isoform (PrPSc). Sporadic CJD (sCJD) accounts for 85% of cases, classically manifesting as a subacute triad of rapidly progressive dementia, multifocal neurological deficits (cerebellar ataxia, visual disturbance, pyramidal/extrapyramidal signs), and prominent startle-provoked myoclonus, culminating in akinetic mutism and death within a median of 4 to 6 months. Diagnostic evaluation has been revolutionized by Real-Time Quaking-Induced Conversion (RT-QuIC) in CSF or olfactory mucosa brushings, which demonstrates >95% sensitivity and ~100% specificity by detecting femtogram quantities of seeding-active PrPSc, supplanting non-specific surrogate biomarkers (14-3-3 protein and total tau). Brain MRI characteristically reveals 'cortical ribboning' and striatal hyperintensity on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI).

standard_knowledge.claim: Real-Time Quaking-Induced Conversion (RT-QuIC) in cerebrospinal fluid detects ultratrace amounts of misfolded prion protein (PrPSc) via in vitro seed-induced aggregation with recombinant PrP, exhibiting >95% diagnostic sensitivity and 99-100% specificity for sporadic CJD, establishing it as the premier diagnostic test.

Brain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) mapping demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy (>90%) for sCJD, characteristically revealing 'cortical ribboning' (hyperintensity in >=2 cortical gyri) and/or asymmetric hyperintensity in the basal ganglia (caudate and putamen), with characteristic sparing of the precentral motor cortex.

Electroencephalography (EEG) demonstrates periodic sharp wave complexes (PSWCs) in approximately two-thirds of sCJD patients, characteristically appearing during the intermediate-to-late stages of disease with a repetition rate of 1 to 2 Hz.

Surrogate CSF biomarkers, including elevated 14-3-3 protein (>2.0 ng/mL) and markedly elevated total tau (>1,150-2,000 pg/mL), reflect acute neuronal destruction; while sensitive, they lack specificity and can be elevated in acute viral encephalitis, hypoxic ischemic encephalopathy, and recent stroke.

page.standard_overview: Exagamglogene autotemcel (exa-cel) represents a transformative milestone as the first approved autologous CRISPR-Cas9 gene-edited cell therapy for severe sickle cell disease (SCD) and transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia (TDT). Rather than inserting a corrective exogenous globin gene via viral vectors, exa-cel utilizes ex vivo CRISPR-Cas9 ribonucleoprotein complexes to introduce targeted non-homologous end-joining insertions and deletions into the erythroid-specific enhancer region of the BCL11A gene within autologous CD34+ hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs). Disruption of this erythroid GATA1-binding motif downregulates BCL11A transcription factor expression, unleashing the gamma-globin promoter and driving robust reactivation of fetal hemoglobin (HbF, alpha2-gamma2) synthesis. High levels of tetrameric HbF prevent the intracellular polymerization of sickle hemoglobin (HbS) in SCD and rebalance the alpha/non-alpha globin chain disparity in beta-thalassemia.

standard_knowledge.claim: In patients with severe sickle cell disease, exa-cel gene editing achieves sustained fetal hemoglobin (HbF) levels of >=40% of total hemoglobin with pancellular distribution (>95% of erythrocytes), eliminating severe vaso-occlusive crises in over 95% of treated individuals for >=12 consecutive months (NEJM 2024 trial).

In transfusion-dependent beta-thalassemia, exa-cel infusion eliminated the need for red-cell transfusions in >90% of patients, maintaining normal or near-normal mean total hemoglobin levels (>=12-13 g/dL) across long-term follow-up (NEJM 2024 trial).

Exa-cel therapeutic execution requires full myeloablative busulfan conditioning prior to edited stem cell infusion to facilitate robust autologous marrow engraftment, exposing patients to standard conditioning risks including prolonged pancytopenia, mucositis, secondary amenorrhea, and sinusoidal obstruction syndrome.

The molecular target of exa-cel is the erythroid lineage-specific GATA1-binding site within the +58-kb intron 2 enhancer of the BCL11A gene, preserving non-erythroid BCL11A expression required for normal B-cell lymphopoiesis and neural development.

page.standard_overview: Intensive Care Unit-Acquired Weakness (ICUAW) is a devastating complication of critical illness that affects 30% to 50% of patients who require mechanical ventilation for more than 48 hours. ICUAW manifests as symmetric, flaccid, quadriparesis with muscle wasting, classically divided into Critical Illness Polyneuropathy (CIP), Critical Illness Myopathy (CIM), or combined critical illness polyneuromyopathy. The clinical diagnostic standard is the Medical Research Council (MRC) sum score; a score <48 out of 60 (or an average score <4/5 across 12 muscle groups) defines ICUAW. Differentiating CIP from CIM is achieved electrophysiologically: CIP exhibits primary axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy with preserved direct muscle excitability, whereas CIM exhibits reduced compound muscle action potentials (CMAPs), normal sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs), and inexcitable muscle membranes on direct muscle stimulation. The only proven preventative intervention is early active rehabilitation and physical therapy.

standard_knowledge.claim: Intensive Care Unit-Acquired Weakness is clinically diagnosed in awake, cooperative ICU patients using the Medical Research Council (MRC) sum score, where a score <48/60 across six bilateral upper and lower extremity muscle groups indicates clinically significant ICU-acquired paresis.

Electrophysiologically, Critical Illness Myopathy (CIM) is characterized by reduced CMAP amplitudes with normal sensory nerve action potentials (SNAPs) and reduced muscle membrane excitability on direct muscle stimulation, whereas Critical Illness Polyneuropathy (CIP) is a primary axonal polyneuropathy with marked reductions in both CMAPs and SNAPs.

Early active physical and occupational therapy paired with daily protocolized interruption of sedation in mechanically ventilated ICU patients significantly improves return to independent functional status at hospital discharge (59% vs 35%, odds ratio 2.7) and reduces duration of delirium and ventilator dependence (Schweickert trial).

Major modifiable risk factors for ICUAW include prolonged deep neuromuscular blockade, systemic corticosteroid exposure, prolonged immobilization, sustained hyperglycemia, and multi-organ failure driven by severe sepsis.

page.standard_overview: The management of moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease has been transformed by a succession of targeted biologic agents directed against distinct inflammatory cascades. Biological therapy is indicated for patients with high-risk features—including extensive anatomical involvement, deep endoscopic ulceration, stricturing or penetrating behavior, perianal fistulizing disease, or corticosteroid refractoriness. Tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-alpha) antagonists (infliximab, adalimumab) represent the first-line biologic standard. The landmark SONIC trial established that combination therapy with infliximab plus azathioprine achieves superior rates of corticosteroid-free clinical remission and mucosal healing compared to infliximab or azathioprine monotherapy. Newer biologic classes—including anti-integrin alpha4beta7 (vedolizumab), anti-IL-12/23 p40 (ustekinumab), and selective anti-IL-23 p19 inhibitors (risankizumab)—offer superior safety profiles with minimal systemic immunosuppression.

standard_knowledge.claim: In patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease naive to biologics and immunomodulators, combination therapy with infliximab (5 mg/kg) plus azathioprine (2.5 mg/kg/day) achieved significantly higher rates of corticosteroid-free clinical remission at week 26 (56.8%) and endoscopic mucosal healing compared to infliximab monotherapy (44.4%) or azathioprine monotherapy (30.0%) in the SONIC trial.

Vedolizumab, a gut-selective monoclonal antibody targeting the alpha4beta7 integrin, blocks lymphocyte homing to the intestinal mucosa by inhibiting binding to mucosal addressin cell adhesion molecule-1 (MAdCAM-1), demonstrating induction and maintenance efficacy in moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease with low systemic infection risks (GEMINI II trial).

Ustekinumab, a fully human IgG1k monoclonal antibody targeting the shared p40 subunit of interleukins 12 and 23, induces clinical remission and maintains long-term response in Crohn's disease patients who have previously failed or are intolerant to anti-TNF agents (UNITI-1 and UNITI-2 trials).

Selective anti-interleukin-23 p19 antagonists (such as risankizumab) demonstrate superior endoscopic mucosal response and clinical remission in moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease refractory to anti-TNF therapies (ADVANCE, MOTIVATE, and FORTIFY trials).

page.standard_overview: Crohn's disease is an idiopathic, progressive inflammatory bowel disorder characterized by transmural, granulomatous inflammation capable of affecting any segment of the gastrointestinal tract from the mouth to the anus, with a predilection for the terminal ileum and ascending colon. The natural history is characterized by recurrent flares that evolve from an initial uncomplicated inflammatory phenotype (B1) toward irreversible fibrostenotic stricturing (B2) or penetrating fistulizing (B3) phenotypes (Montreal classification). Accurate disease staging combines ileocolonoscopy with biopsy, cross-sectional imaging (magnetic resonance enterography, MRE), and objective non-invasive biomarkers (fecal calprotectin). Therapeutic paradigms have shifted from symptom management to a 'treat-to-target' strategy (STRIDE-II) targeting endoscopic mucosal healing to prevent bowel damage, strictures, and surgical resection.

standard_knowledge.claim: Crohn's disease is classified by the Montreal criteria according to age at diagnosis (A1 <17, A2 17-40, A3 >40), anatomical location (L1 ileal, L2 colonic, L3 ileocolonic, L4 isolated upper GI), and disease behavior (B1 non-stricturing/non-penetrating, B2 stricturing, B3 penetrating, with 'p' modifier for perianal disease).

The STRIDE-II consensus guidelines establish a treat-to-target framework prioritizing immediate symptomatic relief, intermediate normalization of biomarkers (CRP <5 mg/L, fecal calprotectin <100-250 mcg/g), and long-term endoscopic mucosal healing (absence of ulcerations on ileocolonoscopy).

Magnetic resonance enterography (MRE) is the preferred initial cross-sectional imaging modality to assess small bowel disease extent, mural thickening, transmural enhancement, strictures, and penetrating complications (fistulae, phlegmon, intra-abdominal abscesses), without ionizing radiation exposure.

In patients with severe fibrostenotic ileocecal strictures causing obstructive symptoms without active inflammatory ulceration, bowel-sparing surgical resection (limited ileocecectomy) or strictureplasty is preferred over continuing ineffective medical immunosuppression.

page.standard_overview: The management of biologic-refractory Crohn's disease has advanced through head-to-head randomized trials and the introduction of advanced targeted oral small molecules. When patients fail initial anti-TNF therapy due to primary non-response, secondary loss of response, or drug intolerance, clinicians must select between alternative mechanisms of action: anti-IL-12/23 (ustekinumab), selective anti-IL-23 p19 antagonists (risankizumab), or oral Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors (upadacitinib). The landmark SEAVUE trial evaluated ustekinumab versus adalimumab in biologic-naive Crohn's disease, showing comparable high rates of clinical and endoscopic remission. In patients refractory to anti-TNF therapy, the head-to-head SEQUENCE trial demonstrated that risankizumab achieved superior clinical remission and endoscopic healing compared to ustekinumab. Furthermore, the oral selective JAK-1 inhibitor upadacitinib (U-EXCEL and U-EXCEED) provides rapid mucosal healing in multi-biologic-refractory disease.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the randomized head-to-head SEAVUE trial in biologic-naive patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease, ustekinumab demonstrated comparable 1-year clinical remission rates (65% vs 61%) and endoscopic remission rates to adalimumab, establishing both as highly effective first-line biologic choices.

In the head-to-head SEQUENCE randomized trial in patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease who previously failed anti-TNF therapy, the selective IL-23 p19 inhibitor risankizumab demonstrated superiority over the IL-12/23 p40 inhibitor ustekinumab for endoscopic remission at week 48 (32% vs 16%) and non-inferiority for clinical remission.

The oral selective JAK-1 inhibitor upadacitinib (45 mg daily induction, followed by 15 or 30 mg maintenance) achieved significantly higher rates of clinical remission and endoscopic response at weeks 12 and 52 compared to placebo in patients with moderate-to-severe Crohn's disease refractory to biologic therapies (U-EXCEL and U-EXCEED trials).

Direct comparative trials establish that targeted selective IL-23 inhibition (risankizumab) and oral JAK-1 inhibition (upadacitinib) yield superior mucosal healing rates compared to earlier generation biologics in anti-TNF refractory cohorts.

page.standard_overview: Acute laryngotracheobronchitis (croup) is the most common cause of acute upper airway obstruction in young children (peak incidence 6 to 36 months of age), typically caused by human parainfluenza virus types 1 and 2. The pathognomonic clinical constellation features a barking 'seal-like' cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, and variable respiratory distress driven by subglottic edema and mucosal inflammation within the rigid cricoid ring. Bedside severity stratification is performed using the validated Westley Croup Score (evaluating inspiratory stridor, chest retractions, air entry, cyanosis, and level of consciousness) into mild (<=2), moderate (3-5), or severe (>=6). The pharmacological foundation of croup management is universal single-dose oral dexamethasone (0.15 to 0.60 mg/kg), which significantly reduces emergency department return visits, hospital admissions, and intubation. In moderate-to-severe croup with stridor at rest, nebulized epinephrine induces rapid alpha-1-adrenergic mucosal vasoconstriction.

standard_knowledge.claim: A single dose of oral dexamethasone (0.15 to 0.60 mg/kg, maximum 16 mg) is strongly recommended for all pediatric patients with croup regardless of clinical severity (mild, moderate, or severe), demonstrating significant reductions in return visits to medical care, length of ED stay, and hospitalization rates (Cochrane Systematic Review).

In moderate-to-severe croup presenting with inspiratory stridor at rest and chest wall indrawing (Westley score >=3), nebulized racemic epinephrine (0.5 mL of 2.25% solution in 3 mL saline) or standard L-epinephrine 1:1,000 (0.5 mL/kg, max 5 mL) provides rapid reduction of subglottic airway mucosal edema via alpha-1 vasoconstriction, with onset within 10-30 minutes.

Following nebulized epinephrine administration, patients must be observed in the emergency department for a minimum of 2 to 4 hours to monitor for the 'rebound effect'—the recurrence of severe mucosal edema and stridor as the local vasoconstrictive effect wears off.

Anteroposterior soft tissue neck radiographs classically reveal the 'steeple sign' (symmetric subglottic funneling and narrowing of the subglottic tracheal air shadow), but routine imaging is unnecessary in typical presentations and should never delay airway stabilization or induce clinical agitation.

page.standard_overview: Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis is an immune complex-mediated small-vessel vasculitis characterized by cold-precipitable immunoglobulins (cryoglobulins) that deposit within dermal postcapillary venules, renal glomeruli, and peripheral vasa nervorum. Under the Brouet classification, Type I consists of isolated monoclonal immunoglobulins (typically IgM or IgG, associated with multiple myeloma or Waldenström macroglobulinemia), whereas Type II (mixed: monoclonal IgM with rheumatoid factor activity bound to polyclonal IgG) and Type III (polyclonal IgM and IgG) account for >90% of clinical vasculitis cases. Over 80% to 90% of mixed cryoglobulinemia is etiologically driven by chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection, wherein persistent viral stimulation drives clonal expansion of rheumatoid factor-producing B cells. The classical Meltzer's triad consists of palpable purpura, arthralgias, and asthenia, frequently complicated by membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis and mononeuritis multiplex.

standard_knowledge.claim: Mixed cryoglobulinemic vasculitis (Brouet Types II and III) is etiologically linked to chronic hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection in >80-90% of cases, wherein sustained HCV-driven B-cell stimulation produces IgM rheumatoid factor that binds polyclonal anti-HCV IgG to form cold-insoluble circulating immune complexes.

The clinical hallmarks include Meltzer's triad (palpable purpura, arthralgias, and profound fatigue), accompanied by characteristically profound consumption of early complement components, resulting in markedly depressed or undetectable serum C4 with normal or mildly reduced C3.

Renal involvement characteristically manifests as membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN) with subendothelial deposits, 'wire-loop' lesions, and intraluminal cryoglobulin thrombi on renal biopsy, presenting with hematuria, proteinuria, and progressive renal impairment.

Therapeutic management is stratified by disease severity: in non-severe HCV cryoglobulinemia, direct-acting antiviral (DAA) therapy alone achieves sustained virologic response (SVR) and vasculitis resolution; however, in severe, life- or organ-threatening disease (rapidly progressive GN, severe motor neuropathy, mesenteric ischemia), upfront B-cell depletion with rituximab (plus plasma exchange and high-dose corticosteroids) must precede or accompany antiviral therapy.

page.standard_overview: Cryopyrin-Associated Periodic Syndromes (CAPS) represent a continuum of rare, autosomal dominant autoinflammatory disorders caused by gain-of-function somatic or germline mutations in the NLRP3 gene (formerly CIAS1) on chromosome 1q44, which encodes cryopyrin/NALP3. Cryopyrin is a central sensor protein of the NLRP3 inflammasome; pathogenic mutations result in constitutive, pathogen-independent activation of caspase-1, triggering massive cleavage and continuous systemic secretion of active interleukin-1beta (IL-1beta). The clinical spectrum spans three classically described phenotypes of increasing severity: Familial Cold Autoinflammatory Syndrome (FCAS, the mildest phenotype, featuring cold-induced urticaria-like rash, fevers, and arthralgias); Muckle-Wells Syndrome (MWS, intermediate severity with persistent daily urticarial rash, progressive sensorineural hearing loss, and secondary systemic AA amyloidosis in up to 25%); and Neonatal-Onset Multisystem Inflammatory Disease (NOMID, also known as CINCA, the most severe phenotype, characterized by chronic aseptic neutrophilic meningitis, papilledema, optic atrophy, and severe deforming epiphyseal arthropathy). Targeted IL-1 blockade is the curative standard of care.

standard_knowledge.claim: Cryopyrin-Associated Periodic Syndromes (CAPS) are caused by gain-of-function mutations in NLRP3 that cause constitutive hyperactivation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, leading to uncontrolled enzymatic processing of pro-IL-1beta by caspase-1 and massive secretion of bioactive interleukin-1beta.

The CAPS phenotype encompasses a continuous severity spectrum: Familial Cold Autoinflammatory Syndrome (cold-induced non-pruritic urticaria and fever), Muckle-Wells Syndrome (unprovoked urticaria, progressive sensorineural hearing loss, and AA amyloidosis), and NOMID/CINCA (continuous aseptic meningitis, intellectual disability, patellar overgrowth, and epiphyseal deformities).

Targeted anti-interleukin-1 therapy (using the recombinant IL-1 receptor antagonist anakinra, the humanized anti-IL-1beta monoclonal antibody canakinumab, or the soluble IL-1 trap rilonacept) induces rapid, complete, and sustained clinical remission, halts progressive sensorineural hearing loss, and reverses secondary systemic AA amyloidosis.

The cutaneous eruption in CAPS is characteristically a migratory, non-pruritic, burning urticaria-like erythematous rash whose biopsy demonstrates a prominent perivascular neutrophilic infiltrate (neutrophilic urticarial dermatosis) rather than the classical mast cell degranulation and eosinophils of allergic urticaria.

page.standard_overview: Cryptococcal meningoencephalitis is an opportunistic fungal infection predominantly caused by Cryptococcus neoformans (in immunocompromised individuals, particularly those with advanced HIV infection with CD4 counts <100 cells/mcL, solid organ transplant recipients, and patients on immunosuppression) and Cryptococcus gattii (in immunocompetent hosts). Cryptococcus possesses a protective polysaccharide capsule (chiefly glucuronoxylomannan) that impairs phagocytosis. Presentation is often subacute with insidious headache, lethargy, fever, and cranial neuropathies. Lumbar puncture is diagnostic and therapeutic: measuring elevated intracranial opening pressure (>200 mmH2O) is mandatory. The Cryptococcal Antigen (CrAg) lateral flow assay provides >98% sensitivity and specificity in CSF and serum, outperforming classical India ink microscopy (sensitivity 60-80%). The foundational ACTA trial established the global induction paradigm: 1 week of amphotericin B deoxycholate plus oral flucytosine, followed by high-dose fluconazole.

standard_knowledge.claim: The lateral flow cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) assay demonstrates >98% sensitivity and specificity in both cerebrospinal fluid and serum, dramatically outperforming India ink microscopy (which has 60-80% sensitivity) and enabling rapid, point-of-care diagnosis.

In the landmark ACTA randomized trial (721 patients with HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis), 1 week of intravenous amphotericin B deoxycholate (1 mg/kg/day) plus oral flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day), followed by 1 week of high-dose fluconazole (1,200 mg/day), achieved significantly lower 10-week mortality (24%) compared to traditional 2-week amphotericin regimens while reducing severe anemia.

Flucytosine (5-fluorocytosine) is converted intracellularly by fungal cytosine deaminase into 5-fluorouracil, inhibiting DNA and protein synthesis; combining flucytosine with amphotericin accelerates cerebrospinal fluid fungal clearance and significantly reduces mortality compared to amphotericin monotherapy or amphotericin plus fluconazole.

Elevated intracranial pressure (opening pressure >200 mmH2O) occurs in over 50% of patients due to fungal capsular polysaccharide blocking arachnoid villi; initial and daily therapeutic lumbar punctures removing 20-30 mL of CSF to reduce pressure to <200 mmH2O (or by 50%) are mandatory to prevent blindness, tentorial herniation, and death.

page.standard_overview: Induction therapy for cryptococcal meningitis has reached its modern zenith through the results of the landmark phase 3 AMBITION-cm trial. Historically, conventional amphotericin B deoxycholate regimens required prolonged, multi-week intravenous access and inflicted severe adverse events—including life-threatening anemia, severe hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia, and chemical thrombophlebitis. The AMBITION-cm trial proved that a single, high dose of liposomal amphotericin B (10 mg/kg on day 1) combined with 14 days of oral flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day) and high-dose oral fluconazole (1,200 mg/day) is non-inferior in 10-week mortality to traditional 7-day amphotericin regimens while dramatically reducing toxicity. In HIV-infected individuals, clinicians must strictly avoid early antiretroviral therapy (ART) initiation: the COAT trial demonstrated that starting ART within 1-2 weeks of meningitis induction significantly increases mortality due to intracranial Immune Reconstitution Inflammatory Syndrome (IRIS).

standard_knowledge.claim: In the landmark AMBITION-cm randomized trial (844 patients with HIV-associated cryptococcal meningitis), a single high dose of liposomal amphotericin B (10 mg/kg on day 1) given with 14 days of oral flucytosine (100 mg/kg/day) and fluconazole (1,200 mg/day) was non-inferior to standard 7-day amphotericin B deoxycholate in 10-week mortality (24.8% vs 28.7%), with significantly fewer grade 3-4 adverse events (13% vs 38% severe anemia).

Current World Health Organization (WHO 2022) guidelines recommend the AMBITION-cm single-dose liposomal amphotericin B regimen as the preferred first-line induction therapy for cryptococcal meningitis in resource-rich and resource-limited settings.

In antiretroviral-naive HIV-infected patients with cryptococcal meningitis, the randomized COAT trial demonstrated that initiating ART early (within 7-13 days of diagnosis) resulted in significantly higher 26-week mortality (45% vs 30%, hazard ratio 1.73) compared to delaying ART until 4 to 6 weeks after antifungal induction, driven by fatal intracranial immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).

Following successful 2-week induction, consolidation therapy consists of fluconazole 800 mg daily for 8 weeks, followed by maintenance/secondary prophylaxis with fluconazole 200 mg daily until CD4 counts remain >100-200 cells/mcL with undetectable viral load for at least 6 months on ART.

page.standard_overview: Emergency interpretation of non-contrast head computed tomography (NCCT) and CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA) represents a core clinical competency in acute triage. On emergency NCCT, rapid identification of acute intracranial hemorrhage (epidural, subdural, subarachnoid, intraparenchymal) is paramount before considering thrombolysis or anticoagulation. In acute ischemic stroke, NCCT detects subtle early ischemic changes—such as the hyperdense MCA sign, loss of insular ribbon, and lentiform nucleus obscuration, quantified by the Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score (ASPECTS <=10). On CTPA, detecting acute pulmonary embolism (PE) requires identifying intraluminal filling defects ('polo mint' sign on axial view or 'railroad track' sign on longitudinal view). Critically, CTPA must be scrutinized for radiographic evidence of acute right ventricular strain—specifically an RV/LV diameter ratio >1.0 in the transverse or four-chamber view, interventricular septal flattening or leftward bowing, and contrast reflux into the inferior vena cava—which stratify normotensive patients into high intermediate risk.

standard_knowledge.claim: On emergency non-contrast head CT, acute intracranial hemorrhage appears hyperdense (50-80 Hounsfield units); epidural hematomas are biconvex (lenticular) and limited by cranial sutures, whereas subdural hematomas are crescentic and cross suture lines but are delimited by dural reflections.

The ASPECTS score (Alberta Stroke Program Early CT Score) evaluates 10 topographic regions of the middle cerebral artery territory on non-contrast CT; a baseline score <=7 indicates extensive early ischemic changes and increased risk of symptomatic hemorrhagic transformation following intravenous thrombolysis.

On CT pulmonary angiography, an enlarged right ventricle with a right-to-left ventricular diameter ratio (RV/LV ratio) >1.0 in the transverse or reformatted four-chamber view, accompanied by interventricular septal bowing into the LV, signifies acute right ventricular strain and is an independent predictor of 30-day PE-related mortality.

Contrast reflux into the inferior vena cava and dilated hepatic veins during CT pulmonary angiography reflects severe tricuspid regurgitation and elevated right atrial pressure secondary to acute pulmonary vascular obstruction.

page.standard_overview: Cushing's disease refers specifically to hypercortisolemia driven by an adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)-secreting pituitary neuroendocrine tumor (PitNET / corticotroph adenoma), representing approximately 70% of endogenous Cushing's syndrome cases. Once ACTH-dependent hypercortisolemia is established, differentiating pituitary Cushing's disease from occult ectopic ACTH secretion (frequently bronchial or pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors or small cell lung cancer) presents a formidable diagnostic challenge. Over 50% of corticotroph microadenomas measure <5-6 mm in diameter and are radiographically undetectable on standard pituitary dynamic MRI. Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) with peripheral and central ACTH measurements before and after desmopressin or corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) stimulation remains the gold-standard diagnostic procedure, exhibiting near-100% specificity. Transsphenoidal selective adenomectomy performed by an experienced pituitary neurosurgeon is the curative treatment of choice.

standard_knowledge.claim: Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling (BIPSS) is the gold-standard procedure to distinguish pituitary Cushing's disease from ectopic ACTH secretion when pituitary MRI is normal or shows an equivocal lesion <6 mm; an inferior petrosal sinus-to-peripheral ACTH ratio >=2.0 at baseline or >=3.0 following CRH or desmopressin stimulation confirms a pituitary source with >95-98% sensitivity and specificity.

Transsphenoidal selective adenomectomy is the preferred first-line curative therapy for Cushing's disease, achieving initial biochemical remission in 75% to 90% of microadenomas (<10 mm) when performed by an expert neurosurgeon.

Immediate postoperative biochemical cure is defined by profound hypocortisolemia (morning serum cortisol <2 mcg/dL [50 nmol/L]) within 48 to 72 hours following surgery, reflecting transient secondary suppression of non-adenomatous corticotrophs and mandating temporary glucocorticoid replacement.

In patients with persistent or recurrent Cushing's disease post-transsphenoidal surgery, second-line options include repeat transsphenoidal exploration, stereotactic radiosurgery, medical adrenal-blocking pharmacotherapy, or bilateral laparoscopic adrenalectomy for rapid definitive hypercortisolemia control.

page.standard_overview: Evaluating suspected Cushing's syndrome requires a rigorous, hierarchical diagnostic approach to establish pathological hypercortisolemia and delineate its etiology while avoiding common diagnostic pitfalls. Step 1 mandates scrupulous exclusion of exogenous glucocorticoids (including oral, injected, topical, and inhaled formulations). Step 2 establishes endogenous hypercortisolemia using at least two concordant first-line screening tests: 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (DST; failure of morning cortisol to suppress below 1.8 mcg/dL / 50 nmol/L), 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC; values >3 times upper limit of normal), or late-night salivary cortisol (>=2 separate elevated measurements reflecting loss of physiological circadian nadir). Once hypercortisolemia is established, Step 3 measures plasma adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) to bifurcate into ACTH-independent (<5 pg/mL, primary adrenal tumors) versus ACTH-dependent (>15-20 pg/mL, pituitary vs ectopic).

standard_knowledge.claim: Initial screening for endogenous Cushing's syndrome requires at least two concordant first-line tests: 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test (post-dexamethasone serum cortisol >1.8 mcg/dL [50 nmol/L]), 24-hour urinary free cortisol (>3 times upper limit of normal), or late-night salivary cortisol (>=2 measurements elevated).

The 1-mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test has high sensitivity (>95%), using a strict cutoff of <=1.8 mcg/dL (50 nmol/L) to rule out hypercortisolemia; however, medications that induce CYP3A4 (phenytoin, carbamazepine, rifampin) accelerate dexamethasone metabolism, yielding false-positive failures to suppress.

Once hypercortisolemia is verified, morning plasma ACTH differentiates etiology: suppressed ACTH (<5 pg/mL [1.1 pmol/L]) indicates ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome (mandating adrenal CT/MRI), whereas normal or elevated ACTH (>15-20 pg/mL) confirms ACTH-dependent hypercortisolemia.

High-dose dexamethasone suppression testing (8-mg overnight or 2 mg q6h for 48h) exploits partial feedback sensitivity in pituitary corticotroph adenomas, where >50% suppression of baseline cortisol supports pituitary Cushing's disease, whereas ectopic ACTH tumors typically fail to suppress.

page.standard_overview: Medical therapy for endogenous Cushing's syndrome plays an essential therapeutic role when surgical resection is non-curative, delayed, contraindicated, or during emergency preparation for surgery in patients with severe hypercortisolemic crisis. Pharmacological options are categorized into three mechanistic classes: adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitors, pituitary-directed agents, and glucocorticoid receptor antagonists. Adrenal-directed steroidogenesis inhibitors represent the first-line medical standard. Historically, ketoconazole and metyrapone served as mainstays; however, osilodrostat (a potent oral inhibitor of 11beta-hydroxylase and aldosterone synthase) has transformed management, demonstrating rapid, sustained urinary free cortisol normalization in the randomized LINC 3 and LINC 4 trials. Pituitary-directed somatostatin receptor ligands (pasireotide) and glucocorticoid receptor antagonists (mifepristone) offer alternatives for specific clinical scenarios.

standard_knowledge.claim: Osilodrostat, an oral potent inhibitor of 11beta-hydroxylase (CYP11B1) and aldosterone synthase (CYP11B2), achieved complete normalization of 24-hour urinary free cortisol in 86% of patients with Cushing's disease in the randomized double-blind LINC 3 trial and demonstrated rapid, sustained efficacy in LINC 4.

Adrenal steroidogenesis inhibitors (metyrapone, ketoconazole, osilodrostat) block enzymatic cortisol synthesis; osilodrostat and metyrapone cause upstream accumulation of 11-deoxycortisol and adrenal androgens, potentially causing hirsutism and acne in females and mineralocorticoid hypertension and hypokalemia.

In patients with acute, severe life-threatening hypercortisolemic crisis (severe psychosis, overwhelming opportunistic infection, malignant hypertension), intravenous etomidate administered in a non-hypnotic ICU infusion achieves rapid suppression of adrenal cortisol production within 12 to 24 hours.

Mifepristone, a high-affinity competitive antagonist of the glucocorticoid receptor (GR-II) and progesterone receptor, rapidly reverses hypercortisolemic metabolic features (improving diabetes and hypertension), but serum and urinary cortisol cannot be used to monitor efficacy, and therapy causes hypokalemia, endometrial thickening, and adrenal insufficiency symptoms.

page.standard_overview: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) is the second most frequent malignancy in humans, originating from malignant proliferation of epidermal keratinocytes. While the vast majority of cSCC cases are indolent and curable with primary surgical resection, a high-risk subset exhibits aggressive biological behavior characterized by local recurrence, deep tissue invasion, and regional lymph node metastasis. High-risk features (defined by NCCN and AJCC-8 guidelines) include clinical diameter >=2 cm, tumor thickness >6 mm or invasion beyond subcutaneous fat, perineural invasion (PNI >=0.1 mm), poorly differentiated histology, high-risk anatomical locations (ear, lip, temple), and occurrence in immunosuppressed solid organ transplant recipients. Surgical management requires Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) for high-risk lesions to achieve complete peripheral and deep margin clearance. For locally advanced or metastatic cSCC unamenable to curative surgery or radiotherapy, anti-PD-1 immune checkpoint inhibitors (cemiplimab and pembrolizumab) have revolutionized therapy.

standard_knowledge.claim: High-risk cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is defined by NCCN criteria: clinical diameter >=2 cm (or >=1 cm on cheeks, forehead, neck; or >=0.6 cm on central face, ears, lips), depth of invasion >6 mm (or invasion beyond subcutaneous fat), perineural invasion (nerve diameter >=0.1 mm), poorly differentiated histology, and immunosuppression (particularly organ transplant recipients).

Mohs micrographic surgery (MMS) provides the highest 5-year cure rates (97-99% for primary, 90-93% for recurrent lesions) and maximal tissue preservation for high-risk cSCC by examining 100% of the peripheral and deep surgical margins via intraoperative frozen sections.

In locally advanced or metastatic cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma not amenable to curative surgery or radiation, the anti-PD-1 monoclonal antibody cemiplimab produced an objective response rate of 44% to 50% with durable responses exceeding 12 months in the EMPOWER-CSCC-1 phase 2 registration trial.

Pembrolizumab demonstrated an objective response rate of 34% to 50% with sustained disease control in patients with recurrent or metastatic cSCC (KEYNOTE-629 trial), establishing anti-PD-1 immunotherapy as the premier first-line systemic standard of care over cytotoxic platinum chemotherapy.

page.standard_overview: Cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (CTCL) represent a heterogeneous group of non-Hodgkin lymphomas characterized by neoplastic clonal proliferation of skin-homing CD4+ mature memory T lymphocytes. Mycosis fungoides (MF) is the most prevalent indolent form, displaying an evolution from erythematous patches to indurated plaques and exophytic cutaneous tumors with classic epidermotropism of atypical cerebriform lymphocytes. In contrast, Sézary syndrome (SS) is an aggressive leukemic variant defined by the clinical triad of generalized erythroderma, diffuse lymphadenopathy, and circulating clonal Sézary cells (>=1,000/mcL or CD4/CD8 ratio >=10). Staging follows the ISCL/EORTC TNMB system. Early-stage MF (stages IA-IIA) is managed with skin-directed modalities (topical corticosteroids, nitrogen mustard, phototherapy, total skin electron beam). In advanced-stage disease and Sézary syndrome, targeted systemic therapies—specifically mogamulizumab (anti-CCR4 monoclonal antibody, MAVORIC trial) and brentuximab vedotin (CD30 antibody-drug conjugate, ALCANZA trial)—have transformed survival and quality of life.

standard_knowledge.claim: In previously treated cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (mycosis fungoides and Sézary syndrome), the randomized phase 3 MAVORIC trial demonstrated that the anti-CCR4 monoclonal antibody mogamulizumab achieved significantly longer progression-free survival (7.7 vs 3.1 months, hazard ratio 0.53) and markedly superior overall response rates compared to vorinostat, with dramatic clearance of blood and skin compartment disease.

In CD30-positive cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, the randomized phase 3 ALCANZA trial proved that the CD30-targeted antibody-drug conjugate brentuximab vedotin achieved an objective response lasting at least 4 months in 56.3% of patients compared to 12.5% with physician's choice (methotrexate or bexarotene), establishing brentuximab as a primary targeted systemic agent.

Sézary syndrome is formally diagnosed by erythroderma involving >=80% of body surface area, generalized lymphadenopathy, and confirmed peripheral blood leukemic involvement (B2 stage: absolute Sézary cell count >=1,000/mcL, CD4/CD8 ratio >=10, or expanded CD4+CD26- or CD4+CD7- T-cell populations by flow cytometry).

Early-stage mycosis fungoides (stages IA-IIA: limited patches and plaques without tumors, erythrodermic, or nodal involvement) is treated with skin-directed therapies (narrowband UVB, PUVA, topical nitrogen mustard/mechlorethamine gel, or high-potency corticosteroids), maintaining an indolent course with normal life expectancy in stage IA.

page.standard_overview: Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive monogenic disease caused by loss-of-function mutations in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) gene, which encodes an ATP-binding cassette anion channel transporting chloride and bicarbonate across mucosal epithelial surfaces. The commonest mutation, F508del (present on at least one allele in ~85-90% of CF patients), causes protein misfolding, defective processing, and premature proteasomal degradation (Class II defect). Triple-combination CFTR modulator therapy with elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (ETI) represents one of the most successful translational breakthroughs in genetic medicine. Elexacaftor and tezacaftor function as molecular chaperones ('correctors') binding distinct sites on the nascent CFTR protein to rescue cellular trafficking to the apical plasma membrane, while ivacaftor acts as a channel 'potentiator' increasing channel open probability. ETI therapy dramatically improves lung function, eliminates exacerbations, and normalizes sweat chloride.

standard_knowledge.claim: In patients with cystic fibrosis aged 12 years and older with at least one F508del CFTR allele, triple-combination elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor (ETI) produced an unprecedented 14.3 percentage-point increase in percent predicted FEV1, a 63% reduction in annualized pulmonary exacerbations, and a 41.8 mmol/L reduction in sweat chloride concentration compared to placebo (NEJM 2019 trial).

In patients homozygous for the F508del mutation who were already receiving dual tezacaftor-ivacaftor, adding elexacaftor yielded an additional 10.0 percentage-point improvement in percent predicted FEV1 and reduced sweat chloride by 45.1 mmol/L (Lancet 2019 trial).

Ivacaftor monotherapy functions as a CFTR potentiator that locks open the channel gate, demonstrating dramatic clinical efficacy specifically in patients with CFTR gating mutations (Class III defects, predominantly G551D), increasing FEV1 by 10.6 percentage points and reducing sweat chloride below the 60 mmol/L diagnostic threshold (NEJM 2011 trial).

Safety surveillance during elexacaftor-tezacaftor-ivacaftor therapy requires baseline and quarterly liver enzyme monitoring (due to drug-induced transaminitis) and baseline ophthalmological screening for cataracts in pediatric and adolescent patients.

page.mentor_intro: CF newborn screening guidance aims to improve sensitivity, equity and timeliness, and the CF Foundation guideline covers CRMS/CFSPID management. German S3 guidance defines chronic Pseudomonas infection, fecal elastase-1 is sensitive for exocrine insufficiency, and consensus exists for following children exposed to CFTR modulators in utero or via breastfeeding.

teaching_points.claim: A US consensus guideline on CF newborn screening aims for improved sensitivity, equity and timeliness.
The CF Foundation guideline manages CRMS/CFSPID designation, noting future research needs on medication, antibiotics and chest imaging.
The German S3 guideline defines chronic Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection and gives evidence-based diagnosis and treatment for CF lung disease.
International Delphi recommendations support follow-up of children exposed to CFTR modulators in utero or via breastfeeding.
A focused update of consensus recommendations addresses prolonged-infusion beta-lactam use in CF, suggesting loading doses when initiating continuous infusion.
Adult chronic rhinosinusitis guidance lists cystic fibrosis among modifying conditions.
Fecal elastase-1 is a sensitive but moderately specific test for pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, suitable for initial screening in high-risk populations.
Probiotics, prebiotics and synbiotics in CF should be considered experimental adjuncts rather than standard.

uncertainties: Long-term effects of in utero modulator exposure.
case_hooks: Infant with positive newborn screen and borderline sweat chloride.

page.standard_overview: Advances in nutritional management, aggressive airway clearance, and CFTR modulator therapies have transformed cystic fibrosis (CF) into an adult medical specialty, with over 55-60% of individuals with CF now living into adulthood. Comprehensive care in adults centers on preventing progressive bronchiectasis, maintaining pulmonary hygiene, and proactively screening for multi-organ complications. Chronic maintenance pulmonary regimens incorporate inhaled mucolytics (inhaled recombinant human DNase [dornase alfa] and 7% hypertonic saline) to restore airway surface liquid depth and cleave neutrophil-derived DNA. Chronic endobronchial infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa demands cycled inhaled antipseudomonal antibiotics (nebulized tobramycin or colistimethate). Adult non-pulmonary complications are ubiquitous: Cystic Fibrosis-Related Diabetes (CFRD) develops in up to 40-50% of adults, exocrine pancreatic insufficiency requires tailored enzyme replacement (PERT), and bone disease warrants serial dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry.

standard_knowledge.claim: Cystic Fibrosis-Related Diabetes (CFRD) is the most common non-pulmonary comorbidity in adult CF (prevalence >40-50% by age 30), requiring mandatory annual screening with a 2-hour 75-gram oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT); HbA1c is insensitive in CF due to high erythrocyte turnover and is not recommended for diagnosis.

Insulin is the only recommended pharmacological therapy for CFRD; oral hypoglycemic agents (sulfonylureas, metformin) are ineffective and not recommended due to primary insulinopenia caused by islet cell destruction from sticky exocrine secretions.

Inhaled dornase alfa (recombinant human DNase, 2.5 mg once daily) and nebulized 7% hypertonic saline are guideline-recommended maintenance therapies that cleave extracellular DNA from degenerate neutrophils and hydrate dehydrated mucus, significantly improving FEV1 and reducing exacerbation frequency.

In patients with chronic endobronchial colonization with Pseudomonas aeruginosa, long-term alternating-month suppression with inhaled tobramycin (300 mg twice daily, 28 days on, 28 days off) preserves lung function and prevents acute infective exacerbations.

teaching_points.claim: ASTCT updated CMV guidelines cover new antiviral treatments, expanded prevention indications and special populations such as CAR T-cell and paediatric recipients.

A Taiwan consensus covers prevention and management of CMV in kidney transplant, including CMV immunoglobulin for refractory disease.
International consensus guidelines cover diagnosis and management of CMV retinitis, with novel antivirals and immunotherapy as second-line options.
Lung transplant follow-up care is built on tacrolimus-based triple immunosuppression, infection prophylaxis, CLAD prevention and bone protection.
Antiviral prophylaxis prevents CMV disease in solid organ transplant recipients, with valganciclovir or IV ganciclovir showing little difference from oral ganciclovir.

page.standard_overview: Cytomegalovirus (CMV) is the single most common and clinically impactful opportunistic viral pathogen in solid organ transplantation (SOT) and allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT). CMV exerts direct pathogenic effects (CMV syndrome with fever, bone marrow suppression, and tissue-invasive disease such as pneumonitis, hepatitis, colitis, and retinitis) and indirect immunomodulatory sequelae (accelerated vascular graft rejection, opportunistic bacterial/fungal coinfections, and decreased graft survival). Risk stratification is dictated by pre-transplant donor (D) and recipient (R) CMV IgG serostatus: D+/R- represents the highest risk in SOT, while R+ represents the highest reactivation risk in HCT. Prevention utilizes two primary strategies: universal pharmacological prophylaxis versus preemptive therapy. In HCT, letermovir has established a non-myelosuppressive prophylactic standard, while maribavir treats refractory CMV.

standard_knowledge.claim: In high-risk solid organ transplant recipients (CMV donor-positive, recipient-negative [D+/R-]), extended universal prophylaxis with oral valganciclovir (900 mg once daily) for 200 days significantly reduced CMV disease at 12 months from 36.8% to 16.1% compared to traditional 100-day prophylaxis (IMPACT trial).

In CMV-seropositive allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplant recipients (R+), letermovir—a novel viral DNA terminase complex inhibitor (pUL56)—administered through day 100 post-transplant significantly reduced clinically significant CMV infection from 60.6% to 37.5% and reduced all-cause 24-week mortality without inducing myelosuppression or nephrotoxicity (NEJM 2017 trial).

Maribavir, an oral competitive inhibitor of the CMV UL97 protein kinase, achieved significantly superior CMV viremia clearance at week 8 compared to investigator-assigned therapy (ganciclovir, valganciclovir, foscarnet, or cidofovir) in transplant recipients with refractory or resistant CMV infection (SOLSTICE trial).

Preemptive therapy relies on serial weekly surveillance of quantitative plasma CMV PCR, initiating therapeutic doses of oral valganciclovir (900 mg twice daily) or intravenous ganciclovir as soon as viral replication surpasses a predefined institution-specific threshold prior to symptom onset.

topic: dabigatran versus warfarin atrial fibrillation stroke prevention

page.mentor_intro: DOACs are as effective as and often safer than warfarin in AF, including CKD (CrCl 15 and above); evidence is weaker in dialysis. DOACs should be standard in low-risk AF needing anticoagulation, with correct dosing, and device-detected AF also benefits modestly.

teaching_points.claim: DOACs may increase efficacy and improve safety versus VKAs in AF with CKD (CrCl 15-90), with at least similar results in kidney failure.
In stage 5 CKD, DOACs showed a significant reduction in stroke and a non-significant trend to less major bleeding than VKAs.
In haemodialysis patients with AF, DOACs versus warfarin comparisons need validation by further prospective studies given thrombotic and bleeding risks.
DOACs should be standard of care in low-risk AF patients needing anticoagulation, with dabigatran showing the best balance of stroke prevention and bleeding reduction in one analysis.
A network meta-analysis found no difference in major bleeding, thromboembolism or mortality between DOACs and VKAs, and no DOAC clearly more favourable than others.
Anticoagulation with edoxaban or apixaban reduces stroke in device-detected AF and increases major bleeding.
Off-label underdosed DOACs, particularly rivaroxaban, were associated with increased ischaemic stroke without reduced bleeding, so on-label dosing should be emphasised.
DOACs may be a feasible option in AF with cirrhosis, pending validation.

uncertainties: Best strategy in dialysis patients.

page.standard_overview: The randomized RE-LY trial (Randomized Evaluation of Long-Term Anticoagulation Therapy) marked the historic transition from vitamin K antagonists to direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) for stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation (AF). Dabigatran etexilate is an oral prodrug rapidly converted by serum esterases to dabigatran, a potent, reversible direct thrombin (Factor IIa) inhibitor. In RE-LY (18,113 patients), dabigatran was evaluated at two blinded doses (150 mg twice daily and 110 mg twice daily) against open-label dose-adjusted warfarin (INR 2.0-3.0). The 150 mg BID dose achieved a superior 35% reduction in stroke and systemic embolism with similar major bleeding, while the 110 mg BID dose matched warfarin's stroke prevention with a 20% reduction in major bleeding. Crucially, both dabigatran doses cut lethal intracranial hemorrhage by ~70%. Idarucizumab provides immediate targeted reversal for emergent bleeding or urgent surgery.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the landmark RE-LY trial (18,113 patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation), dabigatran 150 mg twice daily significantly reduced stroke or systemic embolism by 35% compared to dose-adjusted warfarin (1.11% vs 1.69% per year, relative risk 0.66) with comparable rates of major bleeding (3.11% vs 3.36% per year).

Dabigatran 110 mg twice daily demonstrated non-inferiority to warfarin for stroke prevention (1.53% vs 1.69% per year) while achieving a statistically significant 20% reduction in major bleeding (2.71% vs 3.36% per year).

Both doses of dabigatran (110 mg and 150 mg twice daily) achieved dramatic, statistically significant reductions in intracranial hemorrhage compared to warfarin (0.23% and 0.30% vs 0.74% per year; relative risk reductions of 69% and 60%).

Idarucizumab, a humanized monoclonal antibody Fab fragment that binds dabigatran with 350-fold higher affinity than thrombin, completely reverses dabigatran-induced anticoagulation within minutes in patients with uncontrolled life-threatening bleeding or requiring emergent surgery (RE-VERSE AD trial).

In Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, DBS and responsive neurostimulation may be more effective than vagus nerve stimulation.

page.standard_overview: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is an established, neuromodulatory therapy for advanced Parkinson's disease (PD) complicated by motor fluctuations, disabling 'off' periods, or levodopa-induced dyskinesias refractory to optimized medical regimens. Patient selection criteria are strict: confirmed idiopathic PD with documented dopaminergic responsiveness (>=30% improvement in UPDRS motor scores following acute levodopa challenge), absence of significant dementia or major depression, and realistic expectations. Selecting the anatomical stimulation target—the Subthalamic Nucleus (STN) versus the Globus Pallidus internus (GPi)—requires tailoring to individual patient phenotypes. Multicenter randomized trials (including the VA/NINDS cooperative trial and NSTAPS) demonstrate comparable primary motor efficacy between STN and GPi. However, STN-DBS permits substantial reduction in daily levodopa-equivalent doses (~50%) but carries higher risks of neurocognitive decline, executive dysfunction, and mood lability; GPi-DBS directly suppresses dyskinesia with greater cognitive and psychiatric safety.

standard_knowledge.claim: In the landmark VA/NINDS randomized controlled trial comparing bilateral STN versus GPi deep brain stimulation in advanced Parkinson's disease, both surgical targets achieved identical improvements in 'on' time without dyskinesia (mean increase of 4.1 hours/day) and equivalent motor function improvement on the UPDRS.

STN-DBS allows significant reduction of dopaminergic medications (average 50% decrease in levodopa-equivalent daily dose), whereas GPi-DBS does not permit major medication reduction but exerts direct, potent suppression of levodopa-induced dyskinesias.

GPi-DBS demonstrates superior neurocognitive and psychiatric safety, with significantly less decline in verbal fluency, processing speed, and depressive mood scores compared to STN-DBS, making GPi the preferred target for older patients with borderline cognitive reserve.

The randomized EARLYSTIM trial proved that initiating bilateral STN stimulation at early appearance of motor fluctuations (mean PD duration 7.5 years) significantly improved quality of life and motor disability compared to medical therapy alone, establishing earlier intervention before irreversible vocational disability.

page.standard_overview: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is a major manifestation of venous thromboembolism (VTE) with significant risks of fatal pulmonary embolism (PE) and long-term post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS). Diagnostic evaluation integrates the two-level Wells DVT pre-test probability score with high-sensitivity D-dimer testing: in patients categorized as 'DVT unlikely' (Wells score <=1), a negative D-dimer safely excludes DVT without imaging. In 'DVT likely' patients or those with elevated D-dimer, venous duplex compression ultrasonography (CUS)—evaluating non-compressibility of venous lumina—is the definitive imaging standard. Anticoagulation therapy has shifted from heparin/warfarin bridging to direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs: apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban) as preferred first-line agents. Treatment duration is stratified by provoking factors: provoked DVT associated with transient major risk factors (surgery, trauma) requires strictly 3 months, whereas unprovoked proximal DVT demands consideration of extended anticoagulation.

standard_knowledge.claim: In patients with suspected deep vein thrombosis, a validated diagnostic algorithm combining a low-probability Wells score (<=1) with a negative high-sensitivity D-dimer safely rules out DVT without ultrasound imaging, with a 3-month thromboembolic risk <1%.

Current CHEST guidelines strongly recommend direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, or edoxaban) over vitamin K antagonists (warfarin) for the initial and extended treatment of acute deep vein thrombosis, providing equivalent antithrombotic efficacy with significantly lower major and fatal bleeding risks.

For acute proximal DVT provoked by a major transient risk factor (e.g., major surgery, trauma, or prolonged immobilization), a fixed 3-month course of anticoagulation is recommended; extending anticoagulation beyond 3 months provides no long-term reduction in recurrence while exposing patients to ongoing bleeding risks.

In patients with acute extensive proximal DVT, the multicenter randomized ATTRACT trial demonstrated that pharmacomechanical catheter-directed thrombolysis did not reduce the overall incidence of post-thrombotic syndrome (PTS) at 24 months (47% vs 48%) compared to anticoagulation alone, while doubling major bleeding, restricting catheter-directed interventions to severe limb-threatening phlegmasia cerulea dolens.

page.standard_overview: Degenerative cervical myelopathy (DCM) is the most common cause of non-traumatic spinal cord dysfunction and spastic quadriparesis in adults over age 55. Encompassing cervical spondylosis, disc herniation, hypertrophy of the ligamentum flavum, and ossification of the posterior longitudinal ligament (OPLL), DCM results from chronic static mechanical spinal cord compression exacerbated by dynamic repetitive flexion-extension microtrauma, causing localized spinal cord ischemia, neuroinflammation, and apoptotic axonal degeneration. Clinical presentation is often insidious, featuring loss of fine hand dexterity (clumsiness, difficulty buttoning shirts or writing), wide-based unsteady spastic gait, Lhermitte phenomenon, hyperreflexia, positive Hoffman sign, and Babinski responses. MRI of the cervical spine is diagnostic, revealing canal stenosis and intrinsic cord hyperintensity on T2-weighted images. Severity is classified using the modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) score into mild (15-17), moderate (12-14), or severe (<12). Timely surgical decompression halts neurological decline.

standard_knowledge.claim: Clinical severity of degenerative cervical myelopathy is categorized by the modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association (mJOA) 18-point scale into mild (15-17), moderate (12-14), and severe (<12), directly dictating surgical decision-making and predicting postoperative neurological recovery.

AOSpine North America and international clinical practice guidelines strongly recommend operative surgical decompression for patients with moderate-to-severe degenerative cervical myelopathy (mJOA <15), proving that surgery halts disease progression and produces meaningful, durable improvements in functional scores and quality of life.

In patients with mild DCM (mJOA 15-17), clinical practice guidelines recommend either structured operative decompression or a closely monitored trial of structured non-operative therapy with immediate surgical intervention upon any evidence of functional decline.

Pathognomonic clinical physical examination findings of cervical myelopathy include the Hoffman reflex (flick of distal phalanx of middle finger inducing involuntary flexion/adduction of thumb and index finger), the inverted brachioradialis reflex, gait spasticity, and hyperreflexia with clonus.

page.mentor_intro: Delayed haemolytic transfusion reactions in sickle cell disease follow red cell alloimmunisation, and complement activation drives post-transfusion haemolysis and hyperhaemolysis. C5 inhibitors have been used effectively in hyperhaemolysis, and case reports support eculizumab in DHTR, though prospective dosing studies are needed.

teaching_points.claim: Complement is a key disease driver in post-transfusion haemolysis and hyperhaemolysis and a promising therapeutic target.
C5 inhibitors have been used effectively in hyperhaemolysis and other conditions with bystander haemolysis.
Eculizumab use in DHTR is supported by a case report, while prospective studies are needed for dosing and sequencing.
RBC alloimmunisation in sickle cell disease requires multicentre studies to develop prevention strategies for life-threatening haemolytic transfusion reactions.
Complement plays a role in alloimmunisation and hyperhaemolysis, and complement-modulating drugs may help intervention.
Complement activation in sickle cell disease occurs in both asymptomatic and severe states, with complement inhibition a new therapeutic perspective.
Therapeutic complement inhibition is advancing in haematological diseases beyond PNH.

uncertainties: Optimal eculizumab dosing.

page.standard_overview: Delayed Hemolytic Transfusion Reactions (DHTR) are immune-mediated complications that occur typically 3 to 14 days (up to 30 days) following red blood cell (RBC) transfusion. The underlying mechanism is an anamnestic secondary immune response: the patient was previously alloimmunized to foreign RBC antigens by prior transfusion, pregnancy, or transplantation, but circulating antibody titers subsequently waned below the detection limits of standard pre-transfusion antibody screening. Re-exposure to the cognate antigen on transfused donor RBCs triggers rapid, clonal B-cell proliferation and high-affinity IgG production. The most commonly implicated antibodies belong to the Kidd blood group system (anti-Jka, anti-Jkb), notorious for rapid titer decline and intravascular complement activation, followed by Rh (anti-E, anti-c), Duffy (anti-Fya), and Kell. In patients with sickle cell disease (SCD), DHTR can trigger catastrophic hyperhemolysis syndrome, where both transfused donor cells and autologous recipient erythrocytes are destroyed.

standard_knowledge.claim: Delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions occur 3 to 14 days post-transfusion due to an anamnestic secondary immune response in an alloimmunized recipient whose antibody titers had waned to undetectable levels prior to transfusion, commonly involving the Kidd (anti-Jka, anti-Jkb), Rh (anti-E, anti-c), Duffy, and Kell blood group systems.

Clinical manifestations feature an unexplained postoperative or post-transfusion hemoglobin drop, low-grade fever, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, elevated serum LDH, undetectable haptoglobin, spherocytosis on peripheral blood smear, and a newly positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT) with mixed-field agglutination.

In patients with sickle cell disease, delayed hemolytic transfusion reactions can progress to life-threatening hyperhemolysis syndrome—characterized by severe post-transfusion anemia with hemoglobin dropping below pre-transfusion nadirs, reticulocytopenia, and destruction of both donor and autologous recipient erythrocytes.

Management of severe hyperhemolysis syndrome in sickle cell disease mandates strict avoidance of further blood transfusions (which exacerbates hemolysis), immediate administration of high-dose intravenous corticosteroids plus intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG), and consideration of the terminal complement inhibitor eculizumab for refractory cases.

topic: Delayed puberty: constitutional delay vs hypogonadotrophic vs hypergonadotrophic causes

page.mentor_intro: Inhibin B differentiates congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism from constitutional delay in boys with high accuracy, particularly with testicular volume 3 ml or less. Letrozole is safe and effective for constitutional delay and may be better than testosterone for testicular volume, and FGFR1 and ANOS1 are the most affected genes in absent puberty.

Patients and caregivers identify barriers to endocrine and bone health recommendations, as in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
Serum inhibin B differentiates CHH from constitutional delay of growth and puberty with sensitivity 92% and specificity 98%, especially in boys with testicular volume of 3 ml or less.
Letrozole is safe and effective for improving height and pubertal outcomes in CDGP, better than testosterone for testicular volume and possibly better at delaying bone-age progression.
In males with absent puberty and complete CHH, FGFR1 and ANOS1 accounted for 53.5% of disease-causing variants.
Phthalate exposure is associated with pubertal timing in girls and boys, supporting reduced exposure.

page.standard_overview: Delayed puberty is clinically defined as the absence of secondary sexual characteristics by an age that lies 2 to 2.5 standard deviations above the population mean: specifically, the lack of testicular enlargement (testicular volume <4 mL measured with a Prader orchidometer) by age 14 in males, or the absence of thelarche (breast budding, Tanner stage B2) by age 13 in females. The diagnostic evaluation begins with baseline gonadotropins: serum luteinizing hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). Elevated gonadotropins establish hypergonadotropic hypogonadism, signifying primary gonadal failure (most frequently Turner syndrome [45,X] in females and Klinefelter syndrome [47,XXY] in males; chromosomal karyotyping is mandatory). Conversely, low or inappropriately normal gonadotropins indicate hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, requiring differentiation between Constitutional Delay of Growth and Puberty (CDGP, a benign, self-limited variant representing 60-80% of cases) and permanent Congenital Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (CHH / Kallmann syndrome).

standard_knowledge.claim: Delayed puberty is clinically defined as the absence of initial physical pubertal signs by age 13 years in girls (lack of breast budding, Tanner stage B2) or by age 14 years in boys (testicular volume <4 mL measured by Prader orchidometer), or failure to attain menarche by age 15-16 in females.

Basal serum LH and FSH reliably differentiate the etiology: elevated gonadotropins indicate primary gonadal failure (hypergonadotropic hypogonadism: Turner syndrome 45,X, Klinefelter syndrome 47,XXY, or prior gonadotoxic chemotherapy), mandating immediate chromosomal karyotype analysis.

Constitutional Delay of Growth and Puberty (CDGP) is the most frequent cause of delayed puberty (>60% in boys, >30% in girls), characterized by delayed bone age on left hand radiograph matching height age rather than chronological age, normal predicted adult height, positive family history of late blooming, and eventual spontaneous pubertal completion.

In adolescent boys with severe psychosocial distress due to CDGP aged >=14 years, a short course of low-dose intramuscular testosterone depot (50-100 mg monthly for 3 to 6 months) safely promotes pubertal growth and virilization without compromising final adult height or accelerating premature epiphyseal fusion.
